With built-in Automatic Ground Trac, the Tracker IV balances for mineralization while you detect. The Tracker IV will detect in extreme ground conditions from salt wet beaches to highly mineralized inland sites with no operator adjustments to the circuitry and with no loss of sensitivity.Excellent ground balancing properties for the best results in all kinds of soilSensitivity meter helps to determine signal strengthUser controlled sensitivity and discrimination knobs for varying conditionsHeadphone jack with 1/4" plug can be used with most headphonesKey Features:8" Coin Depth Detection3' Large Object Detection2 9-volt Batteries RequiredIntensity MeterPreset Ground BalanceMotion all-metalProgressive DiscriminationTwo-Tone Audio8" Open Waterproof Coil
profile.reviewText:
This metal detector I purchased is a direct result of watching "The Curse of Oak Island."
I think I might have caught treasure fever from watching that show, I suspect I amore susceptible to Oak Island Treasure Fever as compared to other peoples sine I was born and raised in gorgeous Nova Scotia.
Anyways, we live in the desert where there is oodles of space that could be hiding treasures.....what's under that rock? That sand? That pile of dead cactus? I DID NOT KNOW, because alas I had no treasure stick with which to find treasures.
And by treasures I mean metallic objects of great historical and significant value...like bottle caps, shell casings and nails. Rusty nails...yeah. MY rusty nails now.
I seriously love this unit, for the price it seems a bit like magic...being able to wave it around over the ground and find hidden metal...I don't actually need to find ancient coins from treasure hiding peoples, just finding a nickel or a QUARTER woo to the hooo, is plenty satisfying. Plus there's the whole being out in sunshine, fresh air, beautiful views plus a bit of exercise.

I did find a cool old shell casing which led me down a fascinating internet rabbit hole where I discovered a whole world of people who collect shell casings, who knew? I do now.
I attached some pics of the stuff I found, perhaps not worth a lot (yet) but it was quite exciting each time the metal detector gave me the beep that meant metal.

It's very easy to use. I think it would make a unique gift for people too. I am keeping this in mind for future gifts for people we know.
profile.summary: Treasure stick! And by treasures I mean metallic objects of great historical and significant value..like bottle caps

profile.description: The Tovolo King Cube Ice Cube Trays create generous, 2-inch cubes of ice, mixers, juices, fruits, and more. Its larger size makes the sturdy tray easy to fill and, best of all, the flexible, food-grade silicone allows the cubes to pop out effortlessly after freezing. The tray is dishwasher safe and makes a great housewarming gift. Available in a variety of fun colors, this tray holds six extra-large ice cubes.
profile.reviewText:
Hmmm.....kind of like but the novelty wore off pretty quick.
You know how you get this idea of wanting a Borg cube in your drink..without actually paying for a Borg cube ice cube tray? So I had one of those moments and got it in my head that what's BETTER than a lot of ice in a drink is one massive cube!
This does make big ice cubes but I am now a member of the "didn't read all the details and reviews club, just clicked buy"  (I'm sure Amazon lovvvvvvves that club, the just click buy in the throes of giant ice cubes in your drink fantasies)
Anyways they are not perfect cubes.
Afterwards I read someone elses mention of this...nit picky much self? Yes but in case you were looking for super square cubes these aren't them. This aint them. This is not those? Er...whatever, you know what I mean.
The bottom of the tray actually has a bevel...perhaps to make the cubes easier to release...I dunno but it means it's not a cube it's a whatyamacallit shape.
It also takes a LONG time to freeze. This is okay, this doesn't ding any stars. This is just a fact of nature and physics and volume of waterin a standard freezer....it is worth noting though....
If you get this ice cube tray delivered in the afternoon and think "a ha, I'll finish the evening with some Maker's Mark and a giant ice cube that I will pretend is a Borg cube and all will be right in the world.....
Except, it won't be frozen by then...I'm not talking like 6 hours later, I mean I got it in the afternoon, immediately washed and rinsed and close to midnight the cubes were pretty frozen (frozen enough to use but with pockets of un-frozen water) Overnight freezing is a must so you don't sook over your whiskey or iced coffee or whatevers.
As I mentioned, that's just personal experience and nothing to ding a star over.

The tray does smell....it's weird...I'll see how it does long term but straight away even after washing and rinsing in vinegar it has a weird smell and if you are sensitive to things like that it may be a deal breaker.

The tray is flexible enough to pop the cubes out pretty easily! Yay!
It's also flexible enough the inner sides of the cubes will be a bit deformed if your freezer is un-level or if your tray gets set in there crooked etc....
I guess what I'm saying is this tray is high maintenance.... Also, again this is just the nature of water freezing I guess but the tops don't freeze level...they are quite un-even....no biggy but since the bottom is beveled, the sides deformed and the top is un-even...it's not a "CUBE" in the sense of a real cube...though it is a cube of ice... I am including photos of the ice straight out of the tray so you can see for yourself. I'm nICE like that...bwa ha

But...it makes a big azz cube. Which is fun.

I will confess that after using it a few times I wondered why I didn't just get the Borg cube maker...I mean I expect that to be high maintenance....

Anyways, fun idea.....I guess in practice I'm not sure it was worth the little bit of extra expense, time and hassle for getting a larger cube....if that makes sense.

It does look cool once immersed in your beverage though.
Iced Coffee pictured :)
Also showed a standard cube (in the sense of it being from a regular tray not that it's a true cube) for scale.
profile.summary: Pretty cool....not as great as I was hoping/expecting.

profile.description: This compact Ultrasonic Humidifier provides optimal humidification, both in the office and at home. An integrated hygrostat lets you set the desired humidity  the mist output therefore adjusts itself automatically. The humidity level can be specifically controlled at all times by means of a variable control. As soon as the water in the tank has been used up, an empty indicator comes on. The mist can be distributed in two directions using the double jet nozzle. Additional features: Practical reminder indicator for refilling water, easy handling and cleaning, double jet nozzle, high quality components, includes essential water maintenance accessories (Hydro Cell, Demineralization cartridge and EZCal).
profile.reviewText:
These units are a nose saver when you live in the desert!
I just realized we are going on 4 plus years of use with our air-o-swiss humidifiers! What the what? Times flies when  you live in a place with daily humidity averages (outside) of around 16%. That's today, a February, and in the summer it's just drrrrrryyyyyyyyyy...it's insane.
Sweat? What's that when in it's 116 F outside?
Any ways in such a dry climate we knew moving here that life would be more comfortable (at least indoors) with some controllable humidity.
We bought two of these units and they have been fantastic!
We use them less now as we adjusted to a dry climate but in the beginning we ran them almost 24/7.
They are lovely and make the air feel so moist and soft and are a life saver for my sinuses when allergy season hits us (dang desert dust and pollens, ick)
We have had them long enough we purchased replacement filters but other than some occasional cleaning they just work and work and work.
If you are not going to use them for a while be sure and open the unit up, un-screw the filter so it can dry out completely or else you'll risk an unpleasant mildew-y smell from the moisture trapped inside.
We have only used filtered water in ours to help keep the entire system cleaner and avoid as much mineral deposits as possible. It still happens though, that classic white scale build up on the plastic, no biggy.
Be sure and set your unit at a proper height as well and you'll avoid a damp feeling floor right beneath the area the mist is flowing out over.
We set one of ours on a tall bedroom dresser and the other on a shelf in our living room.
Even with our adjustment to desert living I can't imagine living here without access to a great humidifier like the air-o-swiss.
It makes indoor life soooooooooooo much more comfortable.
profile.summary: 4 plus years of use and still enjoying this humidifier!

top_5.description: Rubbermaid 7J60 Easy Find Lid Square 2-Cup Food Storage (Pack of 6 Containers)

top_5.reviewText:
Poly mailers are so useful if you ship a lot of items.

I love the poly bags for shipping stuff as they minimize the total shipping weight of packages compared to boxes...I can't hardly believe I ever used to ship in boxes...well they're great for breakables but for anything fabric, soft, lightweight, indestructible, poly mailers are the way to go.
I've been very pleased with my orders of these. They take up very little room in my desk drawer. A stack of these, the 100 pack is only about an inch tall....my stacks of cardboard boxes would be a few feet high and no way could I store them in my desk drawer!!!
These are so lightweight that they register as 0.1 oz on my shipping scale, that's like nothing to the shipping weight.

I also find them quite sturdy. I was nervous as first when I switched to poly mailers but I have had no issues. They seem pretty strong for what is basically a tough little plastic bag with sealer strip.

When I run out again I'll be ordering more again.

A couple tips if you're new to shipping with these sorts of bags. You can use a cardboard insert to make a sturdy shipping package, like if you're shipping photos or prints or something.
You can use bubble wrap around your item for extra cushioning, basically creating your own bubble mailer as well.
Only more affordable and you have the flexibility of shipping your items the way that suits them best.
Oh and if you have an itty bitty box that's too small for adhering the online purchased postage to (grrr, I didn't realize when I invested in some super small cardboard boxes that they didn't meet USPS guidelines for surface area for the postage) you can just stick one of those inside the poly mailer. Great for shipping little breakables etc.
top_5.summary: Lightweight, strong, space saving annnnd awesome for shipping small stuffs.

profile.reviewText:
Both my spouse and I travel extensively and use the noise-canceling headphones almost exclusively for watching airplane movies.  Thus our success criteria is how they do in noisy planes, how compactly they fold, and how comfortable they are for several hours in the plane.

Previously we had Chinese-made Noisebuster (NB-FX) Noise Canceling Headphones, and we were pretty happy with them...they folded very compactly, had quite acceptable audio performance in the plane, were modestly comfortable for long movies, and worked with or without a single AA battery.  BUT the rubber on the ear pieces finally gave out after several years...seems to be the generic end-of-life situation for earphones.

So we've both purchased the Able Planet Traveler's Foldable units as replacements...as the previous units are no longer made.  Bottom line: Not as good audio performance, but OK; fold similarly, but not quite as compactly; and aren't as comfortable for long hauls.  Unfortunately a step back for around the same price.

However, after considerable shopping and a couple of false trials, we couldn't locate anything better.
We recommend them as the best available for our use...and wish someone would bring back the old Noisebuster (NB-FX) Noise Canceling Headphones design...it was sold under a couple of brand names around 2006.
profile.summary: Not Bad..but not as good as Old Ones

profile.reviewText:
I finally made it work with sophisticated EMI filtering that I added...but for powering most digital electronics it's a disaster of a design.  For powering a simple motor that doesn't react to high frequency EMI, it may work, but that wasn't my application so I can't speak to experience in that area.

For my application I needed to power a low power sprinkler 28VAC electronic circuit used to measure soil moisture level, soil temperature, etc in the field.  Not finding any battery powered 28VAC supplies, I moved on to the concept of a small 12VDC to 120VAC inverter combined with a 28V transformer (pure transformer..no switching components) to achieve my 28VAC.  At first I tried a semi-square wave inverter (Foval 110V-150 watt inverter) and that didn't work at all, as the level of harmonics and EMI prevented my application from functioning.  So with confidence I went to a pure-sine-wave inverter (the BESTEK 300W pure sine inverter) expecting that to solve my problems.  BUT...the BESTEK didn't help a bit...still the moisture meter failed to function.  So I hooked up the oscilloscope to see what was going on.  WOW!!!!!! continuous bursts of 100 MHz level EMI with peak levels in the 10s of volts.  This was leading to a background of both radiated EMI (thru the air) and conducted (thru the wires) that almost no sensitive electronic equipment could survive and operate properly.

Because I couldn't quickly locate an alternative inverter that I had any better confidence in, I decided to attempt to build a filter to filter out the EMI and allow my application to function.  For those familiar with the problem, filtering out multi 100MHz EMI is nontrivial as it tends to run everywhere in the circuit, and filter components become extremely sensitive to component types, wire lengths, etc.  In my case the high frequency passed right thru my 28V Rain Bird transformer (from Amazon) and the X10 filter discussed next.  After a couple of days of trial and error circuit design I ended up with an augmented version of the X10 XPPF lowpass filter (sold on Amazon) with a number of added lossy inductors to eat the high frequency EMI.  In the end I got my Rain Bird SMRT-Y moisture sensor application to work...but no thanks to the inverter design.

For anyone trying to power sensitive electronics (those in need of a pure sine wave inverter) this unit is unlikely to work for you.  Definitely NOT RECOMMENDED.  If you have a motor or something immune to high frequency EMI it may work for you.  To give the unit some credit, I found the wave form to be a very accurate sine wave at very close to 60 Hz.  Because I had a low power application I wasn't sensitive to efficiency and didn't measure it...my application drew less that 1 amp from my 12V lead-acid battery supply.  Also, the fan is VERY LOUD as others have noted.

As some advice to the manufacturer, this is not a product ready for distribution to those in need of powering sensitive digital/computer based electronics.  Spend some more money to properly filter the device and charge a bit more for it.  I would be glad to pay 50% more to get a usable inverter.  The X10 filter I had to buy cost 50% of the BESTEK unit's cost, and it alone was not sufficient form my application.
One question I had was: is my unit defective? After reading the Amazon reviews it became pretty clear that everyone was suffering from thje same EMI problems...and their oscilloscope images pretty much agreed with mine.  Thus, this appears to be a generic problem with the design.  My only choice was to attempt to fix it for my low-power application...which I did.
profile.summary: Unacceptable EMI for most sensitive electronics

profile.description: Check the rainfall from today or last week from the convenience of inside your home. Self-emptying tilting cups measure from your own backyard displaying current amounts up to the last several months. Indicates the signal strength from the wireless rain bucket. Monitors your current temperatures & displays time in either 12/24 hour mode. Battery operated.
profile.reviewText:
I bought this unit with some trepidation, given the mixed reviews, but it works great.  I have the rain gauge screwed to a second-floor balcony railing about 50 feet from the censor readout, which is on the living room mantel piece on the first floor.  The temp sensor is in the shade in a covered part of the balcony about 5 feet from the rain gauge.  Both signal strengths are strong and the readouts are solid even though they have to pass through a couple of walls.  The multiple readout times are very handy, but require getting used to.  This is because the short-term readouts are running time readouts, i.e the 1 hour and 24 hour readouts are for the period starting now and running back exactly 1 hour or 24 hours from now...it's not what happened during the past period starting at the beginning of the hour or day.  Once I understood what it was doing I found it quite useful.  I don't use the various alarms and timers...just wanted an accurate wireless rain gauge and outside and inside temp sensors.

The fact that all three units work on batteries is a mixed blessing.  It gives great flexibility in placement of all the units, but will require careful monitoring of the batteries to prevent loss of data.  I'm hoping that they make in about a year so I can replace them just before each rainy season, which for me starts in September and runs thru June.

The only thing I miss is an inches/hour readout that tells one how heavy the rain is at the time...I have this on an old Oregon Scientific unit and find it much more useful than the "current" reading available on the La Crosse 724-1710 unit.  The La Crosse "current" rainfall reading is sort of how much total rain came down in the latest cloudburst.  That was hard for me to use most of the time, and one has the amount in the last hour via the "last hour" readout.  I'd rather they programmed the "current" reading for current rain rate in inches/hour.

Still...its a great running unit at a good price point...highly recommended!

February 2017 Update:
We'll my Northern California unit continues to work well and is keeping track of our record-level rains in Northern California this year.  SO-o-o...I decided to buy a second unit for our Southern California house, for mounting on the roof!  For my yard, the top of a roof vent in the center of my home's roof, provides the best possible placement for the rain gauge, free of rain-shadowing structures, garden trees, etc.  However, an important downside of this location is having to scale the roof to periodically replace the rain-gauge batteries.  In contrast to my previous Oregon Scientific unit, which was constantly charged by a small solar panel, the La Crosse unit uses two AA batteries that require periodic replacement.

Thus I began an engineering project to replace the La Crosse's two AA batteries with a small solar powered battery supply.  The La Crosse unit's two AA batteries are supposed to last around a year, so the power demand is quite modest: 3 volts and around 1600 mA-hr total current draw for the year.
Because I'm fascinated with the capabilities of the new Li-ion batteries, I decided to replace the La Crosse unit's two AA batteries with a single model 14500 Li-ion battery with a stated capacity of 1650 mAh.  This 14500 battery is the same size as a conventional 1.5 volt AA battery, but generates a higher 3.7 volts.  To get the 3.0 volts needed by the La Crosse unit requires just one 14500 battery together with the addition of a series diode to drop the voltage 0.7 volts from 3.7 (the Li-ion battery voltage) to the 3.0 volts desired by the rain gauge.
My goal was to use a small 5-volt solar panel to continuously charge the 14500 battery and thus avoid having to scale the roof to replace the rain gauge batteries.
The engineering challenge was thus to connect a small solar panel to the 14500 battery in a manner that efficiently used the power generated by the small panel, and prevented overcharging of the 14500 Li-ion battery.
Li-ion batteries, unlike other rechargeable batteries like Ni-Cd and Ni-Mh, are very sensitive to overcharging and don't tolerate long-term trickle charging.  This has resulted in specialized integrated-circuit charge regulators, such as the TP4056, that have been specifically designed for use in charging Li-ion batteries.  These charge regulators typically charge at a fixed current until a maximum charge voltage of 4.2 volts is reached, then they rapidly turn off all charging current to prevent overcharging.  Miniature circuit boards containing the TP4056 and its accessary components are readily available for plugging into standard 5V USB cell-phone power supplies.  The question is: can these be easily used in conjunction with a 5V solar panel to charge a Li-ion battery?  The short answer is Yes.
In contrast to a 5-volt USB power supply, which supplies an high current at a fixed 5.0 volts, a solar panel puts out a highly-variable, but limited current (proportional to the solar illumination level) with a current-voltage relationship defined by its IV curve.  To efficiently use the output of the solar panel the applied load must operate near the panel's Maximum Power Point (MP) on its IV curve, which is a point near the knee of the IV curve.  Fortunately, a fairly useful means of achieving operation at a panel's maximum power operating point is to use a constant-voltage load (such as that provided by a charging battery), where the constant voltage is modestly well matched to the array's max power voltage.  A constant-voltage load works well because the voltage of the maximum power point does not vary greatly with illumination level.

Now back to our TP4056 IC and how well does it mate to a solar panel.  The answer: very well.  The current-limiting feature of the TP4056 IC is essentially inactive when used with a solar panel, as the solar panel itself limits the input current (unless one uses a very high current array).  What the TP4056 does is draw current from the solar panel at a fixed voltage of around 4.3 volts and terminates battery charging when the Li-ion battery voltage reaches 4.2 volts...just what it should do.  It also prevents backflow of current from the battery into the solar panel when charging is not occuring...thus eliminating the need for a blocking diode.  The only design challenge is to acquire a solar panel with a max power voltage of around 4.3 volts...the input voltage set by the TP4056.  It turns out that this is well provided by many small 5 to 6 volt solar panels.

MY FINAL DESIGN
The attached figures illustrate my final design using a very small (1" x 2")  5-volt 30 ma solar panel connected directly to my 14500 Li-ion battery via the small TP4056 charge controller board.  No additional components were required beyond the series diode (e.g. 1N4001) used to reduce the battery's 3.7 volts down to 3.0 volts to accommodate the 3.0-volt input voltage desired by the rain gauge.  All components (battery and TP4056 board) can be easily fit in the battery compartment of the rain gauge, while the tiny solar panel is mounted closeby with a good view of the sun.

In terms of charging capability, solar availability data for my Los Angeles location indicate around 2800 peak solar illumination hours per year.  Multiplying this times my 30 ma charge current gives me around 84,000 mA-hrs of battery charging per year....way, way more than needed for the rain gauge. A nice small, but very conservative design....and no more climbing up on to the roof.
profile.summary: Good performing Unit at a good price point

profile.description: Compatible with Crusader, Over Head Door Garage Door Openers using the 340 MHZ Frequency.
profile.reviewText:
Works like a champ on my two old Safe Guard garage door openers dating from the 1980s. My two Safe Guard units have the frequency (340 MHz) printed on them, so I was easily able to get the remote control with the correct frequency.  Works reliably from 100 feet away...perfect!  And the new remote is much more compact than the original Safe Guard remotes.  For one opener for which the original SafeGuard remote was lost, I just opened the little receiver box that is attached to the outside of the opener motor housing and noted the dipswitch positions.  I duplicated them in the new remote, and I was immediately up and running with an operational remote for that door.

Highly recommended for these old door openers that require this remote technology!
profile.summary: Works Great on 1980s Safe Guard Door Openers

profile.description: EC-41112024 Color: Pacific blue Features: -Transforms from a compact pouch to a full size daypack.-Zippered main compartment.-Pack in pocket doubles as a front pocket.-Breathable mesh backpack straps.-Key fob. Dimensions: -Dimensions 16.5'' H x 9.5'' W x 4.5'' D.
profile.reviewText: For years I've taken a light 8-oz 12"x16"x6" Wilderness Experience pack with me on trips as a convenient day pack capable of being rolled up and stored in carry-on luggage.  This size is just right for carrying an extra camera lens for my SLR, and adding in a light jacket, lunch, and a pocket umbrella.  I've been unsuccessful in trying to replace my 30-year-old pack until recently, when I discovered the Eagle Creek Packable Daypack.  It's an exact match in size (12"x16"x6") and has a similar 6"x7" single outer pocket for knickknacks like spare SD cards and camera batteries, lens filters, and small camera accessories.  What's better, the Eagle Creek pack only weighs 6 1/2 oz, yet it's very well made of modestly-heavy black nylon fabric with dual high-quality metal-pull Nylon-tooth zippers.  I just returned from 5 weeks in India using it every day while touring temples and museums.  I found my old pack (same size) also perfect for trekking in Nepal when the porters had our main luggage.  So, for both light day hikes and foreign day trips it's a great size...it also easily caries my 10" netbook computer if I want to take it on the plane or to a hotel-lobby hotspot.  As an added attraction, the pack has really comfortable mesh shoulder straps...a big improvement on my old pack.  Note, however, that the fabric is not waterproof...but neither was my old pack. I highly recommend it as a light travel daypack.
profile.summary: Great Little Pack for Travel

profile.description: Juno 440-WH 4-Inch Low Voltage Flush Gimbal Ring Recessed Trim in White Trim features an adjustment of up to 40-Degree to be able to direct the light where you need it more flexibly. Recessed lighting in the home addresses many lighting needs. It is used as supplemental general lighting for entryways, living areas and bedroom, and as task lighting in the kitchen and bathroom. profile.reviewText:
We're adding new 12V recessed lighting around the house...mostly on paintings, drapes, kitchen counters, etc.  A couple of professional lighting designers had recommended going with 4" low-voltage (12V) MR16 lights...so that is what we did. I then spent weeks trying out dozens of different types of trims (eyeballs, gimbals, recessed cones, truncated cones, chrome (clear), white, gold, etc). I didn't find a book to help much with that selection. There are almost hundreds of trim styles and color combinations, but most aren't on Amazon or in the big box stores like Home Depot...you have to go to web wholesale electric sites.

We bought a couple of these Juno 440 Gimbal Ring trims from Amazon to have something quick to experiment with, as they're available from Amazon with Prime shipping available.  They're relatively high quality, but on the expensive side compared to what we paid for most of ours...the trims typically run from about $10 for the cheap imported knockoffs to $45 for the expensive undiscounted name-brand ones like Halo and Elite.

For me the discriminating difference between the various trims turns out to be:

1) The trim's visibility when the bulb is switched off.  The eyeball and gimbal trims show a fair amount by hanging down below the ceiling, where as the cones and truncated cones are recessed back, but often have the cone surface fairly visible on the ceiling.  The various recessed cones can be obtained in different cone and rim colors to tie into one's decor: Typically chrome (called clear), brass (called gold), copper, brushed stainless, white and black).  The polished metal ones provide a fairly visible metal glint on the ceiling which you may or may not like.  The white cones blend into the ceiling color quite well, and the black ones look, well, black.

2) The bulb and housing visibility when switched ON.  With the eyeball and gimbal trims, the bright bulb is quite visible when the bulb is on, and the bulb invariably lights up part of the gimbal trim elements making them shine brightly (white) on the ceiling, drawing attention to the fixtures.  With the white cones and baffles, the bulb is quite well hidden, but the white cone or baffle is lit up and shines brightly on the ceiling.  With the polished metal cones, the cone reflects the light downward and is not lite up when viewed from a distance.  Thus, they blend into the ceiling color when ON...and tend to not be particularly visible.  The black cones act similarly.

3) Some trims can create very harsh unwanted glints when viewed from an angle.  A couple of cone trims we tested created very harsh glints where the bulb filament reflected directly off of a part of the shiny bulb mount assembly when the bulb was tilted off-axis a bit.  These we quickly rejected.  We found that using truncated cones for 30-degree wall lighting solved this problem very well.

4) Most of the trims when used for lighting paintings created distracting halos (rings of light) on the wall.  This is easily corrected by inserting a diffusing lens (Halo L111 filter) in front of the bulb...these filters work miracles.

5) The trim and bulb retention springs vary a bit in user friendliness.  All the trims simply push up into the 4" cans in the ceiling and are retained by their three-spring clips.  The MR16 bulbs are similarly held in place by a two-spring clip assembly.  They all work about the same...but the more expensive trims tend to work a bit easier... some you have to fight with to get the bulb in and out.

 BOTTOM LINE:  For our application, we liked the look of "no lights visible when ON" so ended up with truncated shiny metal cones for the painting lighting and straight cones for vertical down lights.  The chrome look (clear cones) didn't particularly tie into our decor, so we went with gold cones with white rims, as we have quite a few polished brass fixtures in the rooms.  We're very happy with the results...mostly white trims with gold truncated cones that hide the bulb from side view and allow 30 degree angle on paintings (e.g. Elite B1463RB-WH trims).

As noted above, we used Amazon for the early-test gimbal trims (the Junos) and the special Low Voltage Magnetic dimmers that you need to dim the lights. You need the dimmers and a variety of MR16 bulb styles (wattage and angle) to balance the lighting effects in different locations.  I have other reviews on the dimmers.
profile.summary: OK MR16 Gimbal...but Here are some Lessons Learned

profile.reviewText:
We do a lot of off-road travel in the USA southwest desert regions and use a Garmin 60C GPS with Topo USA 2008 software for planning where we're going, tracking where we are, and viewing where we've been. Most of our destinations are not covered with the Garmin street maps so I bought Garmin's Topo USA 2008 to provide detailed maps of the off-road areas we frequent. I also use the map set for in-city travel, but for this there are better products available.  The key point is that Topo USA 2008 provides downloadable maps for the GPS that are fairly highly detailed and relatively accurate so that you have something to display in the off-road areas of the country and something to use on your computer screen when planning an off-road 4x4 or hiking trip.  The map set also does a pretty good job for streets and roads...except for the latest new developments.

Probably my favorite use of the maps is its built-in tie to Google Earth. Once you locate your places of interest using Topo USA 2008 on your computer, you can click on the "View in Google Earth" and instantly view your waypoints and routes in Google Earth with infinite detail and 3-dimensional views. Vise versa, I often use Google Earth to locate or refine detailed GPS waypoint coordinates and copy them into my Topo USA 2008 software for download to the GPS; this provides a workaround for areas where the maps aren't quite up to date or accurate enough. When you get home you can also upload your tracks and waypoints that you acquired on your trip and view them in Google Earth to know exactly where you were and where to post pictures, if you do that. This interactivity with Google Earth provides a great addition to a relatively up to date and solid performing set of detailed topo maps.

My one complaint is with the level of symbols loaded onto the maps by Garmin for Nav Aids, mountian peaks, and parks.  In general I like to leave the detail level high to display other needed info, but the cloud of these symbols tends to obscure the big picture at certain map magnifications.

profile.reviewText:
The Breville unit seems well built, AND after some tweaking, makes a VERY GOOD cup of coffee for us.  Because the as-delivered machine made coffee that was MUCH TOO STRONG, we had to find a way around the available settings, or send it back.

As background, we are not coffee "connoisseurs", but we do roast our own beans to our preferred medium roast, and I go through three to four mugs of coffee per day with cream and sugar...so we care about the coffee we drink, but prefer it at a medium "American" strength level so that 3-4 mugs/day is enjoyable.  In the past we've had a Compresso machine that functions similar to the Breville (grinds the beans as well as making the coffee), but it reached end-of-life, and its coffee was not bad, but not particularly good either...one of the reasons for our hunt to find better beans and doing custom roasting.

When first brewing a caraf of coffee with the Breville, it was WAY TOO STRONG for us.  So, being engineers, we decided to run a number of calibrated tests on the machine to find out where to set it to get OUR strength coffee.  I also researched the "official" preferred ratio of water to coffee off the web to see how we and the machine compared.  The consensus on the web among coffee experts seems to be around 12-15g of water per gram of coffee for European style coffee, and around 18-20 g water/g coffee for American taste.  After running a morning's worth of tests and consuming all our available beans, we came up with the following data and conclusions:

1)  The machine spanned the "coffee experts" recommended water/coffee ratio very well.  The machine's mild setting yielded around 26 g/g, while its strong setting yielded around 15 g/g.  The "Intense" setting would be even stronger, and all were WAY TOO STRONG for us.

2) We ran the same test on our Compresso machine and found that its strong setting yielded 104 g/g (1/4 the amount of coffee of the Breville on mild, and 1/8 the amount of coffee of the Breville on Strong).  Wow, what a huge difference!

3) We called Breville customer service to see if there was a way to recalibrate the unit to yield a more "medium strength" coffee.  The answer was NO, but the Breville rep said that we could just load in a fixed weight of beans, and the machine would grind them and not care that it ran out of beans part way through its recommended grind.  So we tried it and it WORKS GREAT!

4)  After some experimentation we found that adding 20 grams of coffee beans (exactly 1/4 cup) yielded an excellent 8-cup carafe of coffee for our morning coffee.  It tastes far better than the Compresso-made coffee...it has really GREAT flavor and isn't too strong (but, it is around double the coffee used by the Compresso).  For the Breville's 10-cup water level, we use just slightly below a level 1/3-cup scoop of beans.

5) Trying to make smaller amounts of coffee, like four cups, required an alternative work-around.  Breville's use of the flat-bottom coffee filters appears to create a problem with smaller amounts of ground coffee... the coffee runs through too quickly, even with the added "flavor" settings available in the Cup "steeping" mode.  For example, we found that the Breville used 18g of coffee for just a single 8-oz mug (R-1 setting) as opposed to us using 20g for an 8-cup carafe...and the strengths were similar.  What we found worked for making four cups was to switch to the "per cup" brew mode with a "cup size" of XL-2,  a "Mild-2" Strength setting, and a manually measured 10oz (1/8 cup) of beans.  This is pretty close in flavor to our favorite 8-cup carafe mix noted in item 4) above.

MACHINE RELIABILITY and MAINTENANCE
 After a trial period we switched to the standard flat-bottom paper coffee filters that you can quickly pull out and throw in the trash.  We then carefully wash out the Bevillle's plastic basket holder and water spreader...a little hassle but not bad, load in a fresh filter, and add the required measure of beans to the bean hopper.  We have not had any filter overflowing issues, except once when we forgot to change the filter.

That was a disaster, led to coffee overflowing everywhere, and destroyed the machine.  After that incident (a simple mistake) the machine failed to flow the right amount of water to make coffee, and after discussions with the Breville service rep, was sent back under warranty for a replacement unit.  The replacement unit has been working perfect so far.

BOTTOM LINE:  After our tweaked process with hand-measured bean amounts, we are really enjoying GREAT coffee flavor with this machine....and we're hoping in doesn't crap out again!  It's by far the best coffee we've ever had.
profile.summary: Great Coffee...but only AFTER Tweaking.

profile.reviewText:
I didn't need a deer camera...I needed to find out what animals were tearing up our lawn and eating our flowers in the garden.  The camera worked out great for closeup surveillance (4 feet) as well as at its advertised distance out to 50 feet.

I opted for the Bushnell 119445 model because the reviews on the models with the color viewing screen said that the screen was difficult to see and not worth the extra money.  My model 119445 has a B&W LCD display that you use to program the unit and it works just fine...pretty easy to program...and the camera has an adequate range of parameters (like motion-sensor sensitivity and time between pictures) for what I needed.  I just used the camera's default values (single picture per trip, normal sensitivity, and 20s lockout time).  I like that you can increment parameters (like time of day and date) both forward and reverse...eases setting these values.  One minor issue is that the memory is volatile...if you replace the batteries you have to reset everything.

A big question for me was whether the unit would work close up (say five feet) and be triggered by animals as small as a rat, squirrel, raccoon, possum, etc at night.  The answer is yes, it is easily triggered by rats eating our snapdragons at night four feet away and we found that we could also watch the snails as they attacked.

Another question was the image quality...I'm using the camera's 5Mpixel default setting (it can also be set at 3 MP or 8 MP) and the daylight color images are very sharp and easily viewed...comparable to a good point'n'shoot digital camera; each 5MP jpeg is about 630KB in size.  When the light drops off at night the camera automatically switches over and starts taking 5Mpixel B&W images using the IR LEDs as the light source (the B&W images are the same memory size - 630KB - as the daylight color images).  These B&W images are quite easily viewed...sort of like the military night-vision scenes you see on TV.

Did the IR LEDs scare the animals...didn't seem to.  On the second night surveying the snapdragons I ended up with 50 pictures of rats eating snaps between midnight and 4:30 in the morning.

Some Lessons Learned:

1) I got around 100 images each night.  I found that the easiest way to view the pictures was to pull the SD card out and slip it into a one-card reader that plugs into my computer's USB port.  Looking at each image individually, the animals were a bit hard to spot and the slide-viewing process was very slow.  Looking at the thumbnails on the computer, it was very difficult to see the animals.  What worked very well is to view the images as a full-screen slide show using software such as "Windows Picture and Fax Viewer."  When viewed as a slide show in rapid succession, the animals in each image jump out as something new in an otherwise identical scene...this makes the images quick to review and the animals quick to spot.  For a show for friends I integrated the images into a slide show with a 1-second hold between slides...makes a great movie of our garden being devoured by rats and snails.

2) If trying to view the images at a remote location away from a computer, one option is to load the Bushnell's SD card into your digital camera and use the camera's viewer to examine the images.  One reviewer said in disgust that this didn't work with his camera because of compatibility problems...it worked just fine using my Pentax K-7 digital SLR camera, which has a very good 3" 920,000 pixel display.  In fact I didn't reformat the SD card for the Bushnell, I just pulled a 1GB SD card out of my Pentax and loaded it into the Bushnell...worked perfect and even used the Pentax file structure.  However, this may not work with cards for other cameras (Canon, etc).  I also tried using my little Pentax Optio W10 point'n'shoot...it was totally capable of viewing the Bushnell images, but the lower quality 2.5" 115,000 pixel display made spotting the small animals problematic.  For animals that more fully fill the frame, the W10 should be OK.  With respect to the video clips, the Bushnell uses a ASF file type, whereas the Pentax uses an AVI...thus, no viewing of the videos on the Pentaxes.

3) How about batteries:  My application was a short one, so I just loaded four Alkaline AA batteries in the top four battery slots per the directions (the camera will accept 8 AAs for a longer life).  CAUTION: the battery polarity is NOT marked in the battery compartment...only in the instruction book (a bad manufacturer error).  So I marked the polarity in the battery compartment with a silver felt pen.  After three days of shooting 300 pictures...99% at night using the IR LEDs...I measured the battery voltage.  The batteries had dropped from 1.61 volts to 1.43 volts...indicating they still had a good charge, but were definitely discharging.  Not sure at what lower voltage the camera stops working.

4) What's the case like?  It seems very solid with a gasket seal and suitcase style latches...very similar to a Pelican waterproof case.  I didn't test its waterproofness...but was generally impressed with the design.  I mounted the camera on my camera tripod using the units 1/4-20 threaded mount.

5) For those technically oriented, the individual Bushnell images do come with embedded EXIF data...but it's very simplistic (f/2.8 lens, no shutter speed data, 100ASA film speed).  However, the EXIF data contain the date and time of the picture if you failed to turn that function on and want that data later.

Would I recommend it to a friend?...definitely!  Would I buy it again...YES, probably the same model...don't think the color viewer would have helped much for me...but might be worth having if you want to check out any videos while in the field.  At 640x480, the videos are much lower resolution.
profile.summary: Also a Great Garden Surveillance Camera!

The out is stable than switch power less noise. The constant output makes it easy for many usages, it is perfect for lab use or electronic study. What's more, the unit is equipped with coarse and fine controls for adjusting both voltage and current, making it extremely easy to set the output to your desired level. profile.reviewText:
I am in a quandary on the number of stars to give, because it depends very much on the current level used in your applications.  For my low-current applications (often from 10 to 100 ma the Tekpower TO3006D performed rather poorly and is VERY difficult or impossible to use.  For high current applications of 500ma and above it is probably a useful power supply.

As a bit of background, I'm an engineer with extensive familiarity with current+voltage controlled power supplies...and use them all the time.  The one I have now has a number of features that I hoped were in the Tekpower unit...but unfortunately they were not.  A very common application of my present power supply is to charge rechargeable Nicad and Li-ion batteries.  Here one sets the maximum charge voltage and simultaneously the maximum charge current on the power supply.  Depending on the size of the batteries, the charge current ranges from 40 ma to an amp or so.  Other applications I have are powering small electronic circuits, LED strings, etc.  I often use the current readout of the power supply to assess the current draw of the application I'm working with.

The problem with the Tekpower unit is that it can't be reliably set at low current levels and the current readout is limited to two decimal digits (least count of 10 ma).  Thus, it is pretty-much useless for low current applications below 100ma or so where I have a lot of applications.  Compounding the problem, the Fine Current Adjust knob doesn't work at all at low current levels, so setting low current values like 40 ma is extremely difficult.  My present power supply has a dual range switch (0-100ma, 0-1A) that makes setting ma-level current limits easy.  The Tekpower needs to add this function to get 5 stars.

Another feature of my present power supply that I miss in the Tekpower, is a separate switch to turn power on/off to the output leads, as opposed to turning the unit on/off.  This allows one to turn the unit on and set the voltage limits or change them before applying power to the intended application.  Then, when the limits are set and stable, one throws the switch to the output leads.  Similarly, it one wants to quickly power down the application, you just throw the output switch and don't have to turn off the power supply with its unknown turnoff transient.

At higher current levels of 1 A and more, the fine current adjust and two-decimal readout of the Tekpower unit works fine.  Unfortunately, for my whole set of lower power applications I have to have a second power supply.  I was hoping to replace my present unit with this new modern digital unit, now I have to keep my 30-year-old analog meter unit, and waste bench space with this Tekpower unit which is rarely used.
profile.summary: Unfortunately, Not useful for Low-current Applications

Durable Design: All metal housing with IP54 protection. Extended Range: Powerful 26x magnification power allows for a working range of 330 Feet.
profile.reviewText:
Just finished shooting a contour plot of 10 acres of orchards of mine...nearly two hundred elevation points. The level worked great. Key features I liked:

1) The view with this 26x unit is really sharp and crisp making it easy to read the rod to a tenth at up to 300 feet.  I also used it as close as 20 feet and everywhere in between.

2) The auto leveling is superb...leading to quick setups and fast shoots.  I used the level on a professional camera tripod equipped with a sturdy ball head and custom adapter for the level's 5/8-11mount.  For each setup, I just loosened the ball head and quickly roughly-zeroed the bulls-eye level in a few seconds, fine-tuned the bulls-eye with a quick couple of turns of the levels feet, and was ready to shoot.  The auto level took care of all the fine tuning for all shoot directions...very quick.

3) The auto level dampens down very fast (second or two) and didn't bounce at all in the modest winds I encountered.  Very efficient shooting.

4) The focus and lateral translation knobs work very smoothly, and together with the gun-sight, make acquiring and reading the rod a quick matter.

5) I performed a full calibration of the unit before using it...it was dead nuts on as shipped from the factory.

Couple of issues worth noting:

1) The level comes with a clamp to hold the auto level mechanism during transportation, but actuating it requires holding in a pin on the underside of the level.  This is done automatically when the level is placed into its carrying case...thus the mechanism is clamped during transportation in its case.  However, the mechanism is not clamped when carrying the unit around in the field.  Having a manual clamp for field transportation could be good...OR maybe NOT so good.  One would have to remember to release the clamp, or all your readings would be way off.  The clamp would have to block your view or somehow force you to release it before using the instrument.  It worked fine as it is.

2) In a similar manner, I had to be very careful not to take bad readings with the level by using the wrong cross hair.  The level has three horizontal cross hairs: the central one and two widely spaced additional ones for use in estimating distances.  A few times I caught myself using the wrong horizontal cross hair when taking a reading...they're all similar in size and color.  Had to force myself to confirm that I was using the central cross hair.

Bottom Line: Great Level...a pleasure to use...particularly in comparison to the old "non-auto" units I've used in the past.
profile.summary: Great Level...Fast, clear, accurate, and easy to use--a great value!

profile.description: The High-Speed USB File Transfer Adapter is the premier file and data sharing solution for PC and MAC users. The EasySuite utility software is already embedded on the High-Speed USB File Transfer Adapter and will automatically load onto your system. Transfer e-mail, music, photos, videos and document files from one computer to another, at speeds up to 480 Mbps. Compatible with Windows 2000, XP, Vista and Windows 7 operating systems, the High-Speed USB File Transfer Adapter is ideal for those transferring important files to a new computer and also allows you to quickly transfer music or video files to a friend's computer. The High-Speed USB File Transfer Adapter is compatible and provides a direct computer-to-computer file transfer to save time.
profile.reviewText:
I have a lot of devices, but this is my favorite device in that it works perfectly, does what no other device does for me, and is reasonable in cost.

Computer wise, most of my work is on a large-screen desktop computer...where I'm writing right now.  But on trips, I carry a compact Windows Netbook computer with fundamentally the same software, but containing a subset of the files.  The netbook allows me to continue projects when on the road with pretty much full functionality, and protects my main system from loss or damage by leaving it home.  Other folks might use a laptop for both...then not have to worry about syncing files between the two computers.  But I don't really like to work on a laptop or carry a big laptop.

As a result, when I leave on a trip, I need to copy the files that I'll need from Desktop to Netbook.  This is what the Diamond USB PC to PC does very handily.

You first bring up the software on one computer by just plugging the Diamond device into the USB port and then clicking on the OK screen...then you do the same for the second computer using the other end of the device's USB cord.  Takes just a few seconds.  The result is an Explorer-like double-screen which lists all your files and folders for both computers in one window.  To move files, you just drag and drop the files between the file-trees for the two computers...couldn't be easier. When you are finished, you just terminate the device just like using a thumbdrive, and pull out the USB plugs.

Great device...highly recommended!
profile.summary: AHAAA...My FAVORITE Electronic Device

A big adjustable wrench will of course work, but it adds a lot of bulk around the die in tight quarters.

profile.description: The BLACK+DECKER CM2040 40v Lithium 3-in-1 Cordless Mower features (2) 2.5 Ah - 40V Max Lithium Batteries for 30-45 min of mowing time. This mower offers mulching, bagging and side discharge for multiple mowing modes. The variable speed motor allows conserving the battery for greater efficiency and runtime. The EdgeMax deck design allows cutting up to the edge of fencing and flower beds, providing a clean and manicured lawn fast. This mower also features a 20-inch wide cutting patch, with a 6-setting height adjustment that allows choosing the height of cut between 1-1/2 Inch to 4 Inch. It has a 15 gallon nylon collection bag that allows you to check fill levels. This mower is backed by BLACK+DECKER's 2 year limited warranty. What's included: (1) Mower, (2) 2.5Ah - 40V Max Lithium Batteries, (1) grass bag and (1) manual.
profile.reviewText:
I purchased this unit after having excellent experience with B&D's li-ion powered hand tools (chainsaw, hedge shear, etc) and decided to get rid of my 40-year-old professional grade gas-powered mower and edger.  I have a 600 ft2 lawn in Los Angeles and mow it using a single 2.5 Ah battery that came with the CM2040 mover. Even under very heavy growth, I rarely use more than half the single 2.5 Ah battery's capacity.  My standard practice is to move the battery from my lawnmower to my B&D 40V string mower after I finish the lawn and use the string mower to trim the lawn edges. I've never come close to needing the second 2.5 Ah battery that comes with the mower, even with this dual usage.

From a storage point of view, the unit folds nicely into a compact size that fit easily under a lower shelf in my garden shed.  However, I had a difficult time finding the dimensions of the folded unit...they're not even in the owners manual.  So I've attached a drawing with the dimensions to this review.  Basically its 34.25 inches from the back of the rear wheels (which is the furthest back part of the mower when folded) to the front tip of the chassis (which protrudes a bit in front of the front wheels).  From top to bottom, its roughly 17.5 inches from ground to the top of the folded handle and safety release bar.  But the handle could be pushed down another inch to clear a 16.5 in clearance if you had too.  My shelf has a 19" clearance, so the mower fits easily under it.  And, the clipping bag can be stacked on top of the front of the mower in the same space.

Bottom Line: Works very well for me...light weight, easy to push, quick cut, no gasoline hassle, no pull starting, minimal noise, a pleasure to use, compact storage.  Only negative...a bit plasticy ...sort of like a RubberMaid lawnmower...but it works.
profile.summary: Very Convenient Mower, Compact Storage

profile.description: MaxLite's LED Omnidirectional A-Line lamp replicate true A19 incandescents that produces even light in all directions. They are suited to a wide variety of residential and commercial applications, pendants, wall sconces and table and floor lamps. The 15-watt lamps replace 100-watt incandescent and yield more than 84 percent savings in energy.
profile.reviewText:
I bought this unit for a diningroom table lamp where I'm currently using a 150 W regular tungsten bulb inside a 7" diam glass globe.  The Tungsten bulb runs very hot, burns out every few months, and uses a lot of electricity...and expensive proposition.  I've tried using 75-watt-equivalent LED bulbs and they're way too dim...even though they face down, their most efficient use.  This bulb is much more expensive when compared to conventional LED bulbs, but boy does it shine in this application.

1) The bulb is very bright...not up to the 150W tungsten, but close enough, and it has a very pleasant 3000K color temperature without a hint of green that shows with some tungsten-color replacement LED bulbs.
2) The bulb is very uniformly lit, providing a VERY attractive replacement to my previous 7" globe.  Given its 5" diameter, I use this bulb without a globe...so it also stays real cool.
3) As an unexpected added benefit, it works with my previous light timer that needs power conducting thru the bulb when turned OFF.  I was ready to install a new timer that uses a separate continuous power feed, but before I got it installed I found this LED bulb working just like my previous tungsten bulb with the timer.  No need for a new timer, which turns the light on every evening when we're not at home.
4) AND it only uses 15 watts....one tenth of my tungsten bulb...and hopefully doesn't need replacement for many years.

This is a real winner for this application!
profile.summary: A real winner for a dining table downlight

profile.description: 15x zoom range of 18-270mm makes this the ideal all around lens (equivalent to 27.5mm to 414mm in the 35mm format)
profile.reviewText:
My spouse and I do extensive world travel...Africa, Antarctica, Galapagos, Nepal, Vietnam, etc and need a lens with fairly good sharpness and very good zoom range.  When traveling in Africa, or where-ever, we find that we have seconds to grab the best shot before it disappears.  We're constantly on the go, no sitting in a blind waiting for animals...or street scenes.  Changing lenses is a luxury we have to use sparingly for special shooting situations only.  For example I have a 12-24mm for inside shooting in confined spaces...caves, tunnels and churches.

Thus, having an extreme zoom range like this lens has is a MAJOR advantage...as it covers the historic 35mm film range from 28mm wide angle to 400mm telephoto all in one very compact and lightweight lens.  We also shoot from extreme-darkness night scenes to bright snow and find the f/stop range of the lens to be just fine...all hand held.  The Pentax's in-body image stabilization helps with this.  I also have my Pentax K-5 camera body set at a default ASA 1600 and normally use a standard aperture of f/11 with the lens...at very high shutter speeds.  My images are all over the focal length range with many over 200 mm.  I also use the lens in place of a pair of binoculars when scanning for animals.

Another very nice thing about the lens is its extremely close focusing ability...like 20" at 270mm.  Combined with the high shutter speeds I use, it is great for shooting butterflies and insects on blooms and stopping their action.

Before buying this new lens, I used the Pentax 18-250 lens for a few years.  The two are very similar (nearly identical in size, f/stops, sharpness and focal length range).  My spouse still has the Pentax 18-250mm while I'm shooting with the new Pentax 18-270mm...no real discernible difference in our photos.  The ultrasonic focusing (SDM) is a bit quieter, but no big deal...about the same focusing speed.

BOTTOM LINE...I highly recommend this lens to those with shooting demands like ours...I have a dozen Pentax lenses for the camera.  This is the lens that I KEEP on the camera...it's the lens that will be ON it on any trip.  It's a huge advantage over my old film camera lenses...and a huge advantage over what's available for full-frame digital camera bodies.
profile.summary: This is my GO-TO travel lens...Excellent

profile.description: City Navigator Europe NT 2013 DVD
profile.reviewText:
Friday Afternoon...DVD Arrives (April 11, 2014)

First, I've be using Garmin GPS Products for over 10 years.  I really like to use Garmin's MapSource software to preplan routes and waypoints on my PC and then download them to my 60Csx GPS...as a result I want the full DVD version of the maps with the MapSource interfaces.  I have an upcoming trip to Europe so I bought the City Navigator Europe NT to get the full set of maps for Europe to load onto my PC (running MS XP SP3) so I could start the detailed planning process.

RESULT: installation was a NIGHTMARE.  Upon starting the installation process (package says its 2014 version) the installation says that an updated version of the maps is available so recommends downloading them off the web...time = 3 hours on my fairly fast broadband.  After 2 hours software says it's done...but no maps are anywhere on computer where MapSource can find them.  NOTHING is available for my trip planning.  I check Garmin support...closed for the weekend.  Looks like a multi-hour maximum hassle process to get the maps.
Bottom Line:  Watch out for this product...better avoid until I get a better answer (see Below).

SUNDAY MORNING UPDATE (April 13, 2014)
Wow...Wild Ride...But Convergence
After receiving my City Navigator -Europe DVD on Friday afternoon and finding it dysfunctional and Garmin "Help" shut down for the weekend, I started researching the problem on the web.  I soon found that Garmin has switched from MapSource to BaseCamp software for on-screen PC mapping (though many old-time users still prefer MapSource).  I found BaseCamp installed on my system from my DVD installation...but on clicking on Basecamp.exe file, I found it dysfunctional, as it came up with error box noting missing software of some type...no run on my Windows XP machine with SP3.
In my digging thru the Garmin Blogs I noted that BaseCamp was also provided as a free Download by Garmin on their web site.  So I reinstalled their web download version (56MB file downloaded in a few seconds).  Then after nearly an HOUR of installation antics (new Microsoft add-ins, etc...perhaps contacts with the NSA, etc...who knows?) the program was up and running WITH my new European maps AND my previous Garmin map products.

Bottom Line... Disastrous DVD.  In the end, the DVD provided nothing I was able to use directly...the European Maps all had to be updated via web download that took hours, and the BaseCamp software and required computer add-ins all had to be reinstalled via the Garmin free download from their website.  AND...Garmin doesn't have the sense to place a Read-me file on the DVD with any sort of user help or operational description.  BTW...the DVD is labeled as 2014 and my new downloaded maps are version 2014.4, so I think I do have the latest maps now...and they look pretty good.

EXPERIENCE LOADING NEW MAPS to my 60 Csx GPS
Another Wild Ride...another Painful Convergence.  I started by loading the entire European map package on a fresh 4GB SD card in my GPS.  My previous experience with map downloading is that it is an EXTREMELY SLOW process...so I keep different map sets (US Topos, Far East, World Maps, Nepal, Antarctica, etc on separate swappable SD cards.  After 4 hours of downloading...boy what a painful process...the maps were on my GPS...BUT were they?  Yes, the detailed maps at street level were there (12-mile-across screen and below), but there were no high-level maps.  You move over to France and it's a BLANK screen....you zoom in and it's still blank...you have no idea where you are.  Finally, at local-street level, roads magically appear...except you don't know where you are in the context of the overall country.

My guess is that many newer Garmin GPSs have a World Basemap that they use to fill in the higher level maps...but my 60 Csx only has base maps for the US...thus there are NO high level maps when using the Garmin "CityNavigator - Europe" maps on my 60 Csx.
But I had a solution...Combine my "World Maps" set with the "CityNavigator - Europe" set...and luckily Garmin's BaseCamp "MapInstall" software provides for the ability to simultaneously install a combination of maps from different map sets (in fact you can't add maps to an SD card...you have to simultaneously install them all at the same time).  Bottom Line...after another 3-hour install...I now have European detailed maps PLUS the high-level maps I need to navigate at a country level.

TUESDAY MORNING UPDATE (April 15, 2014)
Helpful aide from Garmin tech rep

MAPSOURCE UP & RUNNING with City Navigator

I decided to call Garmin when they got back on line Monday to see if I could get may MapSource software to work with my new City Navigator Europe.
After a bit of a wait, a very helpful rep came on the phone and had me download the latest version of MapSource from the Garmin website...via my existing software's "Check for Software Updates" under HELP on the Windows menu-bar. This brought down the new 56MB MapSource file v6.15.11 in less than a minute and it was installed just as quickly and immediately found all my existing Garmin maps AND my new City Navigator-Europe maps.  Garmin could have put this info on a Read-me file on the CityNav-Europe DVD and saved themselves a one-hour phone call charge.

BASECAMP vs MAPSOURCE
I haven't had a chance to fully compare the features of MapSource vs BaseCamp, but the web is full of unhappiness with BaseCamp...so I thought I'd really like to save my familiar MapSource interface if possible.

As a first test, MapSource quickly wins over BaseCamp when it comes to selecting maps for download to the GPS, something I just had to do to combine my world maps with the new CityNav-Europe maps.  The two map-selection screens work similarly, but the BaseCamp's selection screen is limited to a small (unexpandable) 6"x8" window that prevents seeing all the selectable map elements at once...and you have to use a very awkward joystik pan-icon to move around the screen...a real pain.  With MapSource, the mapselection screen fills my 24" monitor, making map element selection much much easier.  On both you can grab a large number of desired map elements at once by "boxing them" with the mouse, and then individual maps can be removed from selection by left-clicking (MapSource) or right-clicking (BaseCamp).  MapSource turns the selected map elements pink so they're ease to identify...whereas BaseCamp's MapInstall function turns them pale blue...very hard for me to see which are selected on its small MapInstall window.  I definitely prefer the MapSource map-selection interface.

Another key difference between the two programs is the introduction of Garmin's MyCollection filing approach to filing generated GPS routes, tracks, trips etc.  BaseCamp no longer has OPEN and SAVE functions for opening and saving files...everything has to imported into MyCollection.
Since I already have an extensive GPS filing system on my computer with hundreds of GPS-related files (dozens of pretrip planning versions, dozens of raw track files, dozens of edited track files, dozens of GoogleEarth-generated track files, etc from all over the world...this is NOT HELPFUL!  At least leave the OPEN and SAVE file functions (and turn OFF MyCollection) as an option for serious users.

Another NOT HELPFUL feature of both the new BaseCamp and my upgraded MapSource, is that all the WayPoint and POI Icons have been changed to BIG UGLY icons that cover up huge fractions of the maps I'm trying to read.  Since I've got hundreds of waypoints on hundreds of old files, this is a major problem of backward compatibility.  I guess I'll see if I can redo the "modern" Icons to match my old ones.  Don't know if that's possible.  Adding new custom ones won't help with backward compatibility to years of previous GPS files.

SUMMARY
Success...after a VERY painful process.  Is this the best that Garmin can do!

Postscript: As a note, I use my Garmin 60 Csx  to gather track data continuously for wherever I travel in the world.  It runs typically around 3-4 days on each set of two AA batteries and gives me position data about every 15 seconds.  I then use the track data in Google Earth to generate photo-realistic route maps in 3D and to synchronize with photos from the camera...giving me Geoposition data for all my photos.  I'll be using a separate Garmin Nuvi for driving directions while on the road this summer in Europe.
profile.summary: Disastrous Installation ...totally Disfunctional DVD...but eventully success

It also supports both VGA and DVI inputs for greater compatibility and its VESA compatible mounting offers a sleek, space saving option in tight spaces. profile.reviewText:
Nice inexpensive monitor for pairing with my netbook computer.  When I'm away from home, I needed a monitor with 1680 x 1050 resolution, which is the highest that my netbook computer can provide.  For my desktop PC, I use an Asus ProArt 24" monitor with 1920 x1280 resolution.  It has much better color than this smaller Acer, but this is a lot less expensive. profile.description: The Black & Decker BDEG400 4-1/2" 6 Amp Angle Grinder is ideal for sharpening, cutting, grinding, removing rust and surface preparation. This grinder features a metal gear case for durability and longer life. It offers a 3-position side handle that provides added comfort and control for use with various materials and angles. It also has a spindle lock for easy accessory changes. Operates at 10,000 rpm, with a spindle size range of 5/8" - 11 ". Includes: (1) 4-1/2" Small angle grinder, (1) Metal grinding wheel, (1) Spanner wrench .
profile.reviewText:
Had a job of cutting a 3-point hitch away from a carryall steel frame.  I outfitted the B&D BDEG400 with DeWalt 0.045" cutoff wheels and it did a fantastic job of cutting thru the 1/2" x 2.5" in steel bars and various 1.5" by 3/16" thick steel Ls.  I compared it with using my Sawzall and it was no contest...the cutoff was far faster (maybe 10x).  I also used surface grinding wheels with the B&D BDEG400 to level the cut surfaces and that worked very well also.  Lastly I used the  B&D BDEG400 with Flat Flap Disc Sandpaper wheels to smooth out the edge of some flame-cut steel plates...that worked very well also.

In general, using the B&D BDEG400 worked very smoothly as it was easy to handle, easy to turn on and off, and easy to lay down after use...the shield always preventing the wheel from contacting the rest surface.  For the price, this was a major addition to my tool set.  My only concern is how long the bearings on the head are going to last...I sensed what seamed like some loosening of the head bearings during my multihour use.  This is just a sense, but it's something I'll keep my eye on.  However, at the price I paid, the unit has already paid for itself, perhaps several times over.

Very much impressed with its utility...highly recommended.
profile.summary: Very much impressed with its utility...highly recommended.

profile.description: The Style O garage laser parking guide uses dual lasers shine onto vehicle to precisely guide driver to correct spot.
profile.reviewText:
Over the past year I've bought two of the Sierra Tools 2-Car Laser Parking Systems, the first (purchased a year ago) has been working perfectly since I installed it, though I first had to repair a broken solder joint in the transformer power supply.  After the unit arrived, it died completely before I could get it installed.  Because it would cost a bundle of time and hassle to send it back, I decided to try and fix it.  I quickly narrowed the problem down to a dead transformer power supply, which when hacksawed open, was found to have a broken solder connection to the diode circuit board.  I resoldered the wire, glued the unit back together, and it's been working perfectly over the past year with two very bright lasers that make parking a breeze for both of our cars.  The motion sensor also works perfectly in that the laser is always on when we pull a car into position and stays on long enough to fine adjust our parking position.  Our unit is plugged directly into the 120v supply so we left the battery out...its not needed, as when the power goes out, the garage-door opener doesn't work either.
Based on this good performance, I decided a few weeks ago to buy a second unit for the two car garage at our ranch house.  After quickly checking that the unit was functional, I started to install it and found that I couldn't see the lasers on the garage floor to adjust them.  Further checking indicated that both lasers were generating only a very weak light, perhaps 100x less than my good unit at home.  As before, I tore this unit apart to see if it could be easily repaired.  What I found was very sloppy workmanship with very poor solder joints on the main circuit board, and both laser diodes in the unit were defective with no repair possible.  This dim output on the lasers duplicates the issue noted by some of the other reviewers.
Bottom Line:  A great little device if you're lucky enough to get a functional unit, but based on my experience (two dysfunctional units out of two tries), your chances are not good.  It's a real shame, as the unit's performance (when it works) is very good.  Someone needs to step up the quality control on this unit's manufacture...this is not commercial quality.
profile.summary: Great when it works...but horrible quality control

top_5.description: Able Planet Travelers' Choice Active Noise-Cancelling Foldable Headphones. Ideal for the traveler, student or music lover. The latest technology and convenient foldable size. The Able Planet Travelers' Choice Active Noise Cancelling Foldable Headphones features an adjustable headband, superior sound quality and clarity, patented LINX AUDIO technology, in-line volume control for easy adjustment to safe listening levels (no more hunting for the volume control) and state-of-the-art active noise cancellation (ANC). With over 30 International CES and CTIA awards, the sound quality will delight even the most discernible ear. Features: Patented LINX AUDIO technology InWireTM volume control for easy adjustment to safe listening levels State-of-the-art active noise cancellation (ANC) Superior comfort in a foldable design perfect for travel Specifications: Frequency response: 20 Hz-20 kHz Sensitivity at 1 kHz: 115 dB (Off); 121 dB (On) Plug: 3.5 mm Included: 1/4 home stereo adapter One AAA battery Soft carrying pouch Airplane adapter Dimensions: 6.00"L x 3.75"W x 7.00"H Weight: 0.80 lbs.
top_5.reviewText:
Both my spouse and I travel extensively and use the noise-canceling headphones almost exclusively for watching airplane movies.  Thus our success criteria is how they do in noisy planes, how compactly they fold, and how comfortable they are for several hours in the plane.

Previously we had Chinese-made Noisebuster (NB-FX) Noise Canceling Headphones, and we were pretty happy with them...they folded very compactly, had quite acceptable audio performance in the plane, were modestly comfortable for long movies, and worked with or without a single AA battery.  BUT the rubber on the ear pieces finally gave out after several years...seems to be the generic end-of-life situation for earphones.

So we've both purchased the Able Planet Traveler's Foldable units as replacements...as the previous units are no longer made.  Bottom line: Not as good audio performance, but OK; fold similarly, but not quite as compactly; and aren't as comfortable for long hauls.  Unfortunately a step back for around the same price.

However, after considerable shopping and a couple of false trials, we couldn't locate anything better.
We recommend them as the best available for our use...and wish someone would bring back the old Noisebuster (NB-FX) Noise Canceling Headphones design...it was sold under a couple of brand names around 2006.

Designed as a portable power inverter to power up multiple items and most major household appliances. Upgraded 300W DC to AC Power Inverter: A must-have for your road trips, vacations, outdoors, emergency kits and more. Enjoy 4.8A dual Smart USB ports and 2 standard plug outlets for convenient charging on the road. Wide compatibility: DC 12V to Pure Sine Wave AC 110V Converter, ideal for powering Laptops, mobile phones, Christmas LED light strips, power banks, air mattress, breast pumps, electric toothbrush, electric shaver, cameras, PSP, walkie talkies, tablets, GPS units, TV, battery chargers, camping equipment and mobile office equipment Product Specification: Power (2 AC Outlets): 300W Rated, 360W Max, 700W Peak Input Voltage: 12V DC, Output voltage: 110V~120V Dual USB Port Output: DC 5V, 4.2A rated, 4.8A Max. Auto 0~2.4A*2 Indicator: Green-operation, Red-shutdown Over Voltage Shutdown: DC 15V-16V, Low Voltage Shutdown: DC 10V-11V Dimensions are: 4.92 x 3.39x1.93 inch Optimal Use and Precautions: For DC12V ONLY, not applied for DC 24V and airplane use.
