Maha Energys team of engineers developed a brand new Eight Cell, 0.001V resolution, microprocessor. This microprocessor will charge batteries to their maximum capacity without overcharging or undercharging. The new precision microprocessor assures maximum battery longevity. The MH-C801D delivers just the right charge every time! The MH-C801D intelligent system will charge batteries anywhere around the world with a heavy duty switching AC Power Supply. This 100-240V, 50/60Hz universal adapter employs a rugged DIN connector for reliable contact. The MH-C801D is perfect for home, office or travel!
profile.reviewText: I'm a photographer and discharge AA batteries like crazy, especially with flash units. Until now I've just been using a La Crosse BC-9009 (older model of the La Crosse BC1000), which is great, but it only charges 4 batteries at a time. Given that my camera grip uses 6 batteries, I really needed something that could charge at least 6 at a time if not more. So far so good with this thing. I've used it to recondition batteries (I suspect that the La Crosse probably does a better job at that) and charge them in both soft and fast modes (mostly soft). Batteries come out fully charged with no issues. So far I've tried Powerex, Imedion, Eneloop, and some old Energizers that were never very good to begin with. I've also charged AAAs and both AAs and AAAs at the same time with no issues. The recondition process that it uses also seems to be quite fast compared to the BC-9009, though that kind of makes me wonder if that's an indication that it isn't as thorough. One nice thing is that the controls are simple, just one button to put it in soft charge mode (it defaults to fast charge) and another button to put it in recondition mode. That speeds configuration a bit compared to smart chargers with lots of features like the BC-9009, and makes it easy enough to control that my mother could do it. I'm a little skeptical of the "soft charge" mode only being 2h long instead of longer, but perhaps this doesn't matter with the pulse charging technique that this uses. Normally in my BC-9009 I charge at 250mA if I'm not in a hurry, and it takes many hours. (Slow charging is supposed to be better for NiMH batteries long term.) So at 2h for the "soft" charge I'm not sure exactly how soft it is. I'm very happy with this thing at this point, though I've only been using it a few weeks, though I of course plan to keep the 4 battery BC-9009.
profile.summary: Recharges or Reconditions FAST

profile.description: Rosco Photofoil Matte Black Cinefoil (12 inch x 10 feet Roll) is a matte black aluminum material that virtually soaks up light. Ideal for masking light leaks and/or eliminating unwanted reflections.It can be quickly molded to form barndoors, flags, snoots and other configurations. Now available as Photofoil in convenient shorter lengths for still photographers, videographers and students!
profile.reviewText:
I can't say how great this stuff is. It's a deep matte black with practically no reflections, the foil is thick enough that it doesn't collapse too easily, it stands up to heat, and of course it blocks light. Gaffer's tape sticks to it well.

It's very easy to form this into snoots, which is mostly what I've used it for. I don't even plan to buy an actual snoot of any sort, because I can just use this and get exactly the shape and size I want when I want it. It's good for flash and continuous lighting.

Before you buy stuff like barndoors, snoots, etc, get some of this stuff, a roll of gaffer's tape and see what you can do. (Just be careful not to block any ventilation or otherwise cause something to overheat.) For small-time photographers, this length roll is probably all you will need. (You might want to get the wider roll though if you think you might need wider sheets of it.)
profile.summary: Perfect for things like snoots

profile.description: The Lexmark C543dn is the professional color partner small workgroups have been waiting for. Bring your business documents to life with high-quality color output from the C543dn laser printer and drive down costs and inefficiency with paper-saving two-sided printing and included high-yield toner cartridges. Also, with its ultra-compact design and quiet operation, the C543dn is the perfect desktop companion for fast color laser printing.
profile.reviewText: This printer is actually not that bad from the hardware perspective. I've had mine for quite a while with no mechanical problems and it seems to print reasonably fast. Supposedly the TCO isn't anything great from what I hear, but not too bad for this type of printer either. (I can't find reliable figures anywhere, and cost per page is obviously going to depend on what you're printing on each page.) The main problem I have with this printer is very very poor firmware and driver support for printing even remotely accurate colors. The "printer managed color" profiles built in to the printer firmware are horrible, but to make things worse, Lexmark does not provide ICC profiles, and their print drivers (under Mac OS X anyway) don't seem to support ICC profiles at all. The hardware is quite obviously capable of reproducing color with decent (for a laser printer) accuracy because I have profiled mine with a ColorMunki Photo spectrophotometer and, using the resulting ICC profile with Adobe Photoshop and it's built-in color management, I can get color output that often is nearly as accurate as the Fujifilm minilab at the local Sam's Club photo center (depending on the color). The problem is that you shouldn't need to spend hundreds of dollars on Photoshop just to be able to use ICC profiles with this printer and get reasonable color output. The driver should support ICC profiles, and in addition to being able to build custom ones, Lexmark should provide "default" ICC profiles for at least a few paper types. The last person I told about this didn't believe me initially when I told them that Lexmark didn't provide ICC profiles (as their support people confirmed), so it seems that Lexmark is behind standards when it comes to this support. Laser printers are normally quite variable in their color output and normally need to be profiled with a spectrophotometer practically every month to maintain any accuracy, so I wouldn't really expect the built in color management/correction stuff to be that accurate, and I wouldn't expect default ICC profiles to be that accurate if Lexmark actually provided any. But I would expect Lexmark to actually have the driver support necessary for allowing the use of custom ICC profiles with the printer. I've contacted Lexmark support about this issue a couple of times and they can't provide any solutions. About all they can do is ask me to print some test charts, scan them in, and confirm that there's no hardware defect. They are also not very responsive when it comes to answering more difficult technical questions like this. Overall I'd say I'm not impressed with lexmark's technical support offering. The fact that the hardware can print decent color but the capability totally goes to waste because their software/firmware/drivers can't manage color properly is quite sad. From a color perspective, this printer is really only good for people who need to print color charts/graphs and such where they don't really care if the printed colors match anything as long as they look bright/saturated and one color can be distinguished from another. The printer's color "correction" also defaults to "make all the colors bright and pretty regardless of what they're actually supposed to look like" which just further drives home the point that Lexmark really just doesn't seem to care about anything but the printer's ability to print bright, pretty, differently-colored pie slices. Laser printers aren't exactly supposed to make the best photo printers or anything, but Lexmark should be able to do better than they have with the default color handling. If absolutely nothing else, even if they can't do anything with the default color management, their drivers should have proper ICC profile support for those able to profile their own printers. This is just basic stuff expected of a vendor, even for a laser printer. Even if you can't expect them to be photo printers, you should be able to print block graphics with colors that at least vaguely match what they're supposed to. I only bought this printer because I got it very cheaply after discounts, rebates, etc (in fact, I think I essentially just paid the cost of the included cartridges) so I don't feel totally ripped off or anything, but the fact is that next time I buy a color laser printer I won't be getting a Lexmark. Except for getting the printer for a good price when I originally bought it, there's nothing particularly special about it in any way, and the software components that drive the printer are certainly substandard. At the very least I'd rather have both average hardware and average drivers rather than slightly above average hardware and very poor firmware/drivers. So sure, not a bad printer if you want a cheap color laser printer with a typical average cost of operation for this price point, and you have both Photoshop and a spectrophotometer to essentially work around Lexmark's lack of proper driver/firmware color support. It's also OK if you just want bright pie graph slices. Generally speaking though I'd say go for something else if you're looking for a color laser at this price point and capacity level. Even if all you care about is bright, flashy pie slices then you should be able to do better than this. At least go for lower TCO or something.
profile.summary: Very very poor color accuracy

profile.description: VELCRO Brand Sticky Back fasteners deliver strong holding power. Simple peel and stick application. For smooth surfaces such as painted wallboard, glass, metal and most plastics. VELCRO Brand is the original hook and loop fastener. Much better durability and strength than other off brand fasteners. They are available in squares, coins, strips, and tapes and come in a range of colors.These clear coins blend into most surfaces, no color matching required. A must have for any home, school or office. Great for organization.
profile.reviewText: This stuff saves a tremendous amout of trouble when it comes to hanging little bits of equipment (like flash triggers) onto other equipment (like strobes/speedlights). I also made my own "speedstrap" (gel holder) simply by taking 1 1/2' of the tape and sticking the loop half of the tape onto the back of the hooks half (resulting in a strip with hooks on one side and loops on the other). If you need lots of these then you might try velcro cable ties, but I'm not sure how suitable they'd be for holding gels onto the front of a flash or other applications that don't involve cable management. Anyway, the sticky velcro can be used to make cable ties as well as faten other objects together. Serious photographers with lighting equipment will probably want to get 15' of this stuff. It'll probably get used up faster than you think. The only things I wouldn't use these for are certain applications that need a very tight hold. For applications where you need something to practually be glued down to something else, but still need to be able to remove it *sometimes*, Velcro Industrial Strength is much much better. I've used the industrial strength stuff to install some gadgets in my car and the things might as well be glued down, except for the fact that I can remove them (which takes some real force) for maintenance etc and put them back with the same glue-like level of hold.
profile.summary: Essential for strobist photographers

profile.description: Macally iKeySlim is a stylish & clean white slim keyboard. Enhanced low profile keycaps reduces key stroke travel distances and eases pressure on your finger tips.
profile.reviewText:
This is a great keyboard that makes a great alternative to the current super-flat low key travel keyboard that Apple has been selling in the last 3 years or so. It also seems to be the only decent black Mac keyboard in case that matters to you. (In my case, I had colored my mac mini black with a skin, my monitors are black, and my mouse is black or nearly so. As a result I really wanted a black keyboard that would fit in a little better with the rest.)

As some people mention, it doesn't have a power key but in my case I could care less because I leave my computer on pretty much all of the time and usually only need the power button to force a power cycle (which a keyboard power key wouldn't do anyway.)
profile.summary: Great alternative mac keyboard!

profile.description: The ColorChecker Classic target is designed to deliver true-to-life color reproduction so photographers and filmmakers can predict and control how color will look under any illumination. Each of the 24 colors represents the actual color of natural objects and reflects light just like its real-world counterpart. Use it to compare, measure and analyze differences in color reproduction and avoid costly mistakes with trial-and-error color adjustments while editing images.
profile.reviewText:
Just a GretagMacBeth color chart used to cost as much as this product, but this one gives you not only the ColorChecker chart, but you also get a white/black clipping chart, a very uniform white balance card, and software for creating DNG profiles with Lightroom or a stand-alone application. I just wish the software had some options for tweaking the profiles a bit, but you can just use Adobe's DNG profile editor for that.

One bit of advice, do NOT use the gray patches on the ColorChecker chart for white balance. Use the actual white balance card instead. At least one person has found, using a spectrophotometer, that the gray patches on the ColorChecker chart do not reflect a uniform light spectrum (the patches will reflect some wavelengths of light better than others), possibly causing the patches to not be perfectly neutral in some lighting conditions due to metemerism. They aren't that far off, but using them for white balance isn't ideal when you have something else that's designed for white balance.

The white balance card has been tested for spectral uniformity, and it is almost perfect. So it's better to use that for while balance and use the color chart only for profiling.

While the passport case is quite nice and very portable, the lanyard it comes with is way too long. Unless you're Yao Bing or something you'll probably find it useless unless you shorten it somehow.
profile.summary: Good camera callibration for the money

profile.description: Proudly display your art with the Itoya art portfolio advantage presentation display book. The pages of this art display book are made from poly glass pocket sheets to offer a clear view of your art work. This art presentation book has a lightweight black poly cover to keep your art safe. Its pages are fastened to the cover with black anodized metal rivets for enhanced durability. Moreover, this presentation display book features a multi-fold spine that allows you to keep the book flat for convenient presentation. 24 pages for 48 views size: 8.5 in x 11 in acid- and PVC-free archival safe contains recycled polypropylene available in a portrait view.
profile.reviewText:
I've been keeping ink jet prints (Epson R3000, UltraChrome K3 ink, epson paper) in the larger version of these that I bought 8 months ago or so and  no signs of ink transfer or sticking. Prints slide out just as easily now as they did months ago, glossy paper included. At least with the media I'm using, these things just won't stick.

How will the prints look in 50 years compared to unprotected prints? That's obviously rather difficult to say, but if the archival quality of the sleeves matches what I've seen so far then it won't be the sleeves at fault. I'm more suspicious of the paper. (I don't think that even the "Ultra Premium" epson paper is considered archival quality.)

I only subtract one star because the price is kind of high, and for the price I feel like they should have come with hard (box type) sleeves.
profile.summary: These are great, just a little expensive.

profile.description: This stylish camcorder soft carrying case has internal movable partitions and mesh pouches to store both your camcorder and extra accessories.
profile.reviewText:
I bought this case to protect my Lytro light field camera, not a Sony camcorder, so my use case is a bit atypical.

As of this time there's no official case of any sort, and maybe only one expensive third-party case, for the brand new Lytro cameras and i was tired of trying to gingerly carry my Lytro around without damaging it. I saw some people recommend this case on one of the Lytro forums and decided to try it out.

For the Lytro it isn't that bad. The case is maybe 30% larger than needed in all three dimensions, so the fit is a bit loose, but not so loose as to compromise safety. The padding is thick enough that dropping this on the floor with my Lytro in it wouldn't bother me at all, and the stitching and such is solid, so it does work as a Lytro case with the main drawback being that it's bulkier than it needs to be for a Lytro. It also has a little pouch for the USB cable.

If the case were better designed in general though, I'd probably give it at least 4 stars, but unfortunately the overall design of the case is rather medicore regardless of what device you store in it. Problems:

- It has this long shoulder strap that can't be removed without cutting it off (which I'm tempted to do). A shoulder strap for such a tiny case seems awkward to me, I'll never use it, and I hate that I can't non-destructively remove it.

- There is a belt loop, but the loop is oriented to hold the case horizontally which, being a single loop in the middle, isn't sufficient to properly support a case this long. So you can put it on yout belt, but it flops around and is otherwise less wieldy than it would be if the loop allowed it to hang down vertically.

This thing should really be designed more like a "fanny pack", or it should at the absolute minimum be possible to somehow remove the strap without damaging it.

So while this case will do the job of protecting my Lytro for now, I'm not satisfied with it and will continute to look for something better. if you have a Lytro or anything else, you might want to keep looking before you buy this.
profile.summary: An "OK" case for the Lytro

profile.description: Featuring the ability to transfer multi channel digital audio and uncompressed high definition video in resolutions as high as 1440p with a single cable, HDMI has quickly become the latest industry standard for delivering unsurpassed quality. This HDMI to Mini HDMI cable is perfect for hooking up your camcorder or digital camera to your HDTV or any other device featuring a HDMI connection. HDMI is renowned for its ability to deliver crisp high definition audio and video, which remains unrivalled by other conventional cables. HDMI cables will also eliminate clutter, doing the job of several cables with only one. This 15ft cable is certified version 1.3a category 2, allowing it to carry 16 bit color, equivalent to around 280 trillion colors. This helps eliminate banding in images on the screen, allowing for a smoother and more lifelike image. Featuring 24K Gold connectors for maximum conductivity and sturdy construction, this cable is certain to heighten your entertainment experience.
profile.reviewText:
I bought this to use for connecting my Nikon D7000 camera to HDMI compatible monitors and TVs when I'm not at home and need to quickly and easily display photos that I've just taken.  I don't need it very often, but when I do it works well. Gold plated connectors and thick insulation make it a very good value for the price.

Don't waste $50 at some store like Best Buy for a cable that's no better than this one! Cheap analog audio cables can have problems with radio noise degrading the quality of the signal, but with digital data transmission the bits either get there or they don't. RF noise from anything short of a nuclear bomb has no effect because even if it does mess up a few bits of data, digital systems like HDMI have mathemtaical error correction that can detect and correct data transmissions errors. So HDMI cables either work with perfect digital quality or they don't work at all.
profile.summary: Works well on my Nikon D7000

profile.description: NEW! Articulated tip for easy use with SensorKlear Loup with a flexible cleaning tip. The cleaning compound will not spill or dry out and incorporates a unique shaped cleaning tip for those hard to reach CCD sensors.
profile.reviewText:
This is the first sensor cleaning method that I've tried, aside from blowing the sensor off with a bulb. I have a Nikon D7000 (APS-C, 1.5x crop sensor).

This product seems pretty similar to the other Lenspen pens for lens cleaning except that it has a flat triangle-shaped head. I guess you're supposed to use the corners to pick at bits of dust or something.

It basically seems to work once you figure out the right technique, but it's not amazing. I put my camera in mirror up mode, used the blower blub to blow out the aperture area while holding the camera upside down, and then started looking over the sensor with a loupe.

At first I tried just gently brushing at the dust with the lenspen, but this didn't seem to work too well as the thing tended to just push the dust around. After that I tried wiping over the whole thing in rows "squeegee style" and this worked much better. I must have tinkered with the thing trying to find the best technique for 45min to an hour. Eventually I decided the easiest thing to do was remove the loupe, brush across the whole thing edge-to-edge (not stopping or starting in the middle), then put the loupe back on and look to see what was left. Then rebrush those areas with any dust left, always moving from edge to edge. Next time I'll be able to do this much more quickly.

I went back and forth from cleaning to putting the lens back on and taking a test shot (f/32, defocused shot of a brightly lit wall at ISO 100) about 3 times before I was reasonably satisfied, but I still didn't manage to get every single speck off of the thing. When I stopped there were about 5 very tiny specks that seemed to be too small to cause much trouble and I didn't think I was ever going to get the thing 100% free of the really tiny stuff using this method. I also used a blower blub to blow off the tip of the lenspen thing a few times in case that did anything (I couldn't tell). I suspect that the lenspen isn't really capable of always holding on to all dust, so it's probably limited to cleaning off everything but 4-5 extremely tiny bits that won't affect the image enough to matter to most people.

One thing I read said that you probably shouldn't use the lenspen until after you've done at least one "wet" cleaning. So my next cleaning is going to be the wet method and I'll probably reserve the lenspen for certain situations like removing a long fiber or something really big when I don't want to wet clean the whole thing. I'll probably also throw it away after 10 uses or so. I won't try to use it to remove anything stuck on by something other than static electricity.

So the lenspen isn't that great but it isn't totally worthless. It does have the advantage that it doesn't require any liquids or other stuff, but it doesn't seem to attract dust or cancel the static charge that is usually what's keeping the dust from being blown off. The triangle shaped tip seems a bit odd to me; a spatula shape like the swabs would seem to make more sense.

So overall I'd say it's worth trying out since it's pretty cheap, but I should have done a wet cleaning before using it. I don't see any signs of problems after using it, but I wasn't trying to pick off any glued-on crap or do anything else "rough" with it, so I wouldn't really expect any problems.
profile.summary: Not too bad... better than nothing

profile.description: Created to redefine fine art printing, this UltraChrome K3 Vivid Magenta ink cartridge offers superior water, scratch and fade resistance that professionals demand for exhibition quality prints. EPSON UltraChrome K3 with Vivid Magenta technology has advanced magenta pigments for astounding reds, blues and purples with three-level Black technology for outstanding tonal range and phenomenal black-and-white prints. This package contains 1 magenta ink cartridge that is compatible with the following Epson printers: Epson Stylus R3000 Photo Printer
profile.reviewText:
UltraChrome K3 is great stuff, I just wish it weren't so expensive. Since it's the same no matter where you get it, you might as well go for the lowest price.

Regarding yellow ink specifically: keep in mind that your yellow cartridge is going to get consumed faster than the others if your printing is fairly average over the primary colors. This is because you have two shades of magenta ink, two shades of cyan, and three shades of black, but only one shade of yellow. So every other color has 2 or 3 cartridges to draw from while Yellow only has one. This ink will get used whenever red, yellow, or green are printed and green especially occurs very commonly due to the fact that plants are green and plants very often occur in photos.

So even if you just bought a new printer and don't buy any other color ink right away, you might want to just order an extra yellow with your printer because you're most likely to run out of it first.
profile.summary: Yellow.... the most quickly consumed CcMmYkkK ink

profile.description: The Storacell Battery Caddy solves the problem of how to conveniently store your batteries in a compact and easy to find holder. Originally designed for pilots, the Battery Caddy is also great for photography, camping, travel or home use. The Battery Caddy is durable and break resistant and the slim and lightweight design makes it portable. There are no sharp edges to catch on clothing or bags. Storacell's patented locking system snaps batteries into place; batteries snap into place and remove easily. When ready to use, simply push the battery out with your thumb. Keep fresh batteries separate from used batteries by turning them in opposite directions. The Storacell Battery Caddy provides the best terminal protection at both ends. Batteries left rolling around in a drawer, bag or container have the potential to cause a fire. 9V batteries can be a hazard if the double terminal comes in contact with metal objects; an electrical spark can be created causing a fire. The Battery Caddy is great for a variety of uses including outdoor activities, photography bags, emergency kits, by emergency responders and for home organization. Batteries not included.
profile.reviewText:
I love these things. They're much easier to deal with than those little plastic boxes that hold four batteries each.  All you have to do is pull one item out of your bag and pop batteries out of it. Quick and simple, no fumbling with a bunch of little boxes, dropping the batteries, etc.

Unfortunately the first one of these that I ordered was damaged, but that seems to be due to improper packaging. Whoever packed my order put  the storacel in the same box with a larger heavier box inside it, and the air inflated pilow packaging wasn't enough to keep the heavy box from sliding around. So I'm guessing that the heavy box hammered into the storacel during shipping and cracked it. This sort of repeated hammering while the storacel is empty doesn't seem very likely to happen in normal use, so I don't really fault the durability of the product.

I'd rate these 5 stars, but they just seem more expensive than they should be, so I'm subtracting a star for what seems to me like a somewhat inflated price.
profile.summary: Awesome holders, just a little expensive

profile.description: Capable of handling the weight of a professional full-frame DSLR camera with a heavy long telephoto lenses, or even a large format (4x5) field camera, The PRO 700 DX offer professional photographers and advanced amateurs the strength and stability They need while its size, and the use of a. M. T. Alloy, make it lighter weight and more portable than the professional Series. The Pro 700 DX makes setting up easy with secure yet fast speed release leg locks, gearless center column, and 3 position adjustable angle leg locks for easy set up on uneven ground or steps. The PRO 700 DX center column is actually two threaded pieces that unscrew to convert the top piece to a short column. This combined with the adjustable leg angle locks allows the tripod to be lowered to just 15 inches for very low angle or macro photography in the field. The included Pro 700 DX all-metal 3-way pan head has one of the fasted and easiest to use quick release plates in the industry. SLIK Made a Circular quick release plate that can secure the camera to the tripod pointing in any direction, making attaching your camera (once the SLIK quick release plate is attached) more intuitive than most other heads that have squared off or angled plates.
profile.reviewText: The tripod that I had previous to this was a an old half-broken cheap Velbon Victory that someone gave me for free, so as you can imagine the 700DX is a major upgrade that I'm quite happy with. I bought this for use with a Marumi TB-12 Arca Compatible Ball Head which I selected based on price, quality, and Arca QR plate compatibility, and it seems to be a solid combination with these legs. I wish I could compare the legs with ones from other manufacturers at a similar price point, but I'm lacking any experience with those. In any case, this thing is rock solid and gets high marks from everything I've read, and the fact that you can lock the legs into three different positions for various heights is extremely handy. Reversing the center column works quite well, and with a 40mm lens on my 1.5x crop factor D7000 I can extend the legs all the way, reverse the column, slide it to the highest position, point the camera straight down with the legs fully extended in the highest position, and not have any of the legs visible in the frame. So this thing is great for "straight down" angles for copy work or what have you. And for wider angles I'm guessing that locking the legs into the middle position will keep them out of the frame. My only complaint is that the feet don't have spikes, and it seems like there's no option to add spiked feet that I can find. So far I haven't run into any situations that would benefit from spiked feet though, so i can't really say how much of a problem this might be for me.
profile.summary: Solid tripod with flexible configurations

profile.description: The Holga 120N is BACK! The Holga camera was initially introduced to the Chinese public, in 1982, as an inexpensive camera for everyday use. Shortly after its introduction, it became an underground artistic phenomena. Using the Holga is an exercise in breaking free from dependence on technology, precision and controllability. The slight softness of the images, vignetting and random light leaks produce dream-like, one-of-a kind images. The current Holga 120N is modeled after the original Holga camera and features the improved usability found in the latest generations.
profile.reviewText:
I'm a photo student. I'm studying everything about photography. I'm not an urban hipster. I don't look like an urban hipster. I have absolutely no inherent "lo-fi" photography bias due to some sort of artsy hipster social background. It's just something that I'm messing with because I'm sleeping, eating, and breathing all sorts of photography 24-7.

I bought this because it's the prototypical "crappy toy camera" and I wanted to see what I could do with it's limited capabilities. It's part of an optional assignment and I'm playing with film right now, so why not.

The first thing that everyone should know is that this is not really a toy or an inexpensive alternative camera, but rather a modern "remake" of a primitive camera intended to allow those who understand, or are learning to understand, the photographic process in detail to reproduce certain "vintage" photographic styles and push the limits of what can be done with primitive technology.

The Holga 120N has the following features for "advanced" photographers:

- They use medium format 120 roll film. This is film that is a little more than 6cm wide... it is NOT 35mm. Normally this film is used in expensive Hasselblad or Mamiya cameras and is thus not usually sold at drug stores and gas stations. Not every photo lab will process it.

- There IS a "bulb" exposure mode, which means that you can keep the shutter open as long as you keep holding down the shutter button. You have to know what you're doing with this or all you'll do is waste a shot of film.

- Whether "bulb" mode is turned on or off, there's nothing stopping you from exposing the film multiple times without advancing the roll. There's also nothing stopping you from advancing the film too far, too little, or never advancing it at all. Other than the little window on the back, and perhaps counting the clicks of the film winder, there's nothing to tell you how far to turn the thing to get to the next unexposed frame. There's absolutely nothing to tell you if the current frame has already been exposed.

These are all things that can be exploited by advanced photographers to create interesting effects, but for anyone else they're just annoying hazards.

Limitations of the camera that can only be overcome by a somewhat knowledgeable photographer in most situations:

- There are only two aperture settings. To make things worse, the f-numbers that these supposedly correspond to (supposedly f/8 for "sunny" and f/11  for "cloudy" or whatever that icon is supposed to be) are reportedly bogus. They may not be accurate from camera to camera, depending on when it was made. Reportedly all you ever get is f/13, though supposedly on some newer ones the switch actually does do something or the other.
- There's only one shutter speed not counting "bulb" mode: 1/100s
- There's no way to focus visually with the viewfinder and with apertures like f/8 or f/11 the focus ring has to be set somewhat intelligently to have any chance of getting a subject within the in-focus depth of field.
- Aside from using bulb mode or multiple exposures in some situations, you have practically no control of the exposure aside from film ISO and push/pull processing.

If you don't know what I'm talking about, but do want to learn then great! If you don't know and don't care then you probably don't want to buy this camera.

The charming lo-fi features of the camera:

- It has a simplistic high-dispersion plastic lens that softens focus the way transparent plastic does and does little or nothing to correct for the various optical distortions caused by simple spherical single-element lenses. If you're not trying to intentionally take photos with these properties then for the same money you can get a camera with a more modern design that at least has a lens made of glass.
- There's little or nothing in the design to prevent light from reflecting off of slick surfaces inside the camera, contaminating the film with random reflections.
- The gaps between parts (like the back and the rest of the camera) aren't sealed particularly well, so light leaks through and reflects off of surfaces, contaminating the film with stray light.

Some tips for those using these for the first time:

- Tape down the sliding things that lock the back on after loading the camera. The back will come open way too easily if you don't. Light leaks may be hipster cool but having the back come off just results in totally ruined film.
- Light will leak through the little frame number view window (red plastic) in the back and contaminate regular panchromatic film (which responds to red light). How bad this is depends on how bright the ambient light is, and whether or not you're using one of the included (6x6 or 6x4.5) film masks. You can either ignore than and get the hipster light leaks, or you can cover the red window with tape. If you cover it then you can either open it up briefly under subdued light to see when you've advanced the film one frame, or you can figure out how many "clicks" of the winder need to go by before one frame has advanced and count those when winding.
- You may want to write "1/100s" and "f/8 - f/11" on the camera to remind you of what the aperture settings and shutter speed are if you actually believe what the manual says they are.
- You may want to write the approximate focus distances corresponding to each of the icons on the focus ring. I wrote my own focusing scale on the thing using a silver paint marker.
- Use the light meter in a manual mode camera to give you an idea of what sort of lighting conditions are going to work with f/8 and 1/100s with the ISO of film you have in the thing. There's probably no point in walking around metering for every shot, but you should at least get some idea if your film is going to require direct sunlight, shade on a sunny day, work ok with overcast sky, or work inside in rooms with lots of of windows on sunny days. Even at ISO 3200, bright artificial office lighting probably won't be enough for indoor conditions.
- If possible, try to shoot a whole roll of film in approximately the same lighting conditions so you can push/pull process the film to compensate for over/underexposure. For example, if you know that bright office lighting won't quite be enough but you want to try it anyway, shoot the whole roll under that lighting so you can push process the film (to get a higher effective ISO out of it).

Overall I'd say, not bad for $30 if you want to be able to do some of the things that the lack of "idiot proofing" features allow and you want to recreate some lo-fi effects, but don't waste your money on the camera, film, and processing if you don't know what you're getting into. These things are also great for making your own modifications since the worst you can do is destroy the thing, losing $30.
profile.summary: A non-hipster photo student's impressions

profile.description: Introducing the eCraft, the first and only personal electronic cutter that allows you to cut without a mat. Its ease of use combined with advanced technology makes the eCraft the perfect cutting system for all consumers from beginner to expert. It is ideal for scrapbooking, banners, paper crafting, card making, fashion designing, home decor, and so much more. The eCraft's unique design and paper feeder system make it easy to cut materials automatically, without the use of a cutting mat. Use the Paper Tray to stack multiple sheets at a time, or use the Roller to cut 12" by any length. The eCraft is ultra slim, and its lightweight design and onboard storage compartment let you take it anywhere. Use it on its own with SD Image Cards, or attached to a computer with the eCraftshop Professional Design Software that comes in the box. With the large selection of fonts, shapes and designs, anyone can be an expert in minutes. Making great looking projects has never been easier.
profile.reviewText:
I've read reviews here that claim the the eCraft just "doesn't work" and I would dispute that, but it does seem to have trouble with certain patterns especially with no cardstock carrier/stabilizer. The "matless" design is rather ambitious and perhaps a bit too ambitious.

Overall I'd say that what design is going to work or not is probably less predictable with this cutter than with others. Some things are going to be very sensitive to the pressure setting, the tab width and density, and whether or not you use some cardstock under the material you're trying to cut.

PRINT-AND-CUT WARNING: A big feature that's missing from the eCraft is print-and-cut. For some reason I missed that fact before I bought it. There's just no good way to accurately align the page for this, and the rollers seem like they're more likely than usual to adversely affect ink jet printed images anyway. So don't buy the eCraft if you want print-and-cut!

The main limitation of the eCraft (other than no print-and-cut) becomes apparent when you try to cut a full-page lattice type pattern. Because it doesn't use a carrier mat, the paper has to have a minimum amount of stiffness and once you have the whole sheet filled with hole cuts (especially if the average gap between the holes is like 1/4") the sheet becomes weakened to where it doesn't stay flat when it's being pushed by the rollers. Trying this sort of cut at least twice (reducing the density/complexity the second time), it jammed both times. A third attempt trying to get the blade depth set to just barely cut entirely through the paper while using a backing sheet avoided jamming, but apparently I didn't have it set deep enough to cut all the way through in most places. (Basically it got kiss cut maybe 80-90% through in most places.) I had the tab width set to the smallest and least dense settings, and I'm guessing that raising the tab settings to wide and dense would help some, but would probably make removing the "chads" rather difficult.

Interestingly enough, if I use some thin cardstock (like the protective sheet that came in an 8.5"x11" box of Epson photo paper) as a backing sheet, it cuts relatively fine detail (at least in the middle 25% of the page) in 32lb laser paper without any trouble even with the tabs turned off. (I didn't try an elaborate lattice with that yet though.) And that's even with no adhesive.

Of course, having to use a backing sheet kind of defeats the purpose of having a "matless" cutter.

Another annoying thing is that if it jams, there would seem to be no way to release the tension between the rollers so you can remove the crumpled paper. This makes clearing jams pretty difficult a lot of the time.

I also read about problems that seem to be caused by paper lifting up (probably while pushing) in the area under the cutting head as it seems to have nothing there to really keep it held down flat.... like an adhesive backing mat.

It probably works pretty well with adhesive vinyl since that's always kiss cut with it's own backing.

Actually, the lattice that I cut might have worked if the cuts had been made in the best order. It jammed toward the end when it tried to push and pull the whole sheet back and forth trying to make lots of little cuts around the edge after the whole middle of the page had been weakened. (Turning off "prioritize inner cuts" probably would have helped but I'm loathe to try it again since trying to clear the jam the last time was very difficult.) If the vendor's software were smart enough to analyze the rigidity of the page in various areas and optimize the cut order to minimize the amount of weakened area that's pushed through the rollers (such as cutting in rows from front to back, scanning down the page, so it never revisits weakened page areas) that would probably help.

The only way I think they could improve this given the matless design of the cutter is if the software did some somewhat sophisticated analysis to find weakened areas and then perform special optimization on the cutting order and warn you when a particular design is just going to weaken the paper too much to be likely to work with no backing sheet, or at all. The quality of the vendor software is currently rather mediocre overall (which makes the usefulness of third-party software like Make the Cut greater for the eCraft compared to other cutters) so I kind of doubt that we'd see advanced optimization features like this any time soon.

The documentation for both the included eCraft software and the cutter itself is really horrible and lacking in information. I'm an engineer and not only was it not obvious to me what orientation letter size paper should be loaded in the paper tray, I couldn't find a clear answer in the documentation. I had to figure this out by trial-and-error.

While I don't have any experience with any other cutters yet, and I know that all of these cutters have some not totally predictable limitations in some cases and require proper configuration/calibration in all cases, I suspect that the ecraft is less predictable than most. Maybe if people stick to using only simple designs like not too small or intricate flowers that aren't too densely packed on an entire page, or they just use stuff like vinyl, they won't really have many problems, but with lots of other situations, who knows.

Overall Summary

Pros:

- It's less expensive than many cutters.

- Blades are cheap.

- Works fine for the typical case using simple shapes like the ones on the included SD card and standard cardstock.

- Can in theory cut some pretty thick materials (though I haven't tested this personally)

- The cutting head holds both a blade and pen at the same time, so it can draw and cut without having to switch out the blade for a pen.

Cons:

- Does NOT do print-and-cut!

- Matless cutting design is too ambitious for many use cases. You end up having to use a backing/carrier cardstock sheet under your material in many cases.

- What will and won't work without jamming, especially without a backing/carrier, is difficult to predict. While experience with the machine will help with this, I suspect that this one takes longer to learn than most.

- Software is very mediocre. Luckily it imports SVG files, so I'd advise using something like Adobe Illustrator or Inkscape to design things and then import them. Either do that, or buy third-party software like Make the Cut.

- The documentation is very lacking, making the learning curve even worse.

- Has some design flaws and overall it's not quite ready for "prime time" until some design improvements are made.
profile.summary: It works, BUT limitations exist and they're unpredictable

profile.description: Digital lens, filter and compact lens cleaning kit. Safe for use on all optical devices. Kit contains miniPRO II, FilterKlear and LensPen. Patented carbon compound. Over 500 cleanings.
profile.reviewText:
Lenspens seem to work pretty well in most situatons, but until now I've only had the standard sized one. I always wished that I had a smaller one that I could use to clean small lenses like the ones on point and shoot cameras and such, and the normal lenspen never seemed to be flat enough to do a very good job of contacting the surface of a flat filter.

Well, the micro lenspen and the filter lenspen solve these problems. Really the one for filters isn't all that special, though it does do a better job of cleaning filters, but the micro sized lenspen is a huge help when it comes to cleaning some things like the tiny iPhone camera Photojojo add-on lenses that I have, and other little things that are difficult to clean with anything.

If you're thinking of buying a lenspen, I say buy this set instead of an individual standard one unless you're sure you'll never want the others. Almost certainly you'll be glad you bought the specialized ones when something comes up.
profile.summary: The micro and filter pins are worth it.

profile.description: Say goodbye to analog hiss and distortion, and hello to the diamond-sharp digital sound of HD Radio. With an ever-growing range of exciting new channels and program formats to choose from, HD Radio represents the future of free-to-air radio. And what better way to access this audio goldmine than with the UP-HT1 HD Radio tuner? The UP-HT1 sends high-quality digital audio via a single cable to your compatible Onkyo receiver’s Universal Port*. The same convenient cable also powers the tuner unit, saving on cable clutter. The tuner features 40 random presets for FM and AM stations, so there’s never any shortage of entertainment. Lastly, a rear-side Universal Port input gives you the option of “daisy chaining” a second compatible device, such as the new UP-A1 Onkyo Dock for the iPod. *Compatible models: TX-SR507, TX-SR577, TX-SR607, and later models from Onkyo’s 2009 A/V receiver range.
profile.reviewText:
While this does a perfectly good job of decoding HD radio and I have no complaints about the sound quality etc, I don't think Onkyo did a very good job making this integrate with the controls on the receiver or other devices that use the expansion port. I did not find the tuning controls to be very intuitive because they don't appear along with the normal FM tuning display. Instead you have to select "Port" and use different controls that aren't as consistent as they should be with the analog FM tuner controls.

The unit does have a "pass through" for the expansion port, but at least on my receiver this pass through is not "automatic". Basically you have to throw a physical switch on the HD tuner to pick whether you want the HD tuner connected to the receiver, or whatever other passthrough device (such as an iPod dock) connected to the receiver.

What it comes down to is that the integration of this accessory is far from seamless, so if you buy this tuner just don't expect it to be that way.
profile.summary: Receiver integration could be better

profile.description: The 7 Touchscreen Monitor for Raspberry Pi gives users the ability to create all-in-one, integrated projects such as tablets, infotainment systems and embedded projects. The 800 x 480 display connects via an adapter board which handles power and signal conversion. Only two connections to the Pi are required; power from the Pis GPIO port and a ribbon cable that connects to the DSI port present on all Raspberry Pis. Touchscreen drivers with support for 10-finger touch and an on-screen keyboard will be integrated into the latest Raspbian OS for full functionality without a physical keyboard or mouse. Turn your Raspberry Pi into a touch screen tablet, infotainment system, or standalone device. Truly Interactive - the latest software drivers will support a virtual on screen keyboard, so there is no need to plug in a keyboard and mouse. Make your own Internet of Things (IoT) devices including a visual display. Simply connect your Raspberry Pi, develop a Python script to interact with the display, and youre ready to create your own home automation devices with touch screen capability. A range of educational software and programs available on the Raspberry Pi will be touch enabled, making learning and programming easier on the Raspberry Pi.
profile.reviewText:
Not really happy with this touch screen on the RPi 3B. I ended up returning it. The problem is that it doesn't seem to pass enough power through to the RPi itself and I kept getting the lightning bolt low voltage warning. I didn't like the Pimorini frame either since it blocked the USB power out connector on the display. The frame also blocks 2 of the USB ports on the Pi itself.

The only good thing about this is that the GPIO pins are easy to get to. So, if you have an older Pi that doesn't need as much power (my problem could also have been caused by using the GPIO power pins instead of the USB out, USB in on both devices) or have a USB cable that will fit with the frame then maybe this is OK.

Basically this touch screen is more trouble than it's worth. I'd rather just use it headless with VNC and ssh. I probably won't bother with a touch screen again unless I need to mount it on the wall as a UI for something.
profile.summary: No good for RPi 3B and didn't like frame

profile.description: The Aputure Trigmaster is a premium-grade multi-function radio trigger for your flash, strobe and camera shutter. All you need to do is mount the transmitter onto the camera, speedlight flash or your studio strobe flash, to wirelessly control these devices. While in camera mode, the remote is able to do continuous shooting and bulb shooting (the lens remains open as long as you have your finger on the trigger button). The user receives one each of the following triggers TX1N (fits the Nikon D800E, D800, D700, D300, D200, D4, D3X, D3) TX3N (fits the Nikon D7100, D7000, D5200,D5100, D5000, D3200, D3100, D600, D90)
profile.reviewText:
I bought two bundles of two of these (four total) so I could use them as a remote shutter release and trigger 2 flashes. They come with cables that allow you to connect tranceivers to PC connector ports which is what I need to do "corded flash metering" with my light meter. When I got them I did some pretty thorough testing on them.

Unfortunately the PC cables in all four boxes are not designed to spec. The 2.5mm connectors that plug into the transceivers seem to actually be 2mm wide, and 12mm long (instead of 2.5mm wide 10mm long). This causes them to be too loose in the ports causing a really bad connection. If I try to use these cables then the transceivers trigger less than half the time. Pulling the connectors out slightly increases the success rate (apparently the extra 2mm of length, if nothing else, is causing a problem.)

These cables were bad in four different boxes, so this isn't a random manufacturing defect. It seems like they got a whole batch of cables from some bad supplier that weren't manufactured to the proper spec of 2.5mm wide and 10mm long. Apparently they didn't test them with their own connection ports before shipping them out.

I tested all of the cables with my camera, light meter, and all four tansceivers, so I know it isn't a device problem or a problem with the transceivers.

Luckily the 2.5mm to 3.5mm cables work just fine. The 2.5mm connectors on those are actually 2.5mm wide and 10mm long, and they fit very securely into the transceivers.

I contacted their support department about the PC cable problem via email, so we'll see how they handle it. I'll relate my experience and raise my rating to four stars if they fix it without too much trouble.

Aside from that problem, they work pretty well. I have no problem triggering the shutter or flashes as long as I'm using the 3.5mm cables and/or hot shoe connectors. The only things that I wish were different are that you have to hold down the remote's large button halfway and press the channel change button to manually trigger the flash. If you press the large button (shutter release button) it'll just try to trigger the shutter and do nothing if no transceiver is plugged into the shutter release port. This awkward way to trigger the flashes manually wouldn't be so bad except in situations where you need to do multi-flash exposures or otherwise fire the flashes manually for some reason, such as during long exposures. For the awkward manual triggering I'm subtracting one star. Most people may not care about this but I do a lot of multiflash and other manually fired flash exposures.

It's great that they have the 1/4-20 threaded hole in the bottom for mounting the transceivers on light stands with the right threaded post (same size used on tripods) but I really wish they had cold shoe mounts on the bottom also for stands that only have the cold shoe holder.

So aside from the included PC cables that are incompatible with the product they were included with, I think these are pretty good. Considering that they're almost double the price of the [[ASIN:B004YW79F4 Yongnuo RF-603s] though, it's rather disappointing that they come with bad PC cables and lack an easy manual/test firing button.

Last note: I bought the Nikon version. It seems that each transceiver comes in a different box with either the 10 pin shutter cable for the D300's etc, or the "GPS port" shutter cable for the D7000s and below. BUT they've been bundled in sets of two such that you get one of the boxes with the 10 pin, and another box with the GPS port cable. Therefore you get both cables and can use them with both types of connectors if you buy this set. If you buy an individual transceiver though you'll just get one cable or the other. So if you buy the transceivers individually, make sure at least one of them comes with the cable you need.
profile.summary: Included PC connector cables designed improperly

profile.description: Fujifilm FP-3000B is an instant black & white panchromatic film. This "peel-apart" film is ideal for ID photos, commercial photo proofs, medical & scientific applications, and image preview.
profile.reviewText:
BACKGROUND: I've been using this for exposure testing with Hasselblad and Mamiya (medium format) cameras. Yes, some people still use these things without digital backs, especially for educational purposes. For those who aren't familiar with pre-digital medium format photography, these cameras have backs that contain the film which can be removed from the camera without exposing the film. Unlike a 35mm, you can put some instant film into a "polaroid back", load a roll of 120 negative film into a 120 film back, put the polaroid back on the camera to get some instant feedback as to whether your setup is working, take two shots, then switch the back to the 120 for taking the real photos. This was particularly important when you had multiple thousands of dollars invested in a studio setup for a several hour shoot and you needed some assurance that your camera and settings were working properly. You could then switch the backs again when something changed without wasting all of your unused film. This also allowed people to change the ISO on cameras without wasting film before digital sensors. At this point you hopefully have new appreciation for how the average consumer with a $100 camera can now switch ISO settings at will and view their photos immediately.

ACTUAL REVIEW: The FP-3000B works well for what I'm using it for. Using a Sekonic exposure chart, I took a +/- 1 stop 3 shot bracket of the chart with this film to help me calibrate my light meter for the film/camera and test the exposure latitude of the film. The chart basically has gray patches with 50% reflectance in the middle with patches going down and up +/- 2 stops in reflectance in 1/6th stop increments. When properly exposed, the FP-3000B shows detail in the whole 4 stop range of the chart. Given that the lightest patch shows up as barely darker than the white of the paper, and the darkest patch is very slightly lighter than total black, it's clear that the film has a 4 stop (4EV) exposure latitude which is pretty good.

So, if you're using a light meter, just make sure that the darkest significant areas are no more than -2EV from correct exposure and the lightest areas are no more than 2EV from correct and you should get detail everywhere. (If you don't have a dedicated light meter, take a (D)SLR and use the spot meter in that to meter a scene to give you a general idea of what parts of the scene are light or dark enough to render detail.

So, good stuff for fancy expensive medium-formay pro cameras, and no doubt just as good for "vintage" consumer cameras as well. Just don't get the nasty chemicals from the peel-off on your skin or clothing. That stuff is caustic and bleaches fabric.

Glad that Fuji is still making this stuff, even if they've killed off pretty much all other versions of the instant B&W film.
profile.summary: 4 stops exposure latitude and it's still being manufactured

profile.description: Sekonic RT-32 Radio Transmitter Module installs easily, enabling wireless, Selective Quad Triggering of PocketWizard-enabled electronic flash units up to 100' away. Radio Triggering Module RT-32 - The Radio Transmitter Module plugs directly into a built-in compartment behind the battery door. Compatible with both the L-358 and L-608 (also L-608CINE) and the older L-558 as well. The Transmitter module triggers the electronic flash units wirelessly as the meter takes a measurement. Channel ID's are easily selected through the meter's built-in software. (CH 1-16 Single Remote Triggering, CH 17-32 Remote control "Quad Triggering"), compatible with PocketWizard Digital Radio Slaves. No more tripping over synch cords, or fumbling with PC connectors. Compatible with all PocketWizard Digital Radio Receivers. You can also select through the meter's software, - Quad Triggering mode - which provides you with up to four zones of lighting control remotely. Now you can individually measure several flash units wirelessly with the touch of the meter's measuring button, without walking over to each light and turning them on or off. You can even trigger motor driven cameras from the meter. Part of the Digital Wireless Freedom system, the L-608, L-608CINE, L-358 and L-558 are wireless exposure meters and exposure makers.
profile.reviewText:
I wasn't going to buy this thing because it used to cost something like $120 and I normally use cheap Cactus triggers instead of the comparitively super expensive Pocket Wizards, but I started using the studio facilities at school and all of their stuff is Pocket Wizard based. I found that trying to carry around both a full PW transmitter along with the light meter is a real pain whether or not they're connected with a sync cable or not.  Either both hands are full or one hand is fumbling with two unwieldy devices.

Still, I was not willing to spend over $100 for this. However this cumbersome situation was getting really annoying and I started looking around to see if I could find a better price. When I noticed that I could get the thing for $65 I was like "heck yea". I was pretty sure I was going to be using other people's Pocket Wizards enough that this would end up being worth it, even if I don't own any PWs myself.

So far I haven't done much more than test it a few times, but on the L-358 I'm using configuration is quick and easy, and it works. I wasn't able to tell from the documentation alone, but once installed it was immediately obvious that the channel configuration was essentially just another "mode" just like corded or uncorded flash are modes. So basically when you're flipping through modes with the dial and mode button, the channel configuration mode comes up one click before the actual transmit/meter mode. This means that there's no funky stuff with holding down multiple buttons and turning the dial, etc, so setting the channel is very quick, easy, and it's obvious how to do it. If you hand the meter to an assistant who's never seen it before and tell them how to switch the modes, it will be immediately obvious to them how to set the channel with little or no additional explanation.

While the transmitter is "only" supposed to have a 30m range as opposed to the 500m or whatever ridiculous range that the actual PW transmitters have, this is several times what I need for the tiny studio bays I'm normally limited to and it's probably enough for the majority of situations (but hey, I'm new to this so I don't really know how big sets might get). If you occasionally need more than a 30m range then you can always go back to using a regular transmitter at times, as annoying as it is. If you always need more range then perhaps this thing isn't so great. Note that the studio I'm using isn't large enough to test the range on this thing, and I'm not yet allowed to check out location kits that I can use outside, so I haven't been able to test the actual range of my unit. For all I know maybe it works from further away but just fails to trigger half the time when too far away or something.

If I had to pay $120 for this then I'd probably give it 3 stars just due to expense (though compared to the cost of PWs I guess it isn't that horrible), but for $65 the price no longer annoys me so much and it's an easy 5 stars.

Now if only they'd make some module like this for the Cactus or some other cheaper brand of trigger then I'd be thrilled. At least my Cactus transmitter is rather tiny and not as annoying to carry around cabled to the meter.
profile.summary: Extremely convenient even if only limited to pocketwizards

profile.description: The 4.3 Navi Sleeve from Lowepro offers a minimal, yet highly protective approach to protecting a GPS device. Its made of stretchy neoprene and reinforced inside both panels to provide extra protection from impact. Lowepro added a built-in microfiber cloth to protect and polish the delicate touchscreen, as well as soft, brushed tricot lining to safeguard the device from dust, scratches and abrasion. Dual, wrap-around zippers allow access to a GPS device from the top or bottom, plus make it easy to re-charge while its in the sleeve. Designed with an ultra-compact profile, the 4.3 Navi Sleeve neatly fits inside a glove compartment or center console of a vehicle.
profile.reviewText: I have a Lowepro camera bag and I'm quite happy with it, so I was pretty sure I was going to like the construction and protective value of this case. But how well would my new Garmin nvi 3490LMT fit? Well, I can say that it fits nicely. It looks like it could even handle something a little larger, though the case isn't too large for mine. It has plenty of padding like my camera bag, and also like my camera bag it has a microfiber flap of cloth inside for protecting the screen. Given how inexpensive it is, I really didn't expect it to be made as well as my $100 camera bag but it is! I'm glad that I bought this instead of any of the cases Garmin sells because this one has much better protection value which is important, especially since my particular GPS model has a glass screen. I'm not planning to test it, but I'm pretty sure I could drop this thing at least 3' onto concrete and any GPS inside would be undamaged. As a bonus, this case is also a lot less expensive than the official Garmin cases. Anyway, get this case! If your GPS has a 4.3" screen and isn't from 10 years ago then it's very likely going to fit given the extra space it has with my 3490 in it. This Lowepro is the best case I could find after some extensive searching and I'm not the least bit disappointed.
profile.summary: Perfect for my Garmin nuvi 3490 and probably almost anything.

profile.description: The Dremel 225 Flex Shaft Attachment has a flexible, 36-inch shaft that attaches easily and adds an improved level of versatility to your project. The quick connect attach system allows you to easily attach the flex-shaft to your Dremel rotary tool. A 5 bend radius provides more flexibility and fits comfortably in our hand. The integrated shaft lock button allows on the hand piece allows you to easily change your accessory or attachment. The Flex-Shaft holds up to 1/8 shank, and works with both the collet system and the Dremel chuck.
profile.reviewText: I own the Dremel 8000-03 Cordless which is only 14oz. I partly bought it because I wanted a relatively light tool for small work. Most of the usefulness of the flex shaft attachment is in reducing the weight of what you have to hold in your hand for detail work, so this attachment isn't quite as useful to me as it would be if I had one of the corded models that weights twice as much. I bought it anyway, along with the Dremel 575 Right Angle Attachment just so I'd have it around in case I needed to get in to tighter spaces or needed further "weight reduction" over holding the tool itself in one hand. If I were using a corded model it would be absolutely essential for me for what I do. Because it isn't something that I normally need, I haven't used it that much and probably won't use it routinely, so I can't properly speak to its durability. (I usually go back and update these reviews after a while though to update people on that.) But in my testing it feels very sturdy and solid and so I feel confident in its ability to hold up when maintained properly. (Not stored so that it bends at sharp angles, greased at intervals as specified in the manual, etc.) It seems to have no problem working with the Dremel 4486 Keyless Chuck. Attaching and removing the flex drive from the tool itself it is similar to attaching and removing the right angle attachment (you need to replace the collet nut or chuck on the rotary tool with a "drive" adapter that the cable slots into) both of which are pretty easy. I am not entirely sure if it's OK to attach the right angle adapter to the handheld part of the flex shaft as it seems like together they may create too much friction on the drive and thus possibly too much additional load on the motor. (Remember these rotary tools power accessories based on speed, not on torque. High speed low torque often does not deal with too much continuous load very well.) Anyone who knows if this is considered OK or who has long term experience using both together please post a comment. A couple of things that you must keep in mind when using this: 1) You really do want to hang the tool up above where you're working when you're using this flex thing. I can't say exactly why, but most likely it has to do with keeping the amount of friction low (increased when more of the shaft is curved vs straight) and keeping the shaft from bending at too sharp of an angle. If you have the Dremel 220-01 Work Station drill press type thing then that comes with an extendable hanger but I can't see any good reason to buy that thing just to get a hanger. In fact almost anyone could come up with something much less expensive and more secure than using the hanger on that. Screw an eye screw into the ceiling and hang it from a rope or run a "clothesline" across your work area and hang it on a couple of "S" hooks, or something. If you don't hang the tool I doubt the shaft is going to shred itself immediately but I'm sure it won't last as long, will be more likely to get damaged by an accidental sharp bend, and won't be able to run at as high of a speed due to the increased friction. 2) NOTE! In case you miss the little note in the box, you really do want to run this thing at high speed for a couple of minutes with it hung straight down and no accessory attached. It'll make some disconcerting little ticking sounds at first but those will stop after several seconds. I suspect the point of this is that you want to evenly distribute the grease inside the shaft before running it while bent or otherwise doing any real work. Again, I doubt you'll shred the thing if you don't do this, but at the very least you might have a little trouble with your grinding, etc, for a minute if you try to use it immediately since it's going to distribute grease or otherwise break itself in when first used no matter what. It really will run at 35,000RPM and it really is OK to run it like this for two minutes straight without doing anything. It won't whip around or anything so this is pretty safe. (My cats weren't even that afraid of it while it was doing this.) 3) You will need to grease the thing at periodic intervals as the manual says or you will eventually shred the flexible cable inside the jacket. The grease you use for this is as common as dirt at auto parts stores though. So in short, this attachment is pretty important if you want to use a heavier model of a dremel in one hand. The other option in this case is to buy an additional smaller rotary tool for one-handed use but you'll probably end up with less power for more money if you take that option. If you already have a light tool that you can hold in one hand for a sufficient time without much trouble then you might want to hold off on buying this until the need arises. But in any case, this is a solid quality attachment that you'll likely be very happy with if and when you do have a use for it.
profile.summary: For detail work with heavier Dremel models

profile.description: This is a bulk 5 set of a 10 exposure pack of glossy Instant Color Film FP-100C/FP 100C from Fuji. It is a peel-apart-type instant color film with an ISO speed rating of 100. Its ability to produce photos of superb quality makes this film ideal for a wide range of commercial uses, including product photography requiring long exposures, microphotography, CRT image recording, and of course identification and portrait photography. This film, in regular size, can be used in cameras and other photographic equipment that accept instant film with a photo size of 85 x 108mm, and those provided or fitted with an instant camera back.
profile.reviewText:
I'm not going to write the usual review here, because lets face it.... people don't buy this format of instant film anymore just to get photos with the best image quality or the cheapest photos. Though perhaps some customers would be owners of legacy systems that still need this film to keep doing what they've been doing, if you're reading this then you're most likely interested in film photography for some sort of artistic reason.

I originally bought this stuff for test exposures using Polaroid backs for Hasselblad and Mamiya medium format cameras, but later I decided to buy an old 1967 Polaroid 250 Land Camera off of eBay for $60 to see what I could do with whatever of this film is still being made. Best purchase ever!

In the process of messing around I found that people were able to actually reclaim the negatives from these peel-apart films by using household bleach to dissolve the opaque black anti-halation coating on the non-emulsion side of the negative. (The negative is the part that you peel off and normally throw away because once it's been exposed to light and transferred its dye to the print its intended job is done. The thing is that it still has a negative image and you can still use it in an enlarger or film scanner if you can just get the thick black coating off the other side of it.)

So now I basically take some shots on these, keep the negatives rather than toss them out, let them dry, then use bleach to remove the anti-halation coating on them. To see the process, do a search for "Fuji FP-100C Negative Reclamation". There are a bunch of videos on youtube and there's no generally agreed-upon "right way" to do it.

The best tips aren't well documented anywhere I know of, so here's what I've learned so far:

- Using Clorox High Efficiency Bleach Gel or some sort of similar "gel" type bleach works much better than regular bleach, but you can use standard laundry bleach or even bleach-based cleaners like Tilex Mold & Mildew Remover as long as the cleaner contains a high concentration of bleach. Stuff like Goo Gone, Goof Off, etc does not work.

- If you want to get all artistic, you can use a paintbrush to brush the bleach gel on certain areas of the black coating, wait, then rinse the dissolved area away to get interesting borders around the negative. As you might imagine, other techniques are possible as well.

- People use various methods for keeping the bleach off of the emulsion, but I find that if you slap the thing emulsion side down on a wet piece of glass and squeeze the water out from under it (sticking it to the glass) then it's rather hard for the bleach to get under the negative to damage the emulsion. Just make sure to start rinsing the bleach off from the middle of the negative so you don't flush water, and bleach, under the negative while you're trying to rinse the top off.

- you MUST let the negative dry before doing anything, otherwise the emulsion comes off too easily.

- After you initially let it dry, it seems that it's probably better to remove the black coating before washing the excess developer reagent "goop" off of the emulsion side. So use bleach, wash black stuff off, then wash the emulsion side off to remove any excess goop. Assuming you let the negative dry after peeling it off the print, you should be able to rub the emulsion with your finger under running water to get the reagent goop off.

- Bleach will definitely cause the emulsion to come off. You can intentionally apply bleach around the edge of the emulsion to cause this to happen in a somewhat controlled manner to get a border effect or whatever.

- After rinsing the negative off really well, it's best to dip it in photoflo to prevent streaking/bubbling during the drying. I actually don't have any photoflo so I've been messing with Finish Jet-Dry Drying Agent, Turbo Dry which is a very similar non-ionic surfactant.

After all of this is done, you have a negative that you can use in a scanner, enlarger, contact print, etc. The quality isn't exactly perfect but it's better than you'd probably think.

Have fun! I hope Fuji keeps making this stuff!
profile.summary: this + $60 camera + bleach = fun!
