profile.description: Protect your touchscreen against scratches and scrapes with Alpha Glass for Samsung Galaxy S7 Fortified, anti-shatter glass defends your display  reactive touch retains sensitivity. Plus, you get options: Crystal Clear for immaculate clarity, or Privacy Glass for ultimate discretion.
profile.reviewText:
This is the easiest screen protector I have ever installed. Unlike film protectors which cling and trap air, this stiff glass cover just dropped right into place on my first try. Others have complained about the black bars at the top and bottom of the screen - these  made it easier for me to align it correctly. Match the black screen protector bans to the black bars at the top and bottom of the phone screen and the clear spots for the back button and screens button fall right where they need to.

The cover does not go right up to the edge of the screen. However, none of the film covers I've had for this phone or others do that.
This seems typical to me, and not something I'd comment on except that other reviewers have complained about it. I'm not using an Otterbox case, but have a silicone sleeve case. The screen protector works fine with the edges of the case that slightly curve around the front of my phone.

The protector is clear, responsive and sturdy. Unlike other non-matte screens I've used, fingerprints are also not too obvious. I will need to use it for a while to know how it holds up. The only odd part is that in the middle of the screen there's an odd rainbow effect. Wavy colored lines are apparent and they move (but never go away) when I press on the cover. The good news is that these are only visible when the phone is off. They don't show up when the screen is lit and I'm using it. Seems to be some effect of glass-on-glass.

I received this cover in exchange for an honest review; if I were buying my own screen protector, I might pass this one by due to price.
profile.summary: Easy to install; weird rainbow effect appears

profile.description: Samsung 32 inch LED monitor, glossy white finish, 19201080 resolution. Tilt stand, gaming mode, wall mountable.
profile.reviewText: This is the 3rd Samsung monitor that I have had the pleasure of reviewing over the last couple of months. Here is the list. This 32" flat panel = Samsung 32" Screen LED-Lit Monitor Glossy White (LS32F351FUNXZA) 32" curved (previous review) = Samsung 32" Screen LED-Lit Monitor Curved Glossy White (LC32F391FWNXZA) 27" curved (previous review) = Samsung 27" Screen LED Lit Monitor Curved Silver (LC27F591FDNXZA) This review will compare and contrast the three monitors. I will refer to the monitors as the 32" flat, 32" curved, and 27" curved. To see the other monitors and reviews follow the AMazon links below: "Samsung LC32F391FWNXZA" for the 32" curved Samsung CF391 Series LC32F391FWNXZA 32" Screen LED-Lit Monitor "Samsung LS32F351FUNXZA" for the 32" flat Samsung 32" Screen LED-Lit Monitor, Glossy White (LS32F351FUNXZA) "Samsung LC27F591FDNXZA" for the 27" curved Samsung CF591 Series Curved 27" LED-lit Monitor (LC27F591FDNXZA) To summarize the reviews of all three monitors in case you are in a hurry. 1. The 32" curved is great, superb, excellent, and recommended; skip Starbucks for two weeks and buy the curved over the 32" flat. The monitor is bright, sharp, crisp, and with reduced eye strain. The curve may seem like a gimmick but trust me it is not; once you start using a curved monitor you will not want to go back to a flat panel. 2. The 32" flat is very very very good, and recommended second. It is bright, sharp, crisp, meets all of the superlatives of the 32" curved except it is flat. Very very very good monitor. 3. The 27" curved is very very good, and recommended third. It is bright, sharp, crisp, meets all of the superlatives of the 32" curved, it is curved, just smaller. Very very good monitor. In the box. See the attached photos taken as I unpacked the 32" flat box. Also included are images showing the monitors side by side for comparison. Optics. All three monitors are aesthetically pleasing. The attached pictures show the relative size of the monitors and the 1800R curvature of the two curved monitors; 1800R means that the monitor curve represents an arc of a circle with radius of 1800 millimeters (1.8 meters) - so assuming you are sitting 1.8 m from the monitor midpoint the entire surface of the monitor is equidistant from your eyes. The large screen sizes make all three monitors easy to read. Monitor color. The two 32" monitors that I have reviewed are both bright white in color. They are both showing a little dust but I am not a neat person so not really concerned. The 27" is a silver tone; hides dirt much better. I am not a neat freak but will dust the monitors every 3 months or so. Dual monitors. I have put the 32" flat and 32" curved on my desk; I would rather have two curved but the 32" curved/flat fit nicely together, have a common bezel size, and a common tilt range. The 27" curved is obviously smaller and works well on its own; its bezel size is slightly different from the 32" monitors. The 27" is on another desk in the house. Monitor adjustment. All three monitors can be adjusted in tilt only. The monitors do not offer a height adjustment. Resolution. All three monitors have a maximum resolution of 1920 x 1080 in a 16:9 ratio; this is the equivalent of 1080 HD. The 32" monitors have a slightly larger pixel pitch (distance between pixels) than the 27" making the 32" monitors slightly "grainier" than the 27". I upgraded from two 24" Dell monitors; it took me about a day to adjust to the new 32" monitors. The only people I can see this affecting is graphics specialists such as designers, photo specialists, CAD designers, and the like who really require precision control. None of these monitors are designed for that purpose so if you fit one of those categories just be moving on. "Immersive" monitor. The 32" curved is truly "immersive"; the curve takes the monitor out to the periphery of my vision and I can take in my entire Windows desktop at the same time. The 27" curved was good but the 32" curved does it for me. The slight curvature reduces eye strain (at least for me) by allowing the eye to maintain focus at a fixed distance while you scan the display. I wear glasses and the 32" curved, at an ergonomic distance (1800R), fills my eyeglass from the frame on the left to the frame on the right. The curvature keeps you from having to adjust eye focus as you scan across the screen(s); this is really helpful at reducing eye strain with multiple monitors. The 32" flat panel also provides a wide field of view but the desktop is limited when the edges of the monitor go out of the focus range of my eyes. Applications. I opened MS-Office apps, Solidworks CAD, Nikon ViewNX image editor, and a DVD and had great visuals on all three monitors. This is more a function of my laptop (Lenovo L430 Thinkpad) video card than the monitor, but the images were crisp with excellent contrast and there were no artifacts in the image that I could say were the cause of the monitor. The colors were bright and vivid to my eyes. I do not play video games so I cannot comment on how the monitor works there. All three screens are glossy but have been fine to work with beside a bright window in my office - see photos below. Video Inputs. The three monitors all have different video inputs. All three monitors come with an HDMI cable in the box. The 32" curved and 27" curved monitors accept DisplayPort and HDMI inputs; the 27" also has a VGA (15-pin D-sub) analog input. The 32" flat accepts two HDMI inputs. These monitors are NOT compatible with Macs that use the Thunderbolt video interface. However, if the computer/video game/ etc has an HDMI output plug it in and it will work; any device with HDMI interface works. Speakers. The 27" curved includes internal speakers that sound about as good as any monitor speakers can. The 32" monitors do not include internal speakers. The 32" curved has audio in/out jacks so that you can route an audio cable from your computer to the monitor then plug speakers/headphones into the monitor. The 32" flat does not include audio jacks. Power. All three monitors include a power brick; the 27" curved power brick is rated for 35 W; the 32" flat power brick is also 35 W; the 32" curved monitor power brick is rated for 45 W. The power supplies accept 100-240 VAC input and provide 14 VDC output. The power brick ratings are approximately 35% higher than what the monitors require when operating so there is plenty of safety margin; actual and standby power consumption are much less than these values; see user's manuals on Samsung website for additional details. The power bricks connect to the monitor using an ~ 3' long power cord with a small circular connector attached. The power bricks connect to a wall outlet with a ~3' long cable terminated using a right angle, unpolarized, two prong plug. Unpolarized means that the plug can be inserted into the wall outlet either up or down; the prongs are the same width whereas the outlet slots have one slot smaller than the other. Two prong means that the power brick is not grounded. Do NOT freak out over this; the monitor is still perfectly safe; more than half the world uses ungrounded power outlets. All this means is that you can go anywhere in the world, plug in the monitor and it will work. Base stand. The monitors come with a base stand to hold the monitor in place. The angle of the monitors towards or away from the user can be slightly adjusted however the height of the display cannot. The monitor bases are circular and reasonably heavy to keep the monitor in place and prevent it tipping over. The base of the 27" monitor is about 8.25" in diameter and sticks out ~4" in front of the center of the monitor. The base of the 32" monitors are about 9.5" in diameter and stick out ~4.5" in front of the center of the monitor. In a review of the 27" monitor one individual complained that he couldn't get his keyboard close enough to the screen; I do not see that as a concern with proper ergonomics taken into account. Cable clip. The 27" monitor has a neat little cable clip running up the rear post of the base which provides good strain relief for the power and video cables. The 32" monitors do not provide this clip; annoying. VESA mounting (wall and swing arm mounting). The 32" monitors comes with 75mm X 75mm (3" x 3") threaded mounting holes for a VESA wall or swing arm mount. The 27" monitor does not come equipped for VESA mounting. See attached photos and 32" monitor user's manuals on the Samsung site. Control Interface. All three monitors have the same control interface through a small joystick on the lower back right of the monitors. Pressing in on the joystick turns the monitor on. A menu is displayed if the joystick is pressed while the monitor is on; one option here is to power off the monitor. A second option in the menu is to cycle through the monitor inputs; DisplayPort, HDMI, VGA (27" only). The third menu option allows you to adjust the picture, onscreen display, system, and review monitor information. I had some ghosting issues with the 27" curved monitor as delivered, it was also way too bright, so I tweaked those values and everything was great; see my review of the 27" monitor to look up the settings. The 32" monitors had perfect color and focus right out of the box and required no adjustment. Freesync. I do not have AMD Freesync Technology available on my laptop therefore I did not attempt to use any of its features. I have read that not all of the three monitors are actually equipped with Freesync so if you need or want this feature double check before you buy. Upshot: I like all three monitors. Best is the 32" curved; next is the 32" flat; next is the 27" curved. Don't get me wrong - if the 27" was all that I could afford I would buy it. The negative things about the monitors are really not that bad - in fact, negatives are hard to find. The positive good things about the monitors are great. The screen sizes, at three price points, are excellent. Update - look at the prices of each monitor. The 32" curved is less than $25 more than the 27" curved; cut out the morning latte for a week and buy the 32" curved - you will be happy.
profile.summary: Excellent Monitor for General Office and Home Use

profile.description: BLOK Protective Keyboard Case for iPad Air 2 provides drop protection from as high as 6 ft. onto concrete. BLOK iPad case is made of an absorbent polymer structure that supports iPad upon impact and BLOK's square corners are packed with extra polymers to give iPad more protection where it needs it most, the corners. BLOK iPad keyboard case is the all in one iPad case, with a wireless detachable keyboard, any angle stand and cover, it has all the versatility that you need in an iPad case
profile.reviewText:
Up until a month ago my old iPad was working fine and met my requirements for a tablet. It was slow, had no memory, but it worked for email and surfing so it was all I needed. Then I dropped it. Cover glass shattered. End of old iPad. If I had one of these BLOK Keyboard cases for that iPad I would still be using it today. I have now upgraded to an iPad Air 2. Worth a few more bucks. Worth more to protect it.

This keyboard case will protect. It is solid. Rock solid. It will be too heavy for a lot of folks at 1.2 lbs; the iPad Air 2 weighs in at just under 1 lb. You are more than doubling the weight of your portable device.

I have already dropped my new iPad on a hardwood floor; case is scuffed, iPad is fine. Keyboard seems flimsy compared to iPad side of case but no worse than I have seen on earlier Logitech Bluetooth Keyboard/Case combinations. The keyboard is magnetically attached to iPad side so you can pop it off or leave it on and use the flexible joint to keep the two attached. The keyboard is (or seems) slightly smaller than a desktop so you have to adjust when typing - easy to get used to. Standard Apple keyboard shortcuts work - call the Apple "command key" the Windows "control key" and you can pretend it is a Windows keyboard (copy = CTRL-C, paste = CTRL-V, etc.). Does not have a backwards delete key but there is a keystroke combination that I will eventually look up.

The prop up stand on the back of the iPad needs to be broken in (moved back and forth a dozen or so times) to loosen it up - it will not go back far enough until you do. The stand magnetically snaps to the back of the iPad side so it is not flapping around when you are trying to carry it - I like that a lot.

Uses two CR2032 batteries. These are the 25 cent size flat batteries that are available at any pharmacy or hardware store. It comes with qty 2 batteries installed. Just pull out the yellow tab to apply power to the keyboard. The keyboard has a tiny power switch on the front left hand EDGE. Make sure that is showing GREEN to turn the keyboard is ON. That is the switch that you need to get the Bluetooth hooked up to the iPad. Bluetooth connection was so easy I have already forgotten how to do it. If you have hooked Bluetooth up before it is easy. If you have never done it, read the quick start guide and you should be connected within 5 minutes.

I think it provides great protection for my iPad but probably would not buy one for myself. Too expensive to call it a good value.
profile.summary: LOGIcal Protection at a Cost

profile.description: Make your best work even better with Corel AfterShot Pro 3 Photo Editing Software for PC. Manage and edit your RAW photos with this powerful and ultra-fast photo editor. With no importing required, conveniently store and organize all your photos in one place. Load, select, edit and output your photos quickly, with powerful batch processing with controls and presets that allow you to edit one or thousands of photos at once. Watermark, correct, remove blemishes and more with time-saving integrated tools. Image presets automate tedious and repetitive processing work. Correct distortions introduced by different lenses with built-in support, or share and import new lens corrections with the AfterShot Pro community on Facebook.
profile.reviewText:
My husband and I picked up a Nikon DSLR prior to a China vacation in 2014. The D3200 is a low end Nikon equipped with a 24.2 Mpixel sensor, 11-point auto-focus, native ISO 100 - 6400 (extended to 12800), 12-bit RAW files. I have not attached any images processed by this software because, for lack of a better term, Aftershot Pro 3 does not appear to support Nikon cameras. Or if it does support Nikon cameras it is a well-kept secret.

Note: we are neither professional nor overenthusiastic amateur photographers. We try not to use Auto or Scene Modes preferring to set shutter speed and f-stop ourselves; this does not work a lot of the time. We do take a lot of pictures bracketing the image and delete the ones that are fuzzy or obviously damaged. All our images are stored in 12-bit NEF and high resolution jpeg. Coming off the camera the combined images are approximately 30 to 36 MB.

The AfterShot Pro 3 (ASP3) software comes in a square cardboard CD envelope. Opening envelope finds it empty except for a coupon sized piece of paper. The paper identifies website for software download and license key for installation. I used Chrome to reach the website and downloaded the appropriate software version (versions available for 64-bit Mac, 64-bit Linux RPM, 64-bit Linux Debian, and 64-bit Windows) then started the install (on Win just run the file by doubleclicking). I do not know if the license key allows you to download, install, and run versions of more than one operating system.

I am running 64-bit Windows v10 Pro on a Lenovo L430 Thinkpad. After hitting OK a couple times to get past Win v10 security block and select installation directory the next window I saw was installation complete. No problems with the installation of ASP3 on Windows. I hope the same is true for anyone purchasing the program.

Immediately after ASP3 download your browser loads ASP3 Welcome and Resources page. There are Getting Started videos, the pdf User Guide, and links to Video Tutorials. Again works fine and website looks good.

When you start ASP3 for the first time you are asked where to put your config files and downloaded images. During this part of the installation pay very close attention before you automatically hit OK on file/directory locations; think carefully about what you want where particularly if you want your existing images to be used with ASP3. This is your one chance to organize your images otherwise you will end up with a mish mash and ASP3 database files popping up all over the place. The default config folder is located under your user profile directory; you are warned that this set of files/folders is going to get quite large and are given the option to move the folder elsewhere. ASP3 recommends that this folder be placed on a "large, fast drive". The images catalog is created under your Pictures library; it too can be relocated during install.

Note: this is our introduction to image processing. This review is primarily based on what the Corel ASP3 help page and videos can teach two novices in a reasonable amount of time.

The instructional videos keep talking about "workflow." It takes a beginner a while to finally figure out that this means "index your images then play with them (adjust exposure, filtering, color palette)." I am reasonably up on technology but it still took awhile to realize that the image data parameters were all going into an ASP3 database. The keyword here is "database"; ASP3 is a "Non-Destructive Editor" (NDE). My understanding of this follows. You copy or move images off of camera onto your hard drive (I don't know if ASP3 helps with that or not). You then "import" the images into the ASP3 database; import means data about the images not the images themselves. The actual image files stay exactly where you copied them. If you decide to edit the image, say brighten exposure then turn it black and white, a copy is made of the original image, edits are made to the copy, and each edit/change to the image is recorded in the ASP3 database. By keeping track of each change the ASP3 database becomes a large undo/redo system; undo and it goes from black and white to color, undo and exposure is darkened. If you do edit the image and are happy with it you must "Export" the image; there is no "Save" or "Save As" (confusing until you get the hang of the ASP3 terminology). Once you export the image the copy that you edited is now "saved (?)" and you can keep the changes you made; I had a bit of trouble figuring out where the "Exported" images went; I think ASP3 fooled me and they were in the same directory as the original files with a different file name. Note: there is only a limited number of image file types that can be exported; TIFF and JPG being the most recognizable. If you forget to export - bye-bye edits. Note that while doing all this the original image stays untouched, exactly the same as when you copied it off the camera, so you can always go back and start from scratch. I could not figure out if you did steps ABCDE and exported, if you could then go back to C and do XY (ABCXY) then export again. My guess is that you have to go back to the very beginning and do ABC then XY. ABC could be saved as a "Preset" to make it faster.

I reviewed the Getting Started video while following along in the software. As the video played I would pause it and try what I had just seen. Less than a minute into the video and the guy did something without showing how to do it or was going so fast that you couldn't follow what happened. The user manual solved that first problem, regardless, extremely frustrating for a beginner. I continued on to another video to try and learn how to "install" my Nikon camera. Typing "install camera" into the ASP3 help search function came up with nothing. A google came up with an instructional video on the Corel website. The video consists of the same professional photographer zipping through a directory tree on his workstation, clicking a button, and saying voila. It works just great for his Fuji camera where the configuration files are preloaded on his computer. The only reference he makes to configuration files not being there (aka my Nikon) is to "log your [feedback] request directly to the Aftershot Pro dev team"; I assume that they will get back to you.

Not supporting Nikon out of the box pretty much sealed the deal for me. If Corel cannot support a very common Nikon camera I am not going to waste my time any further. I would be happy to hear from Corel should they generate instructions more suitable to beginners and support my DSLR. In the mean time I will use the Nikon ViewNX software that I have been for the last three years. It is a clunky piece of software but it supports my cameras in a simple straightforward manner. It creates sequenced folders, gets images off my camera, renames the files, and copies them to a back up drive. ASP3 may offer this functionality; I don't know, maybe it comes when it installs my camera. ViewNX offers most of the image editing tools offered by ASP3 but without a lot of the batch processing and fancy NDE (non-destructive editing) capability. I simply make a copy of an image in a new directory, edit the copy, then hit "Save"; no fancy undo/redo (I think) but I don't process many images.

There is a ton of functionality in the ASP3 software. Unfortunately for newcomers the resources to teach how it all fits together is not there. I am sure if you spend enough time you will figure out all sorts of cool things. I would rate 4 for professional capability - it can do a lot (I can understand what is being accomplished in the support videos but they do not slow down enough to teach it to you, rate 3 for not supporting my camera out of the box, and rate 2 for lack of explanatory material geared towards new users. Overall a 3.
profile.summary: Lots of features for professionals processing lots of images; Amateurs not so much

profile.description: This brushed twill hanging toiletry kit features mesh, TPU, and zippered compartments. The elastic straps hold items in place and the hanger fits over most hooks and towel bars. It also zips fully closed
profile.reviewText: The Hanging Toiletry kit is neatly organized with sufficient pockets and pouches to hold your items. The twill fabric is dense but it did absorb some water when I ran it under a tap. There is one large mesh zippered pocket inside the kit; all other pockets are of clear vinyl fully stitched along three edges. Over time, with water splashes and condensation, I would expect mold growth; no cleaning instructions accompany the kit. The kit is neatly single stitched (exception zippers are double stitched) with bright orange piping used throughout. All pockets are slightly bellowed making it easy to place three dimensional items inside. The hook is of medium size and has a small pocket to stow it when the kit is closed; this prevents the hook from catching or puncturing your items.
profile.summary: Neat Organization But How Do You Clean It?

profile.description: TRENDnet's Wi-Fi Baby Cam, model TV-IP743SIC, allows you to monitor your baby from any internet connection. After a brief installation, simply open a web browser or app to view live video on your mobile devices, tablets, and computers. TRENDnet's free Cloud View app brings live video to Apple and Android mobile devices. Hear and comfort your baby with the built in microphone and speaker. See your baby in complete darkness with night vision (5 meters, 16 ft.). Setup motion and sound detection to receive video clips via email. Easy Setup - Quick intuitive guided installation. Remote Monitoring - Live video on your mobile devices, tablets, and computers from any internet connection. Two-Way Audio - Hear and comfort your baby with the built in microphone and speaker. Night Vision - See your baby in complete darkness with night vision (5 m, 16 ft.) Free App - See live video on a mobile device with free Apple and Android apps. Motion and Sound Detection Emails - Receive snapshots and video clips (up to 15 seconds) of detected motion and sound via email. Mounting Base - Adjustable mounting base for flat and vertical surfaces. Digital Zoom - Zoom in by a factor of four. Recording - Record video to a remote storage device. Wireless - Requires a home wireless network in order to function. Automatic Updates - Convenient new firmware alerts.
profile.reviewText:
Free product reviewed under Amazon Vine.

This is a fun product, until you try to delve deep into the set up or use Windows v10. I had upgraded to Windows v10 halfway through this review. The camera went from partially working to not working; I have added more to my support ticket and will wait to hear what the verdict is on Win v10.

The camera is relatively easy to get onto your WiFi network offering either WPS or manual set up. I am used to the old manual set up method so I reset the camera, powered it on, and waited until it established its own WiFi network by acting as a hotspot for a new "TrendNet" WiFi network. I disconnected my iPad from my home network and connected to the camera network. Logged into camera, stepped through the set up pages, and once I had entered my network parameters into the camera, rebooted/power cycled the camera, and the camera was on my network. I then switched my iPad back to my network, logged in and completed the camera set up. The camera is fun to play with. I thought it was broken at first because it only showed black and white. It turns out that my stair landing is too dark for colour photography so the camera went into infrared mode. One of the cats loves it - she walks right up to the camera and stares into it with vividly glowing eyes under the IR lighting. No real problem getting the basics to work. Oh - do not bother to get Chrome browser on a PC working. It doesn't seem to be compatible with the camera viewing plug in so just do not bother. I think the browser is hit and miss. On a PC use Internet Explorer. On an iPad use Safari. Otherwise there were too many permutations and combinations to try so I am not going through every one myself. Good luck.

It appears that if you are running Windows v10 you are out of luck; I was unable to get either the MS-Edge browser or the Chrome browser to show any video. The camera has a troubleshooting mode that will take a snapshot - this worked without problems. You are asked to install a couple of plugins to get MS-Edge to display video. I learned that you must reboot the computer, do not open Chrome, go to MS-Edge, delete the plugins first, then install them. Without doing this you would end up going around in circles.

Follow up. TrendNET indicated that they will not be updating their plugins to support Chrome or Microsoft Edge. Chrome is a deal breaker for me. I will not be able to use the camera.

OK, now for the two signature features; camera over the web and recording following motion detection. The camera over the web was setup quickly and worked on Win v8.1. It basically gives you a web address based on your camera serial number, you go to the site and see the video. No problem setting up application on Android phones. Do not have iPhones so you will have to check yourself. Did not check video to email functionality because of what follows.

Web functionality to PC and iPad died with Windows v10 - I am not sure how as the camera should go straight to the web and not through my PC. Weird; likely a configuration problem in the camera but at this point I was trying to get any video to my PC let alone worry about the Web. Web functionality continues to work on Android app. This is because TrendNET no longer supports Chrome on Win v10.

Now the bonus feature, setting up the camera to detect motion and record it. I carefully followed the instructions and no matter what I tried it would not work. I was able to set up the motion detection area on the camera display. When I walked in front the camera would flash that it was recording but the recording would last 10 to 15 seconds before stopping. No video files ever showed up in the designated folder of my server or PC. I tried saving files to my PC, my husband's PC, our file server; no luck. Finally contacted TrendNet tech support. I have been through two support reps and am now working with a third. We have exchanged several emails and screenshots of configurations without success so far. I did not try recording to server since Win v10 but again I am not sure what the problem is there.

My server is brand new, runs on UPS power, has operated 72 days without a fault, is used for the exact same file system as the camera (SMB/CIFS), runs the latest open source software (FreeNAS), and has 12 TB of RAID storage, I have verified every configuration that I can think of and tried copying other files and other videos into the exact same directories created for the camera, and the server has never even so much as burped.

I believe I have tried every permutation and combination of camera configuration on the "Action (stored video setup page in the camera)" without success; camera with and without server account, camera with existing server share; camera with dedicated server share; camera account with and without password; camera with and without folders/subfolders. Can't think of anything more.

Fun product - Configuration Problems - Tech Support Working Hard
profile.summary: Fun Product - Configuration Problems - Tech Support Working Hard

profile.description: 1800R curved monitor with 3000:1 contrast ratio provides a truly immersive viewing experience on a beautiful 32 screen. Featuring a glossy white design, the monitor boasts Game Mode technology which allows users to enjoy smooth images, even during the fastest moving scenes. With HDMI and Display Port inputs, you can easily connect any of your peripherals to enjoy on this Samsung monitor.
profile.reviewText:
This is a great monitor.

I have recently had the opportunity to review the 27" version of this monitor (Samsung CF591 Series Curved 27" LED-lit Monitor LC27F591FDNXZA). Pretty much everything from that review applies to this monitor. I will refer to the monitors as the 27" and 32" where I make a comparison between the two in this review. The pictures below should give a real sense of the difference in size between the two monitors.

The 32" is bright white; not my favorite choice in colors but as long as I don't touch it with greasy, Cheetos, hands it should be OK. In the pictures you can see that the bezel width is different on each of the screens. If you buy two 27"s or two 32"s this will not be a problem. Both monitors have a maximum resolution of 1920 X 1080 which makes a window across the monitor boundary two different sizes - get two monitors the same size and don't worry about it.

The 32" has a resolution is 1920 X 1080 across a rectangle of 27.5" X 15.5". This gives a pixel pitch of 0.014321".

For comparison, the 27" has the same resolution 1920 X 1080 across a rectangle of 23.5" X 13.2" giving a pixel pitch of 0.01226"

The difference in pixel pitch 0.014321" - 0.01226" = 0.002061" is a really small number but it separates the pixels enough that the 32" screen is slightly "grittier", very very slightly, than the 27" monitor. I replaced my existing 24" Dells with the 27" and 32" and while the larger pixels were noticeable at first I have adjusted and now have no problems with either display.

The 32" is truly "immersive"; the curve takes the monitor out to the periphery of my vision and I can take in my entire Windows desktop at the same time. The 27" was good but the 32" does it for me. I wear glasses and the 32", at an ergonomic distance, fills my eyeglass from the frame on the left to the frame on the right. The curvature keeps you from having to adjust eye focus as you scan across the screen(s); this is really helpful at reducing eye strain with multiple monitors.

I opened MS-Office apps, Solidworks CAD, Nikon ViewNX image editor, and a DVD and had great visuals. This is more a function of my laptop (Lenovo L430 Thinkpad) video card than the monitor, but the images were crisp with excellent contrast and there were no artifacts in the image that I could say we're the cause of the monitor. The colors were bright and vivid although that beauty is in the eye of the beholder. I do not play video games so I cannot comment on how the monitor works there. Both screens are glossy but have been fine to work with beside a bright window in my office - see photos below.

Both monitors come with an HDMI cable in the box. Both monitors accept DisplayPort and HDMI inputs; the 27" also has a VGA (15-pin D-sub) analog input.

Both monitors include a power brick; the 27" monitor power brick is rated for 35 W; the 32" monitor power brick is rated for 45 W. Both power supplies accept 100-240 VAC input and provide 14 VDC output. The power brick ratings are approximately 35% higher than what the monitors require when operating so there is plenty of safety margin; actual and standby power consumption are much less than these values; see user's manuals on Samsung website for additional details. The power bricks connect to the monitor using an ~ 3' long power cord with a small circular connector attached. The power bricks connect to a wall outlet with a ~3' long cable terminated using a right angle, unpolarized, two prong plug. Unpolarized means that the plug can be inserted into the wall outlet either up or down; the prongs are the same width whereas the outlet slots have one slot smaller than the other. Two prong means that the power brick is not grounded. Do NOT freak out over this; the monitor is still perfectly safe; more than half the world uses ungrounded power outlets. All this means is that you can go anywhere in the world, plug in the monitor and it will work.

The monitors come with a base stand to hold the monitor in place. The angle of the monitors towards or away from the user can be slightly adjusted; the height of the display cannot. The monitor bases are circular and reasonably heavy to keep the monitor in place and prevent it tipping over. The base of the 27" monitor is about 8.25" in diameter and sticks out ~4" in front of the center of the monitor. The base of the 32" monitor is about 9.5" in diameter and sticks out ~4.5" in front of the center of the monitor. In a review of the 27" monitor one individual complained that he couldn't get his keyboard close enough to the screen; I do not see that as a concern with proper ergonomics taken into account.

The 27" monitor has a neat little cable clip running up the rear post of the base which provides good strain relief for the power and video cables. The 32" monitor does not provide this clip; annoying.

The 32" monitor comes with 75mm X 75mm threaded mounting holes for a VESA wall or swing arm mount. The 27" monitor does not come equipped for VESA mounting. See 32" monitor user's manual page 18 on the Samsung site.

Both monitors have the same control interface through a small joystick on the lower back right of the monitors. Pressing in on the joystick turns the monitor on. A menu is displayed if the joystick is pressed while the monitor is on; one option here is to power off the monitor. A second option in the menu is to cycle through the monitor inputs; DisplayPort, HDMI, VGA (27" only). The third menu option allows you to adjust the picture, onscreen display, system, and review monitor information. I had some ghosting issues with the monitor as delivered, it was also way too bright, so I tweaked those values and everything was great; see my review of the 27" monitor to look up the settings.

[Update 30 Nov 2016 - re: control, multiple monitor and split-screen - this is taken from comment to this original review]

In order to switch between two monitors you reach underneath the bottom right-hand side, find the button (if you do this several times per day you will know exactly where it is), press the button straight down once, tilt it to the left about 3 mm, press again, tilt the button about 3 mm up, select the desired input from a binary list (there are only two inputs - three on the 27" curved), and press the button again. It takes me less than 2.5 seconds and I do not have the switch position memorized; just tried it again and it was under 2 seconds. Problems: you have to have a clear path to the bottom right side of the monitor - no phone or coffee cup; otherwise, there is the possibility of strain by curving your finger up and making a gentle press on a button three times (sorry about the sarcasm). I really do not see this as a big deal. Updating original post to include a picture of the button.

Can the monitor be split screened? I do not know for sure. The manual mentions something about "Easy Setting Box" software - I was unable to find it on the website but did not spend a lot of time searching - that may have the functionality you are looking for. I have dual monitors and a single computer so I do not need this functionality. Here is what the manual states "Easy Setting Box enables users to use the monitor by partitioning multiple sections". If you are using multiple computers is a simple KVM switch suitable? or do you need to see both simultaneously?

[End Update]

Upshot: I like it. I like it very much. Negative annoying things are not that bad. Positive good things are great. The screen size is awesome and truly immersive spanning my entire field of view.
profile.summary: GREAT Everday, Work, and Play Monitor

profile.description: This stylish Seville Classics UltraSlimline Personal Tower Fan is perfect for the office, bedroom or any room that needs a breeze. The tower fan is equipped with three whisper quiet speed settings (high, medium, low) that will leave you feeling cool and comfortable on those hot and humid days. The oscillating (70 degrees) space saving compact design has a footprint of less than 0.2 sq ft and the black satin finish complements any dcor. This mini tower fan measures 4.9 deep by 5.4 wide by 12.25 high. Ideal for use on desks, counters and in small spaces.
profile.reviewText:
Pros: The functions of the big fan are great. In addition to typical settings like speed and oscillation, you can set type of wind, and a timer in 30 minute increments. My favorite feature is the sleep timer which allows me to start with a higher speed setting and step down one speed every 30 minutes until it reaches eco mode. This is great for bedtime since higher speeds cool off the room quickly and the eco speed is perfect for running overnight. The fan also has a remote control and it's got an easy-to-use interface and helpful display. The small fan is fine and functional basic fan.

Cons: The big fan is a little louder than I'd like. Although it came well-packed, there's a big dent in the metal backing. Doesn't hurt the functioning, so I didn't send it back. Also, the fan wobbles a little bit on the oscillating base. Overall, minor issues.

Verdict: Both work well for my needs. The big one is great for cooling off the bedroom at night and the little one keeps air circulating in my home office.
profile.summary: Lots of cool features

profile.description: The unique T-Fal thermo-spot heat indicator (fry pans only) shows when T-Fal pans are perfectly preheated to seal in the flavor of your food. The even heat base allows for even heat distribution for reliable cooking results. The T-Fal excite cookware has a non-stick interior that is scratch resistant making cooking and cleaning easy. Ergonomically designed handles are color-matched and oven-safe up to 350 degrees, allowing for an easy transition from stove-top to oven. This 14-piece set includes 8-inch fry pan, 10.25-inch fry pan with lid, 1-quart and 2-quart sauce pans with lids, 5-quart dutch oven with lid, 5 measuring spoons
profile.reviewText:
We have a guest unit with a small kitchen in our house, and sometimes host guests for extended periods of time. This set is perfect for that space. Given the included pieces (really a 10 pieces set if you don't count the measuring spoons) and the reasonable price, this is a great set up for casual cooks (not chefs). The color is lovely - more of a deep, dark red than the advertised "cherry" - my mom compared it to the color of slightly burned spaghetti sauce.

All of the basic sizes and functions are included: three sizes of sauce-type pans and two sizes of fry-type pans, all with lids. The little "One Egg Wonder" pan is handy for small, quick jobs (in addition to cooking an egg, we've used it to heat syrup and caramel sauce). The non-stick surface works as expected and it's great that the pans are dishwasher safe. It makes for easy clean up.

As mentioned above, this cookware would probably work best for the casual cook, or someone either just starting out or someone downsizing. If you are an avid chef, this set isn't for you - and the price point reflects that.
profile.summary: Good for the casual cook

profile.description: Designed for iPad Air 2, this QODE Ultimate Keyboard Case offers comfortable, natural typing reminiscent of working on a laptop's keyboard. The keys are well-spaced and responsive, so you can type faster and more accurately than you can with your tablet's touchscreen alone. The keyboard also includes iPad specific shortcut keys. Choose from three viewing angles, each secured by dual neodymium magnets that will hold your iPad Air 2 at the exact angle you want it-no shifting or slipping, even while typing on your lap. The keyboard is so smart, there's no need for a power button--it turns on when you need it and off when you don't. The long-lasting battery offers 264 hours of active battery life and 4,300 hours of standby. The keyboard folds away when you don't need it, making it easy to comfortably watch videos or browse the internet. Convenient cutouts in the keyboard case give you access to all the tablet's ports and buttons. You can charge your tablet or snap a quick photo with ease--there's no need to remove the iPad Air 2 cover. The QODE Ultimate Keyboard Case is compatible with iPad Air 2 devices.
profile.reviewText:
I received this product and was immediately nervous. The box was missing its upper flap and the keyboard case was sliding around the shipping box. I then did a quick inspect of the keyboard case. The "premium aluminum keyboard" is a very thin sheet of decorative aluminum cut to fit over the keys; it provides no support or protection it just sits there and looks aluminish. The case is otherwise plastic and it looks like any drop protection is achieved by hitting the floor and transferring the kinetic energy of the fall into the disassembly energy of the case; this is actually a workable design philosophy but do not be surprised if it sends parts flying when it hits the floor. I am not going to test this for my review. In fact my case looks like it had been dropped on a corner and the aluminum was permanently bent up and buckled in that area. The keyboard rapidly paired with my iPad with absolutely no difficulty. I started using the keyboard and found that the '8' key would respond only after eight or nine presses; this improved as I used the key more and more.

Here is the real funny one. Your iPad uses the new Lightning Cable whereas the keyboard, for an Apple accessory product, uses a Micro-USB connector.

My keyboard and case did not work out of the box. The keyboard itself feels good, nice solid key clicks, Just concerned about quality of materials.

Upshot. Too many unanswered questions. I would keep looking.

Updated - Did get it working. Used it for three weeks. Battery capacity steadily dropped until after 4 weeks the keyboard no longer worked. Definitely find something else.
profile.summary: Problems Out of Box - Update

profile.description: Logitech Ultrathin is a perfect accessory for your iPad. It is thin and light, thanks to its high-grade aluminum construction. A new smart hinge lets you tilt iPad like a laptop screen for a perfect typing angle. An improved layout with well-spaced keys and iOS shortcuts make typing familiar, fast and accurate
profile.reviewText:
So I wanted to use this keyboard for a while before reviewing it because I also had an earlier version (for iPad2) and wanted get comfortable with the switch before commenting. This version works well, as expected. It has fairly stiff keys that provide a solid feeling under my fingers, but they can be a little "clicky" sounding. The surface of the keys is a bit textured which gives a bit of grip. The earlier version had smoother keys and less resistance, and I prefer the feel of typing here. It just feels more solid. There's a new set of keys across the top that I never use. Theoretically they add functionality, but I naturally go to the iPad screen for the functions they perform. The most frustrating addition to this version is the key in the upper right hand corner, which locks the iPad screen. Unfortunately, this is where the delete key lived on my earlier version so all too often I hit the lock key accidentally. I've gotten more used to it over time, but I still find myself hitting it too often. Finally, two features of this version makes it a bit less convenient to use: an adjustable bar that allows you to tilt the screen to different angles depending on needs/preference and a streamlined magnet to attach the keyboard to the iPad when closed. Both of these "upgrades" make it less easy to close the keyboard with one hand. You have to push the bar back flush to the keyboard and tip the magnet out to attache it to the iPad to close. Neither a huge big deal, but both are a slight inconvenience.

All in all, the keyboard works will and fulfills my needs. It's more streamlined than most competing products, and has good solid feel for typing. The negatives (new screen lock key, adjustable bar and hidden magnet) are slighly less desirable than the functionality of the previous version. If this is your first Logitech iPad keyboard, you won't notice at all! But overall, I'm happy with this keyboard and expect it will work well for a long time to come.
profile.summary: Comparison with earlier version

profile.description: 3M Easy-On Privacy Filters allow you to view your tablet in public without revealing confidential information. Bubble-free application allows the privacy filter to be quickly and easily applied and reapplied numerous times.
profile.reviewText:
Edited to downgrade rating from 3 stars to 2. As mentioned below, little particles of stuff slip between the screen and the screen protector - dust, crumbs, cat hair, etc. Maybe if I were taking the protector on and off this wouldn't be a problem because I would be able to wipe the screen regularly. After a few days, the build up of junk could be really irritating. After about 2 months I took the protector off and just never put it back on. So much for that experiment.
----------

The security function of this protector works great. It's a horizontal protector so when I'm holding the iPad in landscape mode, the screen appears black to the people sitting beside me. This makes it possible for me to view sensitive information in public places without everyone reading over my shoulder. If I want to share I just turn the screen to portrait mode. I do think the viewing angle is slightly restricted in portrait mode too, so if you share your screen frequently with others, this is not a perfect solution. 3M claims you just take this protector off and put it back on when you want to share, but I don't think that's very practical (more below).

I prefer my protectors to have a slightly matte finish. Shiny ones like this show too many fingerprints and smudges.

Unlike every electronic device screen protector I've ever used, this one isn't sticky all over but just on the corners. This means it offers unique benefits and drawbacks.
1) Super easy to attach.
2) Sticky corner pieces make it possible to lift off and reattach "easily." It comes with a sleeve to store the protector in when you remove it. I do not find it practical to use this feature. The sleeve is one more thing to carry around, and when you take it off, the corners get dust and other particles on them which makes them less sticky over time. An extra set of corners is provided.
3) It hovers slightly above the iPad screen. This doesn't affect the sensitivity of the protector which I was worried about. However, this causes two problem: stuff gets underneath it, and when I lift the case cover my fingers sometimes lift up on the protector too (will this stretch or tear eventually?)
4) It migrates. After a couple of days usage, I find it is slipping off one side or another. Easy to reposition since it's lifts off and reattached easily. And while it's off, I can clean out the particles that have snuck behind.

Overall, it works well, but I don't find the "easy on and off" feature very useful and it results in extra maintenance. I'd rather put a protector on and forget about it.
profile.summary: Unusual concept for a screen protector

This ball has a full grain leather cover, gray wool winding, and cushion cork center. The seam is raised for improved grip and accuracy.
profile.reviewText: Now normally I hate kids. They are smelly, noisy, and if they are playing sports they usually have parents with them. No one stepped up to coach my son's team this year so based on 30 years listening to Vin Scully's apparently I am it. Well, if extensive practice we found that not only were these baseballs real, honest to goodness, Little League baseballs - these baseballs were real, honest to goodness, magic Little League baseballs. Practices picked up pace, hitters averages are up, a glorious double play was turned (someday in a game!), and confidence grew. Nothing better than a warm summer night, the field bright under the lights, the fans fading away into the dark, a cold beverage, a hot dog with onions and sauerkraut, the 7th inning stretch, and giving out baseballs to kids who didn't get a foul ball but never gave up hope. Baseball is the national pastime.

profile.description: The Liebert PSA is an economical, line-interactive UPS system that offers full-featured power protection for small office computers and electronic equipment. Designed with simple controls for easy operation, the psa provides up to five minutes of back-up time at full load, giving ample time to save work and shut down the connected equipment. USB shutdown software and a USB cable are also included, to allow remote alerts and automated graceful shutdown of the connected systems.
profile.reviewText:
This review was written in July 2016.

Emerson Network Power bought Liebert sometime before 2008; in this review I will refer, wherever possible, to Liebert.

The Liebert Model PSA650MT-120U is an old UPS. How do I know? The data sheet for the UPS, found on the Emerson Network Power website, is copyright 2008; the same data sheet indicates that the Communications/Shutdown Software is compatible with Windows 98 (and later!). The Quick Start Guide is also Copyright 2008. The Multilink Software CD-ROM is copyright 2006 and includes a sticker on the sleeve directing you to an Emerson website for the latest version; HTTP Error 404 File Not Found. Oops. You can do a google on "Liebert MultiLink Automated Shutdown Software" and one of your choices will show that the software supports Windows 7, 8, XP and up to Server 2012 (version 1.5.52 dated 22 Oct 2012). Confidence. I am not keen on installing this software on my Windows 10 laptop.

Inside the Liebert packaging is the UPS, a 3 ft long USB A-B cable, and a Quick Start Guide. Note that a separate power cord is not supplied; instead the power cord is attached directly to the UPS and projects straight out of the unit. Likewise the wall plug is a large plug attached straight to the cable making it take up a lot space against the wall when plugged in.

The back of the UPS provides one surge protected outlet (not UPS powered and supposedly protected by a TVSS), three UPS protected outlets, the USB connection for the shutdown software, the critically important RJ45 jacks for protecting modems, a site wiring fault indicator LED, and an input circuit breaker.

The front panel provides the UPS controls that do not provide a battery charging indicator but does include a power ON LED, a fault LED showing RED = Fault and Orange = Overload, and finally, the ON/OFF button.

The UPS is in a pretty standard Mini-Tower case with one exception. The top of the case is divided in half and each half has a very shallow slope down to the sides. Want to put a pencil sharpener, stapler, hard drive, or modem (yes it could be that old) on top? It is going to teeter from side to side.

The quick start guide indicates that the batteries are not charged prior to shipment and must be charged a minimum of 8 hours before use. This entails plugging the unit into the wall and leaving it. Do not press the ON/OFF button. Note there are no indicators to identify that charging is in progress (or complete) whether power is ON or OFF. Repeat, there are no charging indicators; on a UPS? Also, if the batteries have not been charged in 8 years ... ? No manufacturing date is provided on the unit.

So right now waiting on batteries to charge. Or not.

<4 hours pass>

Listening to Amy Winehouse

<4 more hours pass>

I connected the following instruments to the UPS: HP 54645D Mixed Signal Oscilloscope (300 VA), HP 33120A Arbitrary Waveform Generator (50 VA), and HP 5385A Frequency Counter (100 VA - estimated). I then pulled the plug on the UPS. The UPS ran for 14 minutes before slow beeping (3 seconds) indicating it was on Battery. After 18 minutes the UPS began fast beeping (1 second) indicating Battery Low. I then plugged the UPS back in. So for 70% of rated load the UPS lasted 29% longer.

I am not going to let this UPS power anything important like a server but as disposable backup for low priority devices? Sure.

Pros - low cost

Cons - the UPS is 8 years old

The cons have it.
profile.summary: An 8 year old UPS?

profile.description: They're made of 100percent cotton so they're very absorbent and comfortable when you're drying off. At 60 inch x 31 inch there's plenty to wrap up in. Each pool towel provides optimal coverage, absorbency, and versatility. Use on the beach or poolside as a vacation accessory,
profile.reviewText:
The Cara Clark Convertible Beach Towel & Backpack is a good idea that skimped on the details. The package label reads:

"Lusciously Soft French Terry towel which easily folds into a backpack. Features: Hidden pocket for valuables, Measurements: towel 31" x 60", folded/bag 15" x 17.5", Material: 100% cotton, Care: Machine wash tumble dry."

The towel is almost exactly as described. It has a rectangular pocket that you can carefully fold the towel into, and drawstring ties that you can pull over shoulder to carry it like a pack. Who am I kidding? Forget the fold stuff, the towel is just going to get jammed into the bag. This is not a bad thing but the truth shall be told.

More truth. The terry cloth is thin. After washing it and running it through the dryer there are areas of fabric that you can easily see light through. See the photo below where I washed the towel and ran it through the dryer. There was enough lint in the trap for me to knit a dog. My husband will be using the towel for canoeing and camping where the lack of absorbency will not be that noticeable but the ability to fold it away will help keep things compact and organized in his backpack.

Pros: good idea

Cons: really cheap terrycloth

Note: photos to be uploaded soon

No Wrinkles technology gives you a freshly pressed look around the clock and an Individual Fit Waistband offers up to 1" of extra room in the waist. Features a button through front closure, and a permanent front crease for elevated style, double welt button through back pockets and fine topstitching. A super-soft fabric makes these your new workday go-to.
profile.reviewText:
Passed to my husband for review.

The Dockers Men's Signature Stretch Khaki Slim-Tapered Fit Flat-Front Pants are, as one would expect from Dockers, a quality well made product. The material is strong with a soft texture and a slight stretch. The pants are well made. Stitching is even and uniformly straight. Seams are double stitched with fabric edges cleanly overstitched. The front pockets are deep; no chance of your wallet falling out. The rear pockets are less deep but include button closures.

Sizing. I have problems with the sizing; these pants definitely fit small. I have recently lost a lot of weight and can now fit into a 32" waist after wearing as large as a 42" in the past 3 years. Unfortunately Levis and Dockers consistently fit small. I can fit into 32" pants from Eddie Bauer, LL Bean, and Columbia, but Levis and Dockers seem to require 34" to 36". We optimistically ordered these but lost out even with the stretch. The pants are definitely a slim tapered fit.

If you can get the size right, these are a nice quality well made set of pants. I would wear these on casual days and feel good about how I looked. The problem for me is sizing - I would need to order a couple of sizes and return the ones that didn't fit.

Five thumbs up, the problem is my stomach is larger than my eyes.
