profile.description: Micro USB Host Cable (OTG Cable) - Xoom, Galaxy S2, Nokia N810/N900, Toshiba TG01, Archos G9. New Version with more accommodating "L" shaped connector
profile.reviewText:
First of all, the price of this thing at $2, including shipping, should discourage too many negative reviews. For that price, it's a great bargain.

However, in terms of a USB OTG cable, you can do a lot better. First of all, the fit of this thing is sketchy. It's very loose in the port and definitely not the best solution if you plan on using offline storage or devices in a mobile scenario.

If, instead, you are using your device with an OTG cable as part of a desktop application, this is going to be fine: set up your device, plug in the OTG cable and do your thing while leaving your tablet or phone alone. This will get the job done.

But it won't be setting any speed records doing so. I don't know if it's because the generic fittings are loose, if the generic cables are inferior or if the OTG interface is down a few connections on the potential speeds of 11 pin setups Androids are now using. Whatever the reason: this thing is not going to come close to the high end of USB 2.0 file transfer speeds.

If you're a heavy media user, you're going to want to go with something better. However, if you're just transferring files back and forth for text editing or printing, or hooking up a wireless keyboard or desktop, this is going to be fine.

One thing I do like is that the cable and ports feel like they're well insulated with a fairly think coating of rubberized plastic, but the fact that so much metal is left exposed when plugged in to a micro USB port that there is a lot of potential for noise when using external devices for audio or video work.

You always get what you pay for.
profile.summary: It's a good value that works, but you get what you pay for.

profile.description: An incognito camera bag for all your lens and body needs. Fully padded, removable camera insert allows you to magically transform it from a dedicated camera bag to a utilitarian, carry-all messenger bag.
profile.reviewText:
The tag on the bag says something like, "you and your Snoop are going to become BFF." They couldn't be more right.

The only problems with the design are the front panel pockets and the lack of a grab handle (which has been addressed on the 2012 bag). Like people have said about the pockets, when you load one, you load them all. There is definitely some refinement to be done here, but it isn't that big of a problem since this is my dedicated camera bag and I'm not lugging rolls of 35mm or a ton of cables.

Something I would like to see is moving the clear pocket and maybe a mesh pouch to the top of the camera sack. For me, this seems like a better location to stash filters, memory cards, spare batteries, etc. There is enough of a gap established on the lip of the stitching to make this happen.

I would also like some pen loops. Who carries cameras in dedicated bags? Professionals; and we really like to write notes. Instead of the Velcro strip used to hold the camera sack in, they should put in the old pocket. That would be perfect to hold a notebook and some pens, not to mention cables, freeing up more space in the flat-panel pockets. When I'm not using the camera, I have the sack zipped shut as an extra level of environmental protection: it's redundant given the perfect fit the sack enjoys in the satchel.

One of the reasons I almost didn't buy this bag is because it doesn't have any place to hold a Nalgene liter bottle, but the plastic hoop on the side opposite the strap buckle and a cheap karabiner solved that problem for $0.50.

The fabric is bomb-proof: I've had another Timbuk2 bag for more than 15 years and the only difference thorough abuse has made is the fabric is now nice and soft. There have been zero material failures, even with three crashes that left me looking like I had a Turkish massage with a belt-sander. I have no doubt that this bag will fare even better: the TPU seems more durable than it was when Seinfeld was still airing new episodes and I like that it's now in black. If it were legal, I would recommend putting your baby in a Timbuk2 bag before strapping them into a car seat... for safety.

I also like that the reflectors are now built into the flap straps, though I would like some Velcro so I can subdue them.

The Velcro silencers included are a great idea for being able to move quietly. I would have liked another set for the Velcro pieces where the flap hinges over the satchel to make it completely stealth.

Speaking of those Velcro patches at the hinge: awesome. This is the only place I've ever had rain leak into my old Timbuk2, and the Velcro here totally solves the problem. I had my camera and laptop out in a surprise deluge today, the day after getting it, and ZERO water got in. I wish I could say the same about the jacket I was wearing.

While the tripod loops aren't big enough for my favorite tripod, they comfortably hold my other pods that are more appropriate for the cameras I use these days. While lashing on a tripod eliminate the "stealth" look of the bag, I've had plenty of "camera bags" that haven't had any capability for a tripod built into them and now that I have the Snoop, I would never be without them.

I LOVE the strap on this bag, specifically the rapid adjuster. When I was shooting today, I experimented with shortening the strap to bring the bag up on my chest to quickly access my gear. It works great, and a quick pull on the lever drops the bag to comfortably sling it on my hip. It is a very well-designed platform.

I like that the Snoop is pretty much everything perfect about a traditional Timbuk2 messenger: sleek, super-high-quality, comfortable, and stable with the wrap-around strap attached... just with the added specialization for photographers and journalists.

It also looks good: clean enough to look professional, but not in a douchebag way. Granted, douchebags WILL be attracted to this because it looks good and is a manpurse, but Timbuk2 was born when hair metal died and skinny jeans were still chick pants. Just as real punks know Jello Biafra drops Blink 182 and Good Charlotte during his morning constitutional, anybody who's worth knowing knows that Timbuk2 is more about Critical Mass and less about fashionable [donkeys].

This is a great bag from a company that stays in business by making sure every bag they sell you could be the last one you will ever have to buy. I have respected Timbuk2 for a long time, but now I'm in love. There may be a few things I'd like to have different on this bag, but that's what Timbuk2 is about: these bags are platforms for customization... and each little change that will make this bag more mine and less "theirs" will make me love it even more.
profile.summary: It doesn't get much better.

profile.description: Workout Tracker Red [Discontinued 2015 Edition]
profile.reviewText:
This is a thing that costs between $60 and $70. That's what a single personal training session can run you.

Yes: it isn't perfect, but it can be fixed. The first problem that gets mentioned is that the sensor pops out of the strap frequently. This is a three-part solution.

1) order a color you can find. When I was a paramedic, everyone had a black stethoscope because they look cool. I had a hot pink one because I could find it easily in the back of the meat wagon. Same solution with the MOOV: get the red one. If it pops out, you can find it a hell of a lot easier in any environment.

2) use your noodle. Bluetooth has a range of 20-40 feet. If you haven't heard the coaching for a little while, turn around to where you were before. Always check your phone before you leave an area to make sure it is still paired. This is a tool, not a total solution.

3) electrical tape. I use mine ONLY for working out. This is my personal trainer. It goes on at the gym or track or with my cycling cleats. It comes off with them. I've wrapped the sensor pouch with a small piece of tape and I secure the band in a comfortable position with a little bit of paper medical tape around the clasp. Yes: a traditional watchband with a more secure sensor pocket would be best, but guess what? This is an imperfect world.

Don't gripe. Adapt. This is why you should have you kids play with cardboard boxes and duct tape.

My physical therapist recommended that I pick one of these things up to help with a shoulder/back injury that pinches a nerve when it comes. Along with the treatment recommendation of massage and trigger point work, she recommended this to help with the swimming she thought was beneficial in avoiding surgery.

Hello gym membership, trips around the area buying an assortment of random items that was only missing a bunch of bananas and Trojan Magnums. $220 later, I was totally geared out and ready to have my injury take me to the face.

I wear this in addition to the Garmin Vivosmart HR fitness tracker. Between the two, I have all the information I need to make the best decisions I can in the improvement of my physical condition.

I don't consider the Moov NOW to be a fitness tracker. It is more comfortable to use when I sleep, but this thing is my go-anywhere for anylong personal trainer.

The amount of information I've been able to accumulate from this little device is insane. I ride my bike all the time, for miles and miles, and this device has made me a better cyclist by coaching and pushing me. It has also helped me understand how my body moves through water and apply some Google research to retraining my body how to move.

This is the second sensor I'm buying because if I can rehab my shoulder, I want to start boxing again. The boxing cardio program is an awesome feature that I've watched a few people use in the gym with the heavybag. That is, by far, my favorite kind of workout... but it gets boring working a bag without any feedback except from a Tabata timer. The immediate reason I ordered a second sensor, though, is because Moov is, or has, adding dual-sensor support to their swimming app. This will help me see if my bad arm is working correctly and help me make conscious adjustments to get my form correct and non-injurious.

The most impressive feature, though, is that the MOOV Now has made me run more often. I HATE running. It's horrible. I get no benefit from it. It doesn't nothing except make my lungs and back burn. Then I tried the running app and within a single 20 minute workout had a lot of information to digest about my stride and form. By making constant adjustments to my running style based on the information the MOOV provided, I've been able to go running on concrete without suffering the ankle, knee and back pain typical to previous experiments with the activity.

So yeah: this thing isn't perfect, but it is an impressive piece of equipment that offers a lot of benefit for a small price.
profile.summary: Not Perfect, But Totally Worth It

profile.description: Wear today's fitness goal on your wrist with Vivo smart HR, activity tracker1 with Garmin Elevate wrist heart rate technology. It's the touchscreen activity tracker with wrist-based heart rate and a full suite of smart notifications2. The sleek band is comfortable to wear all day, and the always-on display shows your stats, even in sunlight. Displays steps, distance, calories, heart rate, floors climbed and activity intensity1. Receive text, call, email, calendar and other alerts on your wrist when paired with your phone. Wirelessly syncs2 to your Garmin Connect account, our free online community where you can join fitness challenges and save, plan and share your progress.
profile.reviewText:
I've been using the Vivofit HR since January of this year. I've waited to review it because it didn't feel like it was "done" in terms of the Android Connect app and its integration with MyFitnessPal and Strava.

Things have changed quite a bit, and largely for the better, over the last eight months.

I have had no durability issues outside the band starting to show a little cracking. I do wear it a notch tighter than I normally wear wristwatches, however. This is to keep the heart rate monitor honest. It's an optical system that measures what's going on at the capillary level: the sensor needs a close-up of the action, even if the green LEDs make each pulse a black or white issue of fluctuation.

The VivoFit is way more accurate than the FitBit I initially purchased. I don't know if things have changed on their system, but I imagine FitBit is limited by their hardware: they use two LEDs instead of Garmin's 3. Garmin's are also larger and brighter than what I observed on the FitBit. More light = better information when it comes to optical systems. Just ask your eyeballs. The current firmware (3.4 at this time) has also improved the accuracy of the heart rate monitor.

I don't understand how people are reporting a bunch of scratches and damage to the glass on their Vivofits. I'm not a delicate guy: I bartend, work on my car, am in the middle of remodeling my condo, lift weights, box, practice Krav Maga, cycle, etc. In other words: I'm active and engage in things that lead to wear and tear on my body and the things I equip it with. I imagine that there must be some truly hamfisted individuals out there. The only signs of wear from the last eight months of daily use is the previously mentioned cracking of the band and it is no longer matte, having been polished out by use.

When new, the Vivofit HR had a battery life of three days. I considered that acceptable. However, eight months and multiple updates later, I am getting 4 days of use before I need to recharge while working at my laptop. I have push notifications for weather, inbound caller ID, calendar, facebook, twitter, email, and text messages turned on, the move bar, as well as the controls for the music player. I also use it to track 4-5 hour-long workouts in the gym, plus daily 2-3 mile walks with my dog. I use this a lot, especially the resource-intensive workout monitor (it uses the heart rate monitor much more than when in normal activity tracking).

The only thing I have turned off is the automatic backlight. It never functioned without having to sharply snap my wrist, and the only time it seemed to respond to gentler movements is when I was sleeping... and being a light sleeper, sometimes the glow was enough to wake me up. It's not much effort to take a finger and touch the screen to see what time it is. I even tap it to my nose if I'm riding at night or have my hands full with the stinkier bits of being a responsible dog owner.

Considering it takes about an hour or so to fully charge from the battery warning, I consider this to be excellent battery life for a device that offers so many functions.

I have had no problems integrating MyFitnessPal or Strava, but I do admit that it took a while for the different websites to really communicate with each other. I'm curious to see if MFP and Garmin will continue to work as closely together in the future now that UnderArmor has a capable activity tracker on the market.

Strava is a nice app, but I prefer to turn on the Vivofit's cycling tracker and use the Moov Now sensor on my ankle with its coaching chiming in over my music. Same goes for running. The Moov Now is such a capable and informative device that I would never recommend anyone spend their money on any of the full-featured GPS-enabled smartwatches. Even the Vivosmart HR+ is an additional $50-$100, depending on where you shop, and Garmin is the best at GPS tracking.

However, regardless of what you buy (from a running watch to an iWatch to a Google watch), the battery life of GPS-enabled wrist devices is horrible. What's the point of a device offering a sleep tracker if you have to charge it every night, and what's the point of wearing a watch that goes into a coma before you're even ready for a nap?

Considering the Moov Now is around $60, offers real-time coaching on your form and pace (it is absolutely amazing), and can be used to guide you through demanding workouts in both calisthenics AND shadow-boxing (or heavy bag workouts: I put my sensors on under my wraps, don my gloves, and watch the target cues on the TV in the background. Packing a Chromecast in my gym bag comes in handy), it is worth much more than having GPS on your bicycle, on your wrist, in your car, on your phone... seriously: if you don't know where you are at this point in technology, a runner's watch isn't going to help.

Moov also has one of the best customer service departments I have ever had to contact. They are amazing.

With the continued support for the Vivofit HR, the Connect apps, and seeing how refined Garmin is making their product, I can recommend this device easily. The only improvements I would like to see is that the activity tracking resets with the user's sleep schedule, not the coming of midnight. I work late hours and usually turn in around 4am. My activity stats can easily fall short or register as 200% my daily goals because of this, which leads to some wonky adjustments in the goal-minder.

I would also like to see the ability to turn off vibration notices when anything other than a phone call is coming in. I often have my phone charging next to my laptop while working, so I can see the notification light easily. If I'm not working, I'm driving, working out, or sleeping. The vibrations of notifications can cause distractions. I'll think it's a lap-timer, or if my girlfriend is going super-Fonzi with text messaging, it can get incredibly annoying to get 30 buzzes when I'm working with clients, teaching, bartending, driving, cycling, taking a shower... basically doing things that make it impossible to do anything about what I'm being notified about.

I realize I could turn off notifications, but I like to be able to flick through the notifications screen and get a snapshot of what's going on without having to pull my phone out of my pocket. I'd just like the option of turning off the vibration alert for anything other than phone calls.

This is an incredible product, and now that I see how much attention Garmin has given to improving its products through frequent app and firmware updates, I have no problem saying this isn't just the best activity tracker currently on the market, but also the most practical option if you're looking for a smart watch.
profile.summary: Garmin keeps making it better and better!

profile.description: Rostra 250 1755 Complete Cruise Control Kit for Scion xA xB 2004 06
profile.reviewText:
I installed this before moving across the country in order to avoid the ambitious policing of California cars on Midwestern highways.

It was fairly easy to install and adjust to operate properly, however there are a few tips for people attempting a similar job:
1) After going through the nightmare of installing the Toyota alarm system, it is remarkably easier to work behind the dash after first removing the driver's seat. Don't question it, just do it.
2) Get a lamp to wear on your head. It's going to come in handy.
3) Get a tiny tiny pair of needle nose pliers to clip the T-connectors shut, which is a pain even when you completely remove the section of wiring harness you need to access.
4) While you're under the dash, adjust your brake light switch. Sometimes this unit takes two jabs of the brake pedal to disengage, which is an inconvenience when your radar detector goes beep. I've actually found the clutch disengagement to be more responsive, and it doesn't activate the brake lights in case Smokey is on your six.
5) When getting the cruise unit's wiring harness into the cabin, it is a snap to do the following:
a) Grab your filleting knife from the kitchen butcher's block. The blade is long, sharp, thin and blunt on one end.
b) Face the blunt end towards the OEM wiring harness with at least half an inch of distance from it.
c) Push the blade all the way through both sides of the rubber grommet.
d) Take a half inch extension out of your toolbox. The larger snap connector fits perfectly in the female end.
e) Use electrical tape to secure the large snap into the extension, then tape the smaller snap connection behind it so that it won't be pulled free by the snug-fitting grommet.
f) Push the extension through, climb inside, pull it through until you have enough slack to get business done behind the dash.
g) Adjust the grommet's fit on the inside, then the outside.

Now you'll have a teeny tiny surgical incision to seal up with the putty instead of a massive clumsy gash.

And don't even think about pulling the grommet out of place: you'll turn a 45min job into a frustrating nightmare.

There is nothing else you can do to make the wiring easier. It sucks. Small car, massive ropes of wire, giant American meat club arms: you do the math. Swear your way through it.

Now here's the bummer: the Rostra instructions for the 2006 xA indicates the wire that is used for powering the parking and headlights. I clipped into this wire TWICE (burning my spare T-connector), so my cruise only works when my lights are on. Since it's winter and I use my parking lights as DRLs, anyway, it isn't much of an inconvenience. I will clip in to the cigarette lighter wire at some point, but I'm not in a hurry to ever venture under that dash again.

Sometimes the unit will be pretty inconsistent with speed adjustments depending on terrain or when re-engaging, running the vehicle a full 7mph over the set speed before adjusting itself out. Once in a while, the unit fails to set, even with multiple and long presses on the set button.

A simple reset (turning it off and then back on) will solve the problem, but it's still a little puzzling.

I'll be contacting Rostra's customer service to figure out how to adjust the factory settings inside the brain of the unit, but it did her intended job adequately: rolled 2,700 miles ALWAYS traveling 5mph over the speed limit while getting 35mpg.
profile.summary: Good product, unreliable instructions for the xA

profile.description: Zeikos 58mm 3-Piece Ultra Slim Pro Glass Filter Set (UV Ultraviolet, Circular Polarizing and Warming)
profile.reviewText:
Here's the thing: three filters for $15. You are not getting a premium Hoya product, but what you are getting is a very good product that is far better than what I expected to get for the money.

These are better than the plastic (and 50% less) Zeikos filter pack. The housing is metal, it is thin for zero vignetting, and I always trust glass more than I do plastic when it comes to distortion. These are made for wide-angle use, but I haven't noticed appreciable degradation when using them with the telephoto.

The coating on the UV isn't as good as Hoya, but a UV filter is really about protection more than anything else. It's clear, coated, and free from any sort of machining oil that another reviewer wrote somewhere.

The softening filter does its job. It's not as sophisticated as some coating/tint combinations, but it works. It's $5. You can't even get a day laborer to dump garbage in your yard for $5.

The polarizing filter is okay. The action isn't the slickest, but again: $5. Or more like $3.50 considering this kit also comes with a 6 filter case.

Speaking of the case: it's good. Sure, it's bulkier than I would like, but it slips into the random empty slot in my camera bag without any drama and keeps the filters from flying around. That's important because with inexpensive filters comes easily scratched coatings.

If you abuse your gear, you're going to be disappointed with ANY filter, regardless of the manufacturer because people that don't treat their gear well BREAK their gear well. If you are an untrained ape: buy these filters and do whatever you want. Break them all. Love them.

However, if you take care of your stuff and are deliberate with where you put your camera (not to mention good with a lens cap), you won't have any problems with these filters. The image quality is good enough to where your friends that know nothing about photography will be amazed. Face it: 98% of us want to look like photophiles and 98% of us suck at photography. If your pictures suck: it's not the filter's fault. Take a class at the local JC.

The reason why I gave it four stars is because... they aren't Hoya filters and that I have trouble finding individual Zeikos glass filters to round out the kit. For that reason, the best value is with the bigger filter kits.

Pay the extra $15 and get a full filter case.
profile.summary: You get more than you pay for

profile.description: Lightning Jack Adapter
profile.reviewText:
While I didn't have time to verify all the numbers in terms of whether this puts out the voltage advertized, I can say that it did a good job charging both my Android phone and tablet off my solar panel (if you have a Goal Zero Nomad, the 12v charging dongle is awesome for charging devices), so I believe Anker's claims.

However, I had to return it because after an hour inside my satchel, which was stored in my trunk, it stunk up my entire car with some sort of horrible chemical nasty smell. I'll give a different Anker product a try and hope it has a normal smell.

I don't know if this is a normal characteristic of their products, but the best way I can explain it is a combination of a high school basketball player's shoes; an old man's bathroom after a night of fajitas, dark beer and pickled eggs; and low tide at a sea salt flat.

Horrible, but take a chance: you might get one that doesn't make your business attache stink for 48 hours and counting.
profile.summary: Works great, smells like the dumpster behind a Chinese buffet.

profile.description: The Maxpedition Operator Tactical Attache (#0605) is a large tactical computer attach. The main compartment is padded on all sides; has a hook-and-loop divider and sized to fit a 15.4" (Diagonal Screen Size) laptop, and a legal size pad. This is the perfect office go-bag for the Tactical Officer.
profile.reviewText:
I recently purchased a second one of these because I like them so much.

The first one is my grab-bag for photography and PR writing, essentially a portable office. I use a Timbuk2 Snoop camera sleeve in the main compartment that holds a DSLR, two lenses, my backup point-and-shoot, a ZOOM H1 voice recorder/external mic for video and podcasting work, various cables, etc. It works really well for a camera bag.

FYI: you know those Velcro loops on the top of the bag that are made for a Mag Lite? They also carry a full-size tripod with ease while allowing awkward, yet still functional, access to the main compartment.

One tiny detail I LOVE? The keyper snap prevents the main compartment zipper from working open on accident. I REALLY like that since I can sling the bag and feel secure that nobody will be able to get into the main compartment of my kit without alerting me. Definite bonus when riding the bus or metro.

Since the Snoop sleeve eats up the main compartment, I house a small laptop in the back padded case. Maxpedition states that it will fit a 15" laptop, but that's in the main compartment. The rear compartment will barely fit my 14.1" Asus laptop, but there is no padding on the bottom or sides of that compartment. Unless I need to do a lot of multi-media editing on the run, I carry a netbook, which easily fits in the secured notepad sleeve. There is enough room to carry the power brick, too, though I usually use the radio pocket for that and the case for my glasses.

In the front pockets I carry my e-reader/notepad, camera batteries, SD cards, my phone's charging cable, earphones, and a head lamp (they always come in handy when the workday gets a little longer than the sun's). In the main compartment with elasticized shotgun loops, I carry things that come in handy when the day goes sideways: fingernail clippers to address a hang-nail when working outdoors, pocket knife, lighter, a couple of thumb drives, and a wine/bottle opener. Also stored are a few energy bars.

The concealed-carry compartment houses a solar-charger for my batteries, a full-tang knife, and about 1/8 roll of toilet paper (smashed down tube offeres a great way to keep my knife stashed upright). Across the top, I have a number of pens clipped into the pocket.

The Nalgene pocket houses... a Nalgene bottle, and if I'm expecting a long day, I can fit a 2L hydration bag (Osprey) in the main compartment with the rest of my gear.

Besides the limited padding in the laptop/admin poocket, one slight negative I can find is that waterproofing doesn't last the life of the product. That's like complaining that the sun won't survive the life of the universe: I'm sure I'll be long dead before Maxpedition's fabric tears, and I'd put even money on the bag outliving the sun.

I solved this problem with an application of a PTEF waterproofing spray called Star Brite. It's total overkill, but I carry a lot of precious, expensive, and mandatory equipment.

Also: I would like the design to be more messenger-bag than briefcase. A strap sewn around the main compartment would feel a lot more secure than the clip-on strap similar to my gym bag's. I've had one of these break in the field, but nothing was damaged in the ensuing fall (the Snoop is very good at protecting gear).

Maxpedition replaced the strap free of charge: they really stand behind their lifetime warranty.

Excellent product that is incredibly adaptable to any use made by an outstanding company that takes pride in their product as much as they honor the expectations of their customers.

Buy one.
profile.summary: Almost perfect, but perfect enough

profile.description: ATTENTION: Touch Screen Sensitivity *Touch Sensitivity Adjustment: Go to your phone Settings menu - Advanced Features - Turn On Touch Sensitivity *Sensitivity of the Home Button: Go to your phone Settings menu - Display - Navigation Bar , youll see the Hard Press Home Button feature. The default setting is 3, but you can increase this up to a stronger setting of 5. There is a test at the bottom of the screen that lets you gauge the sensitivity at each level, so go with what works for you. Features: Material: Tempered Glass Touch screen will function as normal Prevent scratches, dust, wear and glare Anti-glare, anti-bubble, anti-fingerprint and anti-slip It provides great security at 45 degree viewing angle Offers tough and durable surface while keeping the LCD screen clean Made of high-quality material that is very lightweight and impact resistant Package Content: 2 X Tempered Glass Screen Protectors 2 X Dust Removal Stickers 2 X Wet/Dry Wipes
profile.reviewText:
Okay, so let me be fair: This is a decent-quality matte screen protector that doesn't interfere with the polarization of the screen when viewed through polarized sunglasses in direct daylight.

With that being said, even when following the directions to a T, using the dust sticker, squeezing out bubbles, etc... these screen protectors still manage to suck dust out of the air before they apply to the phone's screen. It took me three protectors to get one that had a relatively dust-free appearance, but that was only accomplished after using my camera's cleaning solution, power blaster, brush, and microfiber cloth. Even then... these just suck the dust up out of the air.

They're also just a tad too large on each side, causing the edges to rest on the Nexus 5's bevel, and introducing a cheap and ugly-looking constant air-gap under the screen protector.

So while they do their job of protecting the screen and protecting from glare, they are a serious pain to get right. The third time.
profile.summary: A decent product that somehow manufactures dust.

profile.description: This 10-foot cord provides a permanent power source for your detector. The bare wires on the end of the cable can be connected to the fuse box or even directly to the battery. It includes an integral fuse holder Hard Wire Kit for Cobra ESD7000, PRO7080, XRS-9300, XRS-9330, XRS-9340, XRS-9345, XRS-9400, XRS-9430, XRS-9440, XRS-9445, XRS-9500, XRS-9530, XRS-9540, XRS-9545, XRS-9600, XRS-9630, XRS-9640, XRS-9645, XRS-9700, XRS-9730, XRS-9740, XRS-9745, XRS-9830, XRS-9840, XRS-9845, XRS-9930, XRS-9940, XRS-9945, XRS-9950, XRS-9955, XRS-9965, XRS9960G, XRS-9970G, PRO-9780 and all other current models. Works with all Cobra radar models - except DSP 9200 BT.
profile.reviewText:
Universal for products are universally difficult to fit. More follows.

Since I now spend most of my work day in my car, I went on a mission to declutter the cockpit.

This did the job, with minor caveats.

The length of the cord is okay, but I'd like the fuse holder a foot or two up the positive cable so behind my dash doesn't look like a work bench at Mission Control during Apollo 13.

I've installed these by soldering, using an add-a-fuse, and T connectors. Save yourself the headache and use an add-a-fuse on the instrument cluster fuse so it only turns on with the ignition, allowing you full use of the accessory switch for making out.

Use a 2.5 or 5 amp fuse, not 10.

If the fuse holder was farther up the positive cable, I could not have three feet of cable wound up and zip tied behind my A pillar.

The connector is also universal fit. It isn't as clean as the cigarette lighter's cable, but it isn't going anywhere unless I'm in Virginia.

Grounding is easy: remove the kick panel under the fuse box and clamp the appropriate ring fitting to go over the ground strap bolt.

It took me longer to mount an eBay cell phone holder than it did wire my radar detector directly to my electrical system. I'm a much happier driver.
profile.summary: Get your man card in 10min

profile.description: Take calls, receive text and email notifications, listen to FM radio, stream music from your Android smartphone and more. Directly store up to 2GB of music on included micro SD card or up it to 32GB. See how a Bluetooth wireless headset can do so much more than take calls when its four fabulous products rolled into one. Use it as an MP3 player capable of holding up to 2GB of music on the included 2GB Micro SD memory card or upgrade to a whopping 32GB of storage if you want more in store. Enjoy stunning stereo sound and crystal clear call quality thanks to renowned Sony sound, plus pick up local radio stations in your area. View text messages, emails, caller names, media titles and more, or have messages read directly into your headset thanks to text-to-speech capabilities. Basic audio and call features enabled on the Smart Wireless Headset pro with all Bluetooth 2.0 capable devices and full features available with most Android 2.1 or higher devices.
profile.reviewText:
Summary
- The Sony MW1 is a great Android accessory that surprises the user with how much forethought Sony put into better serving the smarter smartphone users. While not perfect, the MW1 is a very capable device that serves most of its roles very well most of the time. Don't think of the MW1 as a Bluetooth stereo headset. Think of it as the LAST headset you'll ever need. While a bit overpriced at the MSRP side of the scale, I feel the MW1 is a bargain at $80.

The Good (+10.5 stars)
- Killer display in all lighting conditions (+1.5 stars).
- Support for Android functions is fantastic (+1.5 stars).
- Support for iOS is horrible. Yes, I'm aware I listed that as a plus (+0.25 stars).
- The ear buds are better than Beats, easily tailored to fit your ears and sound amazing (+1.5 stars)!
- The tangle-free design is great when grabbing the headphones out of your backpack or pocket (+1 star).
- Great sound quality when streaming over Bluetooth (+1.75 stars, especially after suffering various stereo Bluetooth headsets from Rocketfish and Motorola)!
- Good connection distance (+1.5 stars).
- Support for up to 32GB micro SD card (+0 stars: I don't reward honesty in advertising).
- Easy to update firmware from the Android phone (+1.5 stars: I'm a firmware slut).
- Smaller than you think Sony could make it (+0 stars: it's small, but kind of awkwardly shaped).

The Bad (-6.25 stars)
- Bigger than you hoped Sony had made it (-0 stars for the same reason as above).
- Crap instructions, product information and website support (-1 star).
- There's no reason to spend the money on the "pro" version of the headset (-1 stars).
- No noise cancelling microphone (-1.5 stars).
- The shiny case pulls fingerprints and smudges from thin air, insulting the awesome display in bright sunlight (-0.25 stars because it remains very legible even when smudged).
- It may just be my phone model, but text messaging has been hit-or-miss (-0.25 stars because I prefer other applications, anyway).
- FM radio reception could be a lot better (-0.1 stars. Who listens to FM? Download I Heart Radio).
- Tangle free cordage means this headset isn't at all discreet in more professional settings (-0.3 stars. The benefits outweigh the detriments).
- While it can support up to 32GB of storage, it can only play mp3 and WAV files, negating some of the advantage of supporting 32GB of storage space (-0.15 additional stars for not having clear instructions regarding this matter plus another -0.2 stars for picking two of the stupidest file formats to support when the music player sounds as good as this one can).
- Finicky fit for the SD card and an absurd place to cut manufacturing costs (-1.5 stars).
-  No weatherproofing (-0.25 because it was never advertised as weather resistant, but would have made sense to design it that way).

THE RATING: 4.25 stars, or an 85% success for those dorks that find the star rating system flawed.

The Review

It took a little while to set up since the manufacture's materials are pretty sparse, but once I got everything downloaded and updated, I was happier than a pig in poop. This is a link that helped me out quite a bit: [...]. I'd skip the computer download update procedure unless you don't have 4G. It took my phone about three minutes to download the firmware package and stream it to the Sony MW1.

It's nice to finally find an accessory that doesn't come with white ear buds and is designed SPECIFICALLY for Android users (especially after Nike announced that it is cancelling Android support for its Smart Band). In a world that has been dominated by cutesy add-ons for the iPhone, it feels good to know that Sony is developing products that Android users never knew they needed.

And what a great Android accessory it is! This is a very sleek and techy looking bit of gear. That being said, it's also a bit too large to wear in more formal settings. This is unfortunate considering there are plenty of people like me that want to freedom of Bluetooth while not looking like that guy that wears his Bluetooth headset. If it was a little thinner and a little longer, it could be used as a tie clip, which would be a pretty sweet way to wear the MW1 in a professional setting!

As it is, though, you're not going to look as lame as the model on the back of the box... but you're not going to look very cool, either; especially when your shiny new neck accessory is covered up by the greasy fingerprints of rocking through Papa Pastrami's lunch bucket bargain. The good news is that that white on black display looks very expensive AND works very well, even in the glare of reflected sunlight and haze of Taco Tuesday finger smudges.

The tangle free cord design doesn't help things look less dorky. However, the image tradeoff is worth the sound quality of these ear buds. Sony has released a set of headphones that sound like... Sony! For those concerned about the sound quality of the Bluetooth audio, don't be. I don't know how Sony did it, but music sounds just as good when it is streamed from your phone as it does when it is played from the MW1's internal memory card!

That may seem to make the memory card redundant.

It doesn't. There are times when I want to be able to listen to music and take phone calls or read text messages or check email or get the latest RSS update from the LA Times... and doing all these things without having to fiddle around with my massive Otterbox encased HTC Rezound. That's pretty much ALL THE TIME... except when I'm jogging, lifting weights, hiking, etc. It's nice to be able to stash my phone deep inside my manpurse or backpack when taking the metro and still have all important social and communication information available at my fingertips. It's just as nice having a standalone music player when I need to unplug from my social tether and zone out to music through secure and comfortable high quality ear buds.

The MW1 handles it all... just some very important things not as well as it should.

Considering the active role the MW1 can serve, I would have liked to see some gaskets and a tighter bottom so I could be more comfortable in the wet. This is, however, a minor issue that can be solved with a plastic bag and prudence.

Another issue is that text messaging and alerts seem to work off and on. This is probably because the Sony text software does not work with my phone. I can solve the problem using a different application like Vlingo or Maluuba, so the issue isn't that annoying.

My major grievance with Sony's design is the lack of a second noise-cancelling microphone. Using this in the wind is going to be problematic, which is a shame considering I use Bluetooth when I'm on the move. Also, plugging this in to your car stereo using the 3.5mm jack is an issue: without noise cancellation, the person on the other end of the conversation is going to get a feedback loop of everything they're saying, creating a very distracting echo. Most disappointing is that this is a flaw that cannot be fixed with a firmware update.

This isn't a problem when using the MW1 specifically as designed with ear buds or other headphones: call quality has been reported as very good so far (as long as I'm indoors and in a quiet space), but it would be nice for Sony to deliver features that are standard on inexpensive Bluetooth headsets... especially when the Sony demands a premium suggested price.

On the subject of price: skip the $150 ($80 when I picked it up) "pro" model of the MW1. You can't do anything with a puny 2GB of storage and you don't need the AC charger. The "lite" model is exactly the same (even including the USB micro SD card reader), minus the worthless micro SD card and pointlessly redundant charger, for $75.

While the MW1 will work on an iPhone, it is only a basic Bluetooth headset/mp3 player.

Speaking of mp3, the MW1 will only recognize either mp3 or WAV file formats when loaded onto the internal memory card. This is disappointing, and something I hope Sony fixes with a firmware update. I'm a fan of using FLAC on my media drive and converting files to the m4a format to play on my phone or laptop. By the time I convert FLAC to 256 bitrate m4a's, I've got A LOT of good sounding music everywhere I go.

The only way I could get my music collection down to 32GB of mp3 files was by using a 96kbps bitrate. While the quality is still adequate for jogging or hooking up to my car's factory stereo and cruising, I would prefer support for file formats that are becoming more and more common. I'm genuinely mystified that WAV is supported: this isn't Zack Morris' MP3 player.

And it isn't a very well designed music player, but THE MW1 IS NOT DEFECTIVE!!! Sony may release poor designs, but they don't make crap. Here are some answers to common issues I've read in other reviews that are due to poor design, instructions and website support material compounded by inadequate user competence. I would have found the following things useful to know:

1) Are my files in a recognized format?

I believe the lack of file format support could be one of the reasons people have reported problems with their SD cards failing to be recognized. There's no way to tell if the card is mounted or not (no formatting options like most stand-alone music players or a mounting option like an Android phone) properly or not from the display. If you're like me and try copying your music library without reading the small (not to mention ambiguous) print, you'd have a hard time knowing what user error is responsible for a poor experience using the MW1 as a music player.

I had inserted a non-formatted card with documents and music when I first got the MW1. I saw that it recognized music files and was happy to know I had received a "good unit" from Sony. I proceeded to reformat the card and copy my entire music library of m4a files. No music was recognized because the file format is not recognized. If I hadn't previously seen music files on the card, I would have probably returned the MW1 due to the impression left by previous (and misinformed) feedback.

2) Is my card properly aligned?

There have been a lot of gripes that only the Sony SD card works with the MW1, or that the MW1 doesn't really support 32GB cards. This isn't true, but rather due to a very stupid design flaw commited by Sony.

The MW1 does not have a traditional micro SD mount with the spring-loaded mechanism. The problem is that it is difficult to tell when the card is properly aligned and seated without the spring-lock hardware. As a result, I got error messages... or the MW1 would not recognize the memory card at all if I did not perfectly center the card. However, once I discovered I could be at least as smart as the MW1, I used a number of microSD cards I have laying around without a problem.

3) Is my microSD card inserted deep enough?

That's right, guys: you're going to have to take some time getting the job done right with the MW1. You've paid attention to the ambiguous clues and gotten the bottom off. Then you went ahead and made sure you put it in gently and the correct way. What else is there?

Bottom out.

The card won't mount if you don't insert it deep enough into the tight dark hole, and without a spring mount it's difficult to tell whether or not your load of music has found a home inside the MW1. You have to go ridge deep, but be gentle: you don't want to bend or break anything.

4) There is a specific way of copying the correct files to a correctly mounted card that works for me. I copy all the artist folders to the root. For example, instead of copying the "My Music" folder to the SD card, I copy "The Beastie Boys," which contains all other album folders, to the root of the SD card. It isn't as organized (at least visually-speaking, for the OCD among us) as it is on my desktop, but the MW1 recognizes the songs, albums, artists and plays them in any requested fashion from the SD card without hesitation... addressing all major grievances of previous complaints.

It isn't all the firmware's fault.

It isn't all Sony's lack of comprehensive instructions fault (and who can blame them for not publishing more than they have to?).

As a matter of fact, writing as someone that took two hours to do a little Googling and experimentation to get the MW1 to work as advertised, 80% of the blame for the negative reviews rests on the shoulders of the reviewers too dense to do much more than complain and give up.

All in all, I'm very satisfied with this purchase and the job Sony is doing to embrace Android users that demand as much utility in their accessories as they do applications. It isn't perfect, but most of my complaints can be solved with firmware updates... of which Sony releases with the celebrated regularity of a gluttonous vegan.
profile.summary: Very good, almost great.

profile.description: Wix Air Filters remove soot, carbon, abrasives and contaminants from the air before mixing with the fuel. They are made of pleated paper and are placed inside a plastic box which is connected to the throttle body. These filters are highly durable and can be easily installed.
profile.reviewText:
I first purchased a FRAM from an auto parts store to replace the air filter in my girlfriend's 2006 Acura TL and found it too small for the filter box. After reading some good things about the Wix filter, I ordered it from Amazon for less than the POS FRAM cost!

The filter is a perfect fit and it seems to work really well. The unit installed by a mechanic at the last B12 service seemed restricting and the motor would occasionally knock at the upper RPM range when under full throttle. The motor seems much more relaxed with this filter, and the high RPM knocks have gone away. Thanks to some random freak weather in Southern California, I've tested it under full throttle in sub-freezing temperatures as well as at 100 degrees. This seems like a very good product, which is in line with my previous experiences with the Wix brand.

Here's a bonus hint that addresses some of the complaints about replacing the filter: get out at Philips screwdriver and remove the piece of plastic along the ridge of the inner fender. There are two retainers. Unscrew them, carefully pull the plastic piece away from the fender and set it aside. THEN undo the filter box screws and lift the top to expose and change the filter. It's still a tight fit, but it's easy to navigate what was previously impossible.
profile.summary: Perfect fit for an '06 Acura TL

profile.description: Pollen, allergens, various fuel-based contaminants from the outside road environment all pass into and are filtered by your vehicle's Cabin Air Filter, or CAF. A TYC CAF is designed to have the same or better filtration efficiency as the original equipment filter: its identical dust load capacity ensures the same amount of particulate-collecting power, while factory-correct level of pressure drop ensures proper air flow through the vehicle's cabin. Each TYC CAF also comes with step-by-step installation instructions for ease of replacement.
profile.reviewText:
This is the OEM cabin air filter for the 2006 Acura TL, and trust me: this thing does what it's supposed to do. I couldn't believe how much crud this thing had caught between the B12 service on my girlfriend's 2006 TL.

One thing I will say is that this is a PITA to replace. After disconnecting the glove compartment door and removing the two screws and push fittings securing the assembly to the console, pull the console down. Directly down. That means sit in the passenger seat and apply equal force to both sides of the assembly... or you'll break a tab and your interior will never be the same. I've seen two people make the mistake of busting the tabs loose right to left. Don't be another.
profile.summary: Perfect fit for the 2006 Acura TL

profile.description: AEM Synthetic Air Filter Cleaner loosens and dissolves dirt and grime build up on synthetic filters so they can be rinsed clean with water. This cleaner is perfect for AEM Dryflow air filters and other synthetic air filters.
profile.reviewText:
First of all, I purchased an AEM filter to avoid having to use the two step K&N recharge process. I grew tired of walking the balance between inadequate oiling leading to dust particulate along my intake runner or over-oiling leading to fouled MAF sensors. Taking five thousand miles to find out if I got the oiling correct is too much of a concern when it comes to a daily driver.

Enter the AEM sythetic media filters (and I went with a heavy duty model because I frequently drive on roads that are less traveled for a reason): Saturate with cleaner, backflush with water, air dry and go drive without any concerns until you need to service your filter again. I love it.

This is the first time I've used the cleaner, and it does the job it's supposed to do. The dirt came out without much of a fight, leaving the gray media... gray, and I feel confident that using the AEM product will keep my filter treated properly between services.

Some people use Formula 409 or Simple Green. I prefer to stick with OEM: the small additional expense is more than worth it for a component as important as your air filter.
profile.summary: Does the job well.

profile.description: Walker Resonators and Welded Resonator Assemblies provide precise tuning technologies to ensure excellent flow characteristics and OE-style sound. They feature 100% aluminized construction for longer life, quality appearance and favorable acoustics. These are OE-style resonators that fit, perform and sound like the original system.
profile.reviewText:
I used this to replace the straight-pipe the previous owner of my car installed to make an inexpensive import sound like an inexpensive imported angry insect.

The bends are perfect and it is indeed quiet. At 75mph, all I can hear is road and wind noise. Under acceleration, all that comes into the cabin is a faint growl that is attributed to the cold air intake that is also installed. I like that noise, however, as it is reminiscent of Subaru's boxer motors.

Now for the bad: It's NOT stainless, so count on replacing it every few years or moving out West. I'm not sure if this will work, but I coated mine with a few layers of inexpensive BBQ paint in order to protect it from the environment. A few years will let me know if this tactic succeeds, but for $40 you're getting a resonator that seems quieter than the stock piece and doesn't seem to restrict flow too much.

The mounts for hanging on the rubber mounts don't have caps welded on, so make sure everything is good to go when you're doing your 5k services. Not a big deal, but something to be aware of.

The inlet is sized awkwardly if you're installing it behind the OEM cat. Be prepared to cut it down (or get perilously close to the second O2 sensor if you decide to butcher the stock pipe, which I recommend against: it's way thicker) in order to get it to fit, then break out your welder (or have fun finding the right clamp adapter). This is made to mate with the Walker aftermarket cat assembly, not the OEM one (which includes the resonator for the reasonable sum of $700), so it's not a surprise it doesn't fit perfectly.

Also, the outlet is sized to fit with the Walker muffler, which I also installed. It fits perfectly, just make sure you order the gasket. Check out the Walker website for your part numbers.
profile.summary: Not stainless, but church-mouse quiet

profile.description: With The Polaroid Adapter Tube you will be able to add to your camera (model specified above) wide angle, macro, telephoto, fisheye conversion lenses & all different type of filters to increase your photo options.
profile.reviewText:
My primary reason for buying this was to protect my P7000's lens and give me a more stable "SLR-like" shooting grip.

The protection side of things works well. I don't shoot in wide-angle very often, so the slight vignetting for the first 20% of the zoom doesn't matter to me. I feel more comfortable lugging this camera around in my bag with the additional protection to the most vulnerable part of the camera.

As for a stable grip, I can't trust this as much as I would like to. There is far too much wobble (and I'm talking a degree or two, which is TOO MUCH for something custom-made for a specific camera). While I still use it to hold like I do my SLR, I'd like some more heft to the package. I may be able to fix the wobble with an o-ring or something from the hardware store, but the fit is definitely not the equivalent of the Nikon piece.
profile.summary: It's okay. That's it.

top_5.reviewText:
This is a fine case for traveling with your tablet. It is constructed of quality materials with plenty of high quality and heavy duty protection, and it is large enough to store a Samsung Note 8.0 tablet in the main compartment and a full-size folding Bluetooth keyboard in the pocket. Not quite enough room to also store a charger, but I've never found myself using one while traveling, anyway.

The case firmly holds the tablet in a landscape perspective, and if your turn the case over you have multiple viewing angles... pretty slick. The anchors for the tablet are thinner than the bezel of the Note 8.0, so it doesn't interfere with any of the functions of thhe tablet. All keys are readily accessible, the screen is stable enough to use the S-pen, and the viewing angles are comfortable in any situation from using it on a table, in bed or on an airplane's folding tray table.

Another bonus is that the case amplifiies and deepens the sound coming from the Note 8.0's speakers a little bit. I usually wear headphones, so this is a minor bonus, but I thought it was pretty cool.

That capacity and protection also contributes to the case's main fault: it's just too big for most daily users. This is a case for traveling: throw it in your suitcase or backpack and go to your flight without much concern. You can toss it on the x-ray machine without worry. You can drop your luggage without concern. You could probably even throw your tablet like a Frisbee and come out golden as long as you weren't playing against a wall or on concrete.

But it's too big for an office person, and the brown tweed is not that attractive in professional settings, unless you're a college professor with suede patches on the elbows of your 1972 sports jacket.

That being said, I LOVE suede elbow patches, worn fedora hats and even houndstooth. My problem with the fabric is that it's not the gray illustrated in the photos, but rather a very brown brown. If you know how to wear suits, you know that gray goes with everything: it's the complete absense of color.

Brown, on the other hand? It's too casual unless its leather, which this is not.

Traveling or carting your tablet around in a backpack: A+

Professional environments or keeping your tablet in a well-organized attache that already provides good protection: C-. Wrong color. Wrong size. Overkill protection.

Overall: a solid B performer.
top_5.summary: While the color is off, the quality is good.

top_5.description: The Mountain has been in business for over 30 years and printing t-shirts for over 21 of those years. From our earliest days, we have worked to be a responsible company. We have a green philosophy and every day we strive to run our company and produce our products in a way that protects the environment, gives value to our customers and supports our employees and the artists.
top_5.reviewText:
This isn't a review written in a way that makes me sound as witty as everyone else. I have a beard. I know my beer and bourbon. My manhood is adequate: I also drink wine and I believe in equal pay for equal work..

What I will say is that The Mountain has taken it to the next level with their Dubya Shark in ways that make me actually look forward to the results of the 2016 and 2020 elections.

Political beliefs aside, this is a great shirt that everyone has reacted to positively. While the other shirts seem to satirize "'Mer'ca" as much as they do the president depicted, this shirt looks to be a direct shot at George Dub. That being said, even my most hardcore conservative friends like this shirt as a joke, whereas the other shirts seem to actually work as a sort of political mating call, especially at outfitter stores and car shows.

This shirt has proudly taken its place in the mix of my Mountain collection, and I can't wait to see what the future brings for the Obama edition.

top_5.description: This is the maintenance product manufacturers recommend most! Only '303' beautifies as intensely, protects as powerfully or lasts as long. This provides powerful UV screening protection for colored gel-coat fiberglass, inflatable boats, vinyl, clear vinyl windows, rubber, plastics and leather.? Just spray on and wipe dry!? Treated surfaces repel dirt, soiling, staining, water spots, salt water and mildew. Note: Each bottle of 303 is sold separately.
top_5.reviewText:
PROs

- Great product for a good price.
- Painlessly restores exterior black plastics.
- Doesn't smell horrible.

CONs

- Attracts a lot of dust.
- Doesn't smell good.

THE REVIEW

After reading and hearing about 303 for quite a while, I finally caved and purchased it. The first thing I noticed is that it applies and works in a very similar way to the "nano" line of Turtle Wax products that were available a few years ago. The best way to describe how plastic looks after application is to say it resembles freshly exfoliated skin.

It just looks healthier.

Part of the benefit is that the plastic is clean and free of dust. The other part of the benefit is that 303 actually penetrates the plastic and restores it's chemical properties that are slowly eroded by the sun, pollution, and the elements. I was a skeptic of this claim initially since it seems to "science" to be non-fiction, but 303's claims are true. The black plastic on my cowl was severely oxidized and damaged from the previous owner's use of Armor All (HORRIBLE!!!). One application of 303 brought back the deep rich black and it has lasted through two months of 100+ heat and rainy days in the 50s.

This is a fantastic product.

I use it after cleaning my plastic with a mixture of Simple Green diluted with distilled water. Forget the combination cleaner/conditioner sprays. Outside of smelling good, they offer no real lasting benefit. The stuff that cleans weakens the stuff that conditions, and vice versa. I clean with Simple Green once a week and treat with 303 once a month. I treat the exterior plastic whenever I wash my car. This schedule has restored my car's interior and maintained her exterior... and I don't care that it will never be considered on a collector's list!
top_5.summary: This stuff works great for making plastic pretty and attracting dust.

THE REVIEW

I was looking for a sweet mullet for a ski-resort McGuyver costume. This fit the bill in both color, volume, and texture: it screams mid-80s Philadelphia hockey goon. I love it.

Anyway, after some experimentation and the fact that my beard was in heat, showing a luster that was both sublime and outstanding simultaneously, my fat ski-resort McGuyver costume was substituted by Ray "USA!" Jackson. Granted, the color was off, but I explained that with some self-tanner: Ray Jackson after enjoying a month of rehabilitation at a Fiji ocean cabin. This also required two hours of crossed eyes and some gauze.

If you don't know Ray Jackson, you deserve a vicious beating by Chun Li.

This wig falls apart pretty easily, but I believe that's because the mullet is attempting to breed, spreading itself in spores like a cultural mold. Like most mushrooms, edible or hallucinogenic, it's cheap at a little under $16, so some flaws in durability are excusable.

The mullet is also hot. Like REALLY hot, though this could be due to the large amount of Jagermeister consumed over the course of two days. The antics of said two days could also explain the molting, but I'm hoping to get another season out of it because I just found the perfect fat ski resort McGuyver ski jacket at a thrift store and that costume NEEDS to happen.

top_5.description: What's Better than a quart of luscious homemade ice cream, sorbet or frozen yogurt? Two quarts! The fully automatic Cuisinart Pure Indulgence makes 2 quarts of your favorite frozen desserts or drinks in as little as 25 minutes. It's easy - an intergrat
top_5.reviewText:
I love my little Cuisinart ice cream maker!

If you've ever used an old-school ice cream machine with ice and salt, you are going to flip the $%&# out with how easy it is to make ice cream with a frozen cylinder. All you do is freeze the tub, assemble the machine, turn it on, slowly add your batter, and hang out.

While the newer models of nearly all brands offer separate settings for frozen yogurt and sorbet, you really don't need more precise equipment than your own eyeballs to make really good frozen deserts. For the price, this thing is a great device, and the extra half quart over the older models is awesome.

One complaint I have is that this adds a little too much air to the batter for my taste. This is intentional because the recipes in the book call for fairly lower-fat options (this is ice cream: "lower" fat is a relative term), where I prefer my batters to be closer to frozen custards. The extra air with all that fat gives the results a slightly chewy, almost taffy-like quality.

My guess is that this machine rolls in about 40-50% air into the final mixture if you let it run long enough, which is totally fine. The extra air helps your flavors escape sooner, leading to very good desserts using modest amounts of extracts. That makes homemade ice creams less expensive, and definitely way better than store-bought varieties.

I prefer my air content to be down around 15-20%. This leads to a denser, richer ice cream that satisfies my sweets cravings with far smaller servings. And I'm a total ice cream machine. I usually can't get enough of the stuff during the summer, and have been known to smash prodigious amounts during the winter, too. Anything I can do to keep my portions down is good.

How I solve the air problem is simple: I don't let it churn as long as the directions call for. I'll let my custard chill in the fridge overnight, then move it to the freezer (in a thin-walled brownie tin) for about an hour before churning it. This allows for the temperature to drop just above the point of crystal formation, so when it hits the frozen cylinder, it freezes almost instantly.

This is also why I like to turn on the machine before adding the mixture: otherwise I'd end up with a custard slushy.

Churning takes about 9-12 minutes, depending on the butterfat content of what I'm making. Then I transfer the soft serve rapidly into a pre-chilled container and let it hard set for a few hours. Easy as pie, and the final result is always awesome.

I use the same technique for making sorbets, though I prefer higher air contents in frozen yogurt for some reason. Regardless of what I'm making, or how I want it to come across while consuming, this machine always gives me great results. You just have to use your peepers, and after watching a few batches transform in the rotating cylinder, you'll know exactly what to look for when conducting your own tasty experiments.

Buy it. Play with it. Get fat. It's fun.
top_5.summary: This thing makes the @&#$! out of ice cream!

input: Generate the review text written by a reviewer who has a given an overall rating of "5.0" for a product with description "ICED EARTH have returned with a vengeance! With "The Glorious Burden," the legendary US heavy metal band have delivered one of the true heavy metal gems of 2004: an epic and conceptual tour-de-force that showcases the riff-mastery of Jon Schaffer and the vocal prowess of former Judas Priest singer Tim "Ripper" Owens.". The summary of the review text is "Astounding.  Spellbinding.  Stellar.  Any of those words".
output:
"Good God!" were my first words when I listened to the approx 30 minute long, 3-song spanning EPIC trilogy chronicling the Battle of Gettysburg.  And that wasn't even the entire CD!

I admit I'm not a big fan of Iced Earth (mostly because I rarely heard of them before).  I don't even want to dip my foot into the whole reviewer controversy I think I see about the Matt Barlow vs Tim Owens debate between Iced Earth fans.  In my own opinion, based upon the songs in "The Glorious Burden" and other Iced Earth songs from Barlow's time, I'd say Tim Owens is a much better vocalist in my opinion...

But this album is spellbinding.  One of the best I've ever heard.  The first 9 tracks are beautifully melodic masterpieces chronicling various events in world, and primarily American, history

1- Star Spangled Banner: Terrifying to our foes, glorifying to Americans, etc, blah, blah, wine, blood.  Pretty much what I expected; the star spangled banner played on guitar, kinda like what Jimi Hendrix did

2- Declaration Day (9/10): great way to start off an album.  A song about the Declaration of Independence signing.  A great thrumming beat goes throughout the song which fits in well with what the colonists must have felt that day.

3- When The Eagle Cries (8/10): Good song about 9/11 attacks, with little biasedness.  It is greatly written, with the right words at the right time and place.

4- The Reckoning (10/10): Excellent single, pure rock song about Justice and vengeance.  The highpitched vocals are stellar and just "wow"

5- Greenface (9/10): Song which keeps bringing John Kerry and the game Battlefield Vietnam to mind.  Assuming by the lyrics, name, and picture in the CD booklet, I'd say this has to do with the Vietnam war.  Nice sound with good vocals.

6- Valley Forge (10/10): Great ode to the Colonial soldier suffering at Valley Forge.  Also good lyrics criticizing our lazy and apathetic nature towards our government today ("Would he look upon us now in anger and disgust?") ("Will we let ignorance and laziness bring our demise?")

7- Attila (9/10): A ballad to our favourite Hun conqueror!  A song about the man who dominated nearly an entire continent, it is powerful.  What else should I say?

8- Hollowman (7/10): I still can't figure what this song is about, but it has a good sound to it

9- Red Baron/Mad Max (7/10)

Gettysburg

10- The Devil To Pay (10/10): Day 1 of battle.  An astoundingly beautiful song, beginning with a lone bagpipe and drum playing the star spangled banner, Anthem of the Union.  Some seconds later, a banjo playing dixie, Anthem of the Confederacy, joins in.  And then begins the cannonfire.  The song is well put together and chronicles the events of the first day, when not in lyrics, then in music.  Also has a moving rendition of "When Johnny Comes Marching Home" at the que of General Reynold's death.  It goes on to play several variations of the song, mixed with Dixie later on.  The song ends with solemn sounding drum beats which leads into Day 2

11- Hold At All Costs (10/10): Day 2 of battle.  Song begins with a moving ballad based upon two generals who fought that day, one on the Union, one on the Confederates, who were like brothers, now forced to do battle.  The song is more heavier and rough-around-the-edge than the first and third.  The song ends with a climactic drum beat which leads into Day 3

12- High Water Mark (10/10): Day 3 of battle.  The high point of all action is focused primarily in this song.  It's also the only song with dialogue between Generals, with Tim Owens and Jon Schaffer (or Matt Barlow I think) as the other.  The dialogue fits in with the music and even rhymes.  The song plots General Lee's plans, and General Longstreet's faithlessness in Lee's plan.  It goes on with the battle raging about, with several orchestral and overall instrumental parts raging on, with the occasional sound effects of cannonfire.  Then comes the final attack of the Confederacy, with a speech from a field general ("We're almost there my boys, I've never worked with finer") etc.  A bridge then plays, and ends with the shout "CHARGE!!", then the sound of thousands of men rushing forth, followed by gunfire, and then bayonet fighting in a climactic instrumental battle scene worthy of Hollywood fame.  The climax ends with a tragic monologue by General Lee (voiced by Tim Owens), where he pleads for God's forgiveness for his faulty planning ("It's all my fault, their blood is on my hands") ("God forgive me, please forgive me") ("It's over now, we are retreating, I never thought that we'd be beaten")("Is this God's will after all?").  It goes on to play a climactic outro which slowly fades into a sad violin soli of the initial melody of The Devil To Pay.  A majestic way to end a majestic trilogy.

Spectacular!  Worth ever half penny I paid for this album!

profile.reviewText:
Note: The version I am watching is 1 hour and 34 minutes long, so it is apparently the Special Edition 94 minute one.

My only knowledge of Babylon 5 comes from great and rave reviews about its great writing and storylines and story arcs, and the charges that "Star Trek: Deep Space Nine" plagiarized the idea.

Hopefully the series lives up to its reception and to the reception its allegedly ripped-off Star Trek equivalent has received, because this intro movie is horrid on almost every level.

Starting on the most unfair level; the visual effects.  Considering this came out in 1993, it's unfair to complain about bad effects because CGI technology was very new.

But considering that this was also the time in which Star Trek was dominating the Sci-Fi circuit with TNG winding down and Deep Space Nine beginning, the look of the two shows from one to the two others is like the difference between a finely crafted guitar and a shoebox with fishing wire on it.

From what I hear and know, the only CG used in Star Trek at that point was for the phaser effects.  Everything else was standard visual effects and the use of models and miniatures.  By comparison, this TV movie uses full CG.

And it looks horrid.  In space, the ships all look flat, with no substance or shading and stiff, blocky shadows that look as artificial as everything else.  It's as if there are lights shining in all directions.  It's all on par with the sort of things you'd see in Doom or Duke Nukem 64, rendered again and again to completely remove any and all traces of realism, grit, or even believability from these shots.  Every time a shot from space is played, it's like having your head slammed into a table and jerked back up, a total break from the immersion and you're left gawking at how awful and pathetic that looked.

Moving on to the fairer things: The acting.

The acting is BAD.  The only person who is a decent actor is the Vorlon guy who was on Star Trek as a Romulan commander.  This Jeffrey Sinclair person sounds like his acting experience comes from watching TV and movies and then being given a script for the first time and told to act.  He's either completely emotionless or so horribly forced, it utterly kills scenes that are supposed to be tense or emotional.

But he's not alone.  The guy playing Garibaldi sounds almost exactly like Randal Graves in "Clerks", and even speaks in almost exactly the same tone and temperament.  It's impossible to take him seriously with the name of an Italian war hero and the voice of a snot-nosed punk clerk.

Londo Mollari, whose actor clearly IS an actor, but with hair that is two feet tall, fanning out the back of his head, and utterly bald everywhere else, I was shocked to learn he's supposed to be an alien.  Straight out from under the Iron Curtain, based on that scruffy "Generic East European" accent he chomps on so hammily, it's more annoying than humorous, if he's even supposed to be the humor character.

Takashima and the telepath, with all the personality of a goldfish between them, are somehow even worse than Sinclair's actor, with virtually all of Takashima's lines sounding as lifeless as a middle school drama student being asked to sight-read a monologue without any preparation.

All the rest are too stale and below average to warrant special attention, aside from the doctor's hilarity-enducing "Now will someone please tell me what tha HELL is going on around here!", but the description mentioned above, of amateur drama students acting for the first time pretty accurately describes everyone in every role, except for Andreas Katsulas and Peter Jurasik.

But maybe they all sound vapid and confused for the reason that they don't understand what the hell they're reading and speaking.  I know I don't.  "What the hell is going on around here?" is a pretty accurate statement for the entire first hour and 15 minutes, as names, alien species, and events are dropped liberally and at random, with almost no explanation or understanding, and immediate events unfolding involving an attempted poisoning of an ambassador and a shapeshifter apparently responsible.  Exactly what else is filing in the other 60 minutes of that 10 minute plotpoint is purely speculation on my part.

Don't misunderstand, I LOVE it when science fiction chooses not to dwell on exposition, going by either "show, don't tell" as with Battlestar Galactica, or letting relevant information be covered with relevant dialogue, or as Star Wars does, leave background information to be filled in (for better or worse) by expanded universe novels, video games, and comics, to make for a richer experience with the movies that is not needed to go along with it, as well as making more money by producing more work.

Whatever Babylon 5: The Gathering is doing in its first 75 of 94 minutes, it sure as hell ain't any of that.  Events unfold and you're expected to follow along, then try not to act surprised when something else happens that makes no sense or comes out of nowhere.  Add to that the horrifyingly bad acting, and far too many scenes of droning expository dialogue, and you're bored into submission long before you can figure out what is happening and why.
profile.summary: Sincerely hope the series is good

profile.description: Extreme Championship Wrestling is back with a vengeance. After a four-year hiatus, the maniacal Paul Heyman and his band of Extremists have returned, delivering the "anything goes" Extreme Rules matches that sports-entertainment fans have come to love. ECW: Extreme Rules will deliver some of the best matches of today, mixed with incredible early ECW matches that set the standard. This two-disc collection is hosted by Tazz and Joey Styles, and includes their alternate commentary of the legendary Extreme Death Match between Tazz and Sabu from Living Dangerously 1999 to unify the FTW and ECW championships. Also, Tommy Dreamer and Jonathan Coachman provide alternative commentary of the jaw-dropping Scaffold Match between Dreamer and Brian Lee from High Incident 1996.
profile.reviewText:
Like some of us, after the wild success of ECW One Night Stand 2006, I had high hopes for ECW on Sci-Fi---it was on a cable channel, and it was on late at night.

It's been more than half a year.  And I'm watching an hour-long extension to RAW and/or Smackdown.

Owning just about everything to do with ECW, Vince McMahon had a potential hit on his hands, and while he skimmed us in the One Night Stands by editing some ECW superstars' music and having his WWE talent barge in and compete (2006) or just whine and bitch that ECW sucks (2005), it was still extreme, and spellbinding to watch.

ECW on Sci-Fi is not a shell of old ECW---it's another brand of WWE with an ECW sticker slapped onto the screen.  The only original ECW wrestlers ("brilliantly" labeled "ECW Originals") are the Sandman, Tommy Dreamer, Sabu, Rob Van Dam, and Balls Mahoney.  Tazz doesn't wrestle.  The "brilliantly" labeled "New Breed" has some impressive-looking characters like Kevin Thorn and CM Punk, but the rest are the same stale WWE circus show of sad, unlikeable gimmicks like the extraordinarily dull Elijah Burke or the amazingly lame Mike Knox or the ever-present career-jobber Hardcore Holly (who seems to have been shoved into ECW brand simply because of his name "Hardcore")

Titles are likely to change hands maybe once every three or four PPVs, just like in WWE, matches feature an all-time low on athletics (save for when Sabu and RVD are at work), and an all-time high on pillow-strikes (wrestling term for cheap fake punches and stomps) and the storylines are as easily predictable as in WWE.

Disk 1 has matches from Old ECW.  Good.  But this DVD collection isn't about Old ECW.  It's about new ECW.  If you want a great collection of old ECW matches, try Blood Sport ECW: Most Violent Matches.

Tell Vince McMahon that he's made a mistake with this "new breed" of ECW, and with the firing of Paul Heyman, it's only gotten... just as dull as ever.  Don't support more of this.
