profile.description: Windows 7 Professional Upgrade
profile.reviewText:
Three month update:
(1) I'm changing this rating of this from three to four stars (after solving my biggest lingering issue; this was principally an eSATA hardware issue, not a Windows 7 issue, but which available support offerings did little to help resolve).

(2) I finally isolated the recurring --but intermittent-- shutdown, non-responsive task manager and disappearing external hard drive issues that plagued this install of Windows 7. They were directly related to known issues with the eSATA interface of this Western Digital My Book Home 500 GB USB 2.0/FireWire 400/eSATA Desktop External Hard Drive WDH1CS5000N. Online research reveals an extended history of users experiencing a wide variety of performance issues with that hard drive's eSATA interface. In my case, when I switched from eSATA to USB 2, my Windows 7 immediately became stable and trouble free.

My other experiences in the upgrade from Vista to Windows 7 lead me to recommend this: don't wade into this upgrade unless you have confidence in your operating system troubleshooting kung fu. You'll probably need your best tricks should you have an obscure issue. But get through it...and Windows 7 is as good as any Windows operating system I've used (going back to Windows 3.1).

End of update. Original review content follows:

--------------------------------------

...just don't expect annoyance-free operation. It may be Windows 7, but it's first name remains "Windows". My experience: the benefits marginally outweigh the issues. But Windows 7 is not issue-free; don't consider unless you're a confident Windows troubleshooter.

Technology pundits wrote at length about Windows 7 in assessing the pre-release offering. Opinions abound, offered by both sycophantic Windows 7 fanboys and the zealous Windows haters (who seem to never tire of reminding Windows users that they are oh-so-cool with their overpriced Mac hardware or exotic distributions of Linux).

Market share alone tells the rest of the story: most of us --for whatever reasons-- are in a long term relationship with Windows operating systems at both home and work. If we're lucky, somebody else carries the upgrade decision and headaches of execution at work. As for home: even if we're in the market for a new computer (or just tired of Vista's quirks on an existing machine) and not yet ready to re-stock your entire applications catalog to go with Mac or Linux: then we're going to be dancing with Microsoft for a while.

What follows are the highs and lows of one user's experience.

This review focuses on the upgrade process, which began the day after the regular release. I'm still exploring some of the interface features.

Caution: mild geek-speak appears below:

This upgrade was for an 18-month old Dell XPS 420 desktop machine (similar, but not identical to the linked one. The machine receiving the upgrade holds a dual-core Intel E6850 CPU (3 GHZ), 4GB of RAM, two 500 GB (non-RAID) internal hard drives, an ATI Radeon HD 2600 XT graphics card with ethernet and audio integrated into the motherboard).

A long-term problem on this machine has been a conflict between Vista and the graphics adapter preventing me from *ever* successfully updating the graphics drivers; some of the attempted work-arounds have been very painful...and all unsuccessful. This was my primary reason for choosing to go from Vista to 7 (and to be fair, this problem is as much ATI's fault as Vista's; ATI user forums provide abundant discussion showing I was not alone in this situation).

Preparations for the upgrade took about an our to complete. My data files are regularly archived to an external hard drive, so this wasn't a big deal. If you're not as diligent about regular backups, you'll probably need more time.

My upgrade path (Vista Home Premium to 7 Professional) required the "custom" install approach, requiring a full reinstall install of your applications and data which won't make the trip from Vista to 7 (in truth it's only the installed applications that are sure goners; if had a senior moment and really forgot to backup valuable data, it may still be available in a folder named "windows.old" after the upgrade --but don't count on it; do your backups beforehand). I would have selected this choice even if the direct upgrade had been available; direct upgrades of Windows, with the seeming benefit of preserving your current applications and data are notorious for being buggy afterward.

I also went online to check for Windows 7-specific drivers for a scanner and two printers (a monochrome laser and an color inkjet) that are hooked to this machine. Two of these devices already had Windows 7 drivers available; the web site of the other promised "November" availability (and the Vista drivers worked perfectly well for the one still waiting for its Windows 7 update).

Once my data was backed up, the new drivers saved and I had collected the applications I would need to reinstall (some were on CD, some were downloaded executables) I started the journey from Vista to Windows 7.

Timeline (from loading the install DVD):
-5 minutes: notification that "upgrade" option (retaining files and applications) was not available and that the "custom" option was required.
-18 minutes: blue screen of death following long Vista shutdown sequence; not sure if this was normal or not.
-20 minutes: "starting Windows".
-29 minutes: installation "completed"; first automatic restart.
-32 minutes: installation "completed"; second automatic restart, and visual progress bar appears at bottom of screen.
-75 minutes: installation *really* complete, and initial Windows setup options offered.

Windows 7 immediately recognized my wireless mouse and keyboard; the printers and scanner drivers were installed the devices available within 45 minutes.

As a veteran of several earlier operating system upgrades, installs on new machines, or reloads on older machines, this was by far the easiest (to this point). No drastic solutions were needed that had occurred following other Windows OS upgrades due to disconnects between Microsoft and hardware vendors (including a very scary BIOS upgrade during an Windows ME to XP upgrade, and the required purchase of a new printer to replace one that simply wasn't supported by Vista).

Immediate improvements:
-The Start menu has been simplified (get this: selecting the Start | Shutdown sequence actually *SHUTS DOWN* the computer now, instead of launching a THIRD window (and you can speed this up further with readily available desktop gadgets that take you direct to shutdown)
-The programs listing is far easier to manage and customize, and the taskbar navigation is greatly improved. The taskbar permits greater control over its contents (and even if it can't keep an application for loading there, you can control which ones you see!).
-User access control is much less problematic than in Vista (the only warnings I've received is when trying to run executables).
-Folder navigation is far more intuitive, and I no longer feel like I'm managing my operating system at the same time I'm managing my tasks.

Immediately after installation, this Windows 7 machine shut down in 20 seconds. Start up now takes about 55 seconds from the BIOS/POST sequence to the first appearance of the OS splash screen, and the menu of users is available about 90 seconds after powering on. The user desktop is ready to work (mine is fairly cluttered, with a dozen or so shortcuts and six separate desktop gadgets) about 10 seconds after the user selection is made.

But it's not all sunny and mild with Windows 7:
Microsoft has presented us with far too many upgrade paths, and even a powerful machine will be constrained somewhat by the operating system if you try too much multitasking. Also, see below for a discussion of Adobe products and their compatibility with Windows 7.

2-week update:
More flaws emerge:

After three days, I developed shutdown hang. Went through Microsoft's chat support offering...but should have used the phone (as multiple restarts were required, adding additional time to re-establish chat with the same agent...and the technician surely should have suggested this). We spent about 90 minutes checking services via msconfig. I disagree with their suggestion to begin by assuming that all Microsoft services are not potential suspects for this, and that it's a non-MS service causing the hang. Bottom line after this is the problem has improved from being constant (when it first appeared) to intermittent.

When I finally upgraded the video card driver (the primary reason for making the move), the shutdown problem became less intermittent...but still present.

Since then, I've changed the power management setting from "balanced" to "performance" (not an issue with a desktop on AC power) and updated both the CPU chipset drivers and BIOS. These steps have collectively reduced --but has not eliminated-- shutdown issues. The chipset and BIOS tweaks are not things most users are going to want to mess around with (and the BIOS update always carries the risk of turning your motherboard into a paperweight should the power go out while its underway).
Other issues:
(1) sometimes the task manager won't launch
(2) sometimes the task manger won't end frozen processes
(3) sometimes it won't access data in an attached external hard drive (eSATA interface)...even though the drive itself is still recognized. This always clears up upon restart.
Presumably these are known to MS and will be corrected in an update or the first service pack.
(4) If you are running older versions of Adobe products (in my case, Acrobat 8, Photoshop Elements 6 and Premier Elements 4): you may have compatibility issues with these versions that Adobe does not "officially" support in Windows 7. While I place this issue firmly in Adobe's court, if you are using Adobe applications, do your homework. Adobe products are generally intrusive (in terms of both activation requirements and footprint within the tender areas of a PC operating system) and definitely not cheap. I think I've resolved this, but it wasn't free of trouble, cost or time to do so.

Please note that I experienced NONE of these things under Vista.

Finally:
If you are buying a new laptop or desktop with Windows 7 already installed:
you'll probably be a happy camper until you run into your first case of "we don't support Windows 7" (yet...or at all) with your version/model of software/hardware.
profile.summary: What Vista could have been; don't attempt upgrade without strong geek skills!

profile.description: Logitech Inc (966185-0403) Harmony 688 Remote Control
profile.reviewText:
...you won't be needing them after you trade in the confusion of many for the simplicity of one...

I've been using this remote since early 2006, and it has stood up to the test of time (and changing components!).

Unpack a shiny new piece of consumer electronics, and you often confront yet another remote soon after opening the box. Then it joins the constant struggle to avoid being lost (or crushed under the expanding pile of its partner remotes).

The H-688 can't eliminate reliance on remote control of your components, but it can get you to a point where you only have to worry about the location and status of one.

It does this via Logitech's online database of components. You'll need Internet access for initial set-up, when you add or change controlled devices, or if you want to check Logitech's support site for firmware updates.

Getting the Harmony to assume control of multiple devices is a four-part process:

(1) Install the associated software (Windows or Mac operating systems) either from CD or direct from Logitech; you'll be asked if you want to check online for a more current version.

(2) Create a user account with Logitech and enter information (function, make and model) about the components you want the remote to control into the application you just installed. The software uploads this to Logitech, and then then takes you through a menu-driven series addressing component and input options for each task ("watch a movie", "watch TV", "listen to CD", etc.). The software offers very sound  default options that are usually correct, but also lets you modify them for different configurations (for example, TV audio output to a CD audio input) that you might have.

(3) After you submit your component and task functions, the Harmony's firmware is updated from Logitech via a USB cable.

(4) The software then asks you to test each tasks, and offers troubleshooting and modification options. All of my components and tasks worked correctly the first time immediately, so I did not get to exercise these.

When set-up is complete, this remote has both fixed function controls for common activities, and a scrolling LCD display for others.

I completed this entire process in less than 30 minutes. My environment for this includes a TV, a home theater receiver and a gaming console (a Wii, which it can't control, but can manage the A/V inputs into the TV for Wii output). While the hardware environment is relatively simple, the task list is complex (watch TV, watch a DVD, listen to CD, listen to radio, play Wii). The Harmony gets everything synched so you can focus on your entertainment, and not managing your big pile of remotes.
profile.summary: Keep those old remotes in a safe place...

You won't need to stock up on lithium batteries or make sure you have a USB cable for charging...because these options aren't available. For modern Canon DSLRs, the primary variables are the abmient temperature the camera is used in (colder air = reduced operation time), use of the camera's integrated flash and the following shooting modes: (1) through the viewfinder *without* using the EOS "Live View" feature (the user guide estimates ~800 images with no flash at 73 degrees (F) and ~750 at 32 degrees (F). With 50% flash use, these numbers decrease to ~700 and ~650, respectively. (2) with EOS Live View: 240 images (no flash at 73 deg (F), 220 with 50% flash use (these decrease to 230 and 210 at 32 deg (F)0. (3) movie mode: ~110 minutes recording time at 73 deg (F) and 90 minutes at 32 deg (F). Charging time when new is around two hours, and generally under an hour after the initial charge. profile.description: Philips Revolution Motorized Portable Speaker Dock for iPhone/iPod: Motorized dock rotates for watching movies and videos. Wireless remote controls all basic functions. Class D digital amplifier with Dynamic Bass Boost. Advanced speaker technology for rich, static free sound. Runs on batteries or AC adaptor (included).
profile.reviewText:
This quirky device offers a combination of useful and puzzling features. While it produces sound that is clearly better than that the tinny, tiny sound that emerges from most laptop and netbook computers, there may be docking speaker units available with better sound that cost less. Combine this with at least one neglected --and badly needed-- interface feature, and the shortcomings of this product become apparent...especially as you ponder the ultimate utility of the "motorized" part of its name.

The good and useful:
-Accepts boths iPods and iPhones (bot not an iPod Nano); uses separate, interchangeable cradle adapters for the iPod and iPhone.
-Recharges the iPod/iPhone when it is docked.
-Remote control mirrors the familiar 4-way ring controller found on iPods.
-Sound quality is OK when compared to what you can get from most notebooks or netbooks. However, at this price, your are beginning to reach the entry point for decent entry-level bookshelf speakers and this unit can't compete with their quality. Yes, I realize the speakers don't charge personal music players and require a an audio programming source...but the sound output is the primary feature here, so the comparison is important.
-Also accepts audio from a laptop or desktop computer via a 3.5mm mini stereo plug (male-male; included). See above comments for its ability to improve that audio experience.
-Works on both AC power and 8 "AA" batteries.

The puzzling:
-The motorized dock. If you watch videos on your iPod/iPhone, the cradle on the front of this unit rotates 90 degrees to shift between portrait to landscape views. This is done using the included remote control. I just don't understand why this function is included. A user sitting far enough away to need the remote is unlikely to be able to make out much on an iPhone screen anyway. I'm trying to imagine the marketing and design sessions that led to this "feature", and my imagination comes up short...or assumes that it came out of a focus group of 8-year olds.

The missing:
-A big circular backlight frames the cradle in the center of the unit. While this cool enough, it doesn't provide any actual feedback about the device (except that it's powered on...and not even then, since it can be turned off separately from the speaker unit). Yet absent is any user feedback into how far you have turned the volume up or down. A scaled indicator should have been part of this backlight. This is primarily an audio output device; insight into the amount of output a user has dialed up would be nice.

Issues:
-Documentation: Ikea-like pictograms and a few bulleted text items raise as many questions than they answer.
-The AC adapter is a blocky "wall wart". Since the speaker unit weighs almost seven pounds, Philips should have internalized the AC-DC converter and returned precious space near electrical outlets to the consumer.
-Carrying handles are on the sides. I'm not sure why this would be better than a single handle on the top. I am sure that this makes the footprint of this device on a table or desk wider than it needs to be. It also forces it to be carried vertically. If the person carrying it this way is shorter than about 5'5", then it's going to be close to or in contact with the ground if carried by one of the handles on the end.
-The remote control is rather small. Thanks to commenter Jeff Kraus below who pointed out that it does fit into a magnetic storage slot on the rear of the unit.

Overall:
Hey: it's better than the sound from a portable computer. But for the money, docking/speaker alternatives are abundant (including many that will leave you with some money left over to download some new tunes to your iPod/iPhone).
profile.summary: Acceptable sound; puzzling features included and needed features missing...

profile.description: Language: Dutch / Synopsis: A young psychology student is drawn into the dark and fearful world of a diabolic and mysterious App that starts to terrorize her, distributing compromising photographs, videos and text messages about herself and delves deeper and deeper into her personal life, flawlessly exposing all of her deepest secrets.
profile.reviewText:
...and you won't have to subject your eyes and ears to lame writing, vapid characters, unresolved plot points and an utterly absurd concept.

In a nutshell (all spoiler: you'll thank me for it!):
Anna and Sophie are two 20-something best friends and college students. Anna rides a motorcycle. Anna's brother (Stan) is partially paralyzed from a motorcycle accident (although Anna still rides her Honda, wearing a black helmet a la Lisbeth Salander). Anna and Sophie are also taking scuba lessons together. Anna and Sophie go to a party where only the most naive movie watcher on the planet would not realize that Anna's ex (Tim) has installed on her phone an evil app named Iris. Anna is inexplicably failing at least one of her classes. Hilarity ensues as video of Sophie's in flagrante delicto encounter with a professor is released to social media (Sophie forgives her). When another video of a male student's same-sex encounter with another professor, meets the same fate, the professor publicly takes his own life. Anna can't delete the app from her phone. The app can not only transfer content to to other devices its in proximity to, but it can also provide glimpses into the future (but apparently only if those glimpses involve death).

Over time, Iris becomes more powerful. It can take control of SCADA systems, change traffic lights, lock building doors, control elevators. The trail of destruction grows. Anna's sympathetic guy pal: dead. The grey market phone dealer who replaces her malware infected phone (but transfers the SIM card...go figure): dead. Sophie: dead (in a swimming pool scuba-diving accident while the instructor has inexplicably left her underwater in the pool by herself in contravention of the number one rule of any water safety environment).

But wait, there's more. Suddenly we learn that ex-boyfriend Tim is in cahoots with Stan's doctor to implant a device (described to Anna by the doctor as...wait for it..."the implant") in Stan's spine to let him walk again. Who knew? Not us, until Tim and the doctor start debating the marketing plan for their evil plan that will somehow make both the doctor and boyfriend rich. Naturally, when Anna confronts the doctor about this: more people will die soon. Apparently in The Netherlands, everybody knows everybody.

Anna catches on to their evil plan, disconnects Stan from his post-surgery medical monitoring devices, and then in a rooftop showdown, the doctor and Tim get theirs, courtesy of both Anna and --wait for it-- Iris.

We close with Stan walking normally (what?), on his way to a week Barcelona with Anna on a southbound Boeing 757. The trail of destruction at the hospital is unresolved, including Anna's brutal attack on an innocent bystander nurse.

I'll give you three guesses which app suddenly cackles to life in the glass cockpit of their Spain-bound 757 as the movie ends?

This movie claims to be the first to incorporate the "Second Screen" viewer experience, and download an app that will provide additional interaction as the film progresses (but the invitation to do so assures us that you'll have a fine experience without this). Do yourself a favor: this flick is so bad when fed via a single screen, you don't want to add to the experience with a second one.

Avoid.

Note: this DVD provided for review purposes.
profile.summary: Don't install the disc in your DVD player...

profile.description: Barbara and Myrick Land, internationally distinguished journalists, have collaborated on six books, including A Short History of Reno. In addition to her articles and newspaper columns, Barbara Land has written four books. Myrick (Mike) Land was an editor of LOOK magazine and a prolific journalistic who published eleven books. Mike Land, who died in 1998, had recently retired as professor of journalism at the University of Nevada, Reno.
profile.reviewText:
During preparations for a trip to Las Vegas, my daughter asked the question: "How did something like Las Vegas end up growing in the desert?"

While I had been to Las Vegas before, I had only vague awareness of the forces driving its explosive growth in the post WWII years. "A Short History of Las Vegas" is an excellent resource for clearing up some of that vagueness.

Myrick and Barbara Land take a straight-ahead chronologically ordered approach to laying out the history of Las Vegas. They begin with the archeological evidence of its pre-history, take us through the first native American, Mexican and European discoveries that have accompanying historical data. Then they walk the reader through the exploration of Fremont, the growth of the railroad (attracted by the fresh water springs that gave rise to the city's Spanish name..."the meadows"), the construction of the Hoover Dam, the growth of legalized gambling and liberalized divorce laws, and WWII and post-WWII growth from the growing entertainment (and organized crime!) and nuclear testing industries. Whew.

They close with another portrait of Las Vegas, the place that houses more than a million residents who not only make the gaming and entertainment industries work, but the place that serves as a suburban home for those who work there.

This is a book that is free of agenda, and doesn't offer a judgement on the goodness --or lack of-- in the illusion-manufacturing that drives much of the regional commerce. There is perhaps a little too much emphasis on the destruction of older gambling properties in favor of describing the town's second and third generation development...but this does not diminish the overall usefulness of the book in grounding the reader in the essential history of Las Vegas.

Whether you've been there, going there, or just have in interest in famous American places: if you want a fundamental understanding of how Las Vegas became what it is today, this book is a good choice.
profile.summary: Objective, no-frills account of an iconic American destination...

The USB rechargeable built-in battery, charges fully in 2-3 hours to provide up to 4 hours of uninterrupted sound while youre on the go.
profile.reviewText: The SP5500 Bluetooth speaker delivers very nice sound from a Bluetooth source (within the usual limitations of lossy source files and typical Bluetooth compression schemes). Overall, its operation is very intuitive. It immediately recognized and accepted pairing from an HTC EVO 4G LTE. The sound from this speaker offers good presence, strong midranges. It is (thankfully) free of any over-emphasis on bass, and it is beefy enough to keep the high end from sounding cheap or tinny. As for the the fold out stand: I'm not sure what this really adds to the user experience. The product images show it being used (in its folded position) to position the speaker vertically. When doing so, it does it with a slight rearward cant, and it seems slightly unsteady (cat owners will find it more than slightly unsteady!). When folded out to accommodate a tablet or phone, it doesn't include any kind of charging port or friction mount. Again this is a case of not adding confidence to the resting position. This is a minor issue. Lay it flat, give up the space that your source device is going to take up on its own, and enjoy the music. Note: This item was provided for review purposes.

profile.reviewText: So: you scored yourself a shiny new HTC EVO 4G, and laid down something between $179 and $499, depending on who sold you the hardware and the state of your contract. As you closed the deal, your provider offered a monthly insurance plan and you started doing the math, adding up the total for your new data plan, the monthly fee for 4G services, and everything else that comes along as you adopt "convergence". If, like me, you rolled the dice and passed on the insurance, this can offer a modest bit of piece of mind. It fits nicely around the Evo, while offering easy access to all display surfaces, the four soft keys, data ports, camera, speaker and kickstand. A thin rubber membrane covers the side volume keys and top power button; the membrane has raised areas providing tactile feedback on the location of those controls, which still work normally through the cover. Will this protect your Evo from everything that comes its way? Not a chance. Will it keep it from an uncontrolled slide off your car seat or table top? Probably so. Will the thin rubber rim save your screen from some scratches. Almost certainly. The "fishbone" name comes from nice combination of colors contrasting the hard and soft plastic sections. One minor gripe to keep this from 5 stars: The bottom rubber piece (between the four soft keys and HDMI/USB ports could have benefited from some reinforcing to make it stiffer; it flexes easily as you slide your fingers around those keys. Not a serious flaw, and I liked this case enough to buy a second one in Red for the other Evo user at home. It won't save your Evo from total mayhem...but might buy you one more careless moment:-)
profile.summary: Good enough to buy two...

Guaranteed* to kill mice, Tomcat Press 'N Set Mouse Trap can be a powerful ally in your fight to get rid of rodent pests in your home. After baiting the trap, place it where mice are active. After catching a mouse, simply use the trap's grab tab to dispose of the rodent. *Satisfaction guaranteed or your money back.
profile.reviewText:
We have a cat who is a very good mouser, but who doesn't have regular access to an unfinished basement storage area where I recently discovered signs of mice. While I don't have any fundamental gripe with mice, I have a healthy respect for the risk of disease that comes from their droppings, and prefer not to have the things I have stored get chewed and re-purposed into nesting materials. Co-existence within the house isn't an option...so mouse traps are the answer.

I deployed three varieties of traps in multiple locations. Pictured is one placed on utility shelving where I saw recent droppings. I used peanut butter in the bait well, and have had three kills in the first 24 hours of use. While I wasn't present for any of the catches the jaws made their contact with the mouse in the rear head/neck area. I'm highly confident the dispatch was quick (and I hope the frequency of catches decreases as the herd thins).

Easy to set, does an unpleasant job effectively.

Select with confidence.
profile.summary: Three for three in the first 24 hours...

profile.description: The D-Link AC3150 Ultra Wi-Fi Router (DIR-885L/R) is packed with advanced features, like 4x4 data streams, dual band speeds of up to 3,150Mbps (1000Mbps in 2.4GHz and 2167Mbps in 5GHz), Smart Connect and Advanced AC Smart Beam technologies to deliver premium performance for today's most demanding tasks like HD streaming and gaming to multiple devices. The AC3150 is designed with four high-performance external antennas and high power amplifiers to deliver maximum range around your home and yard. The DIR-885L is equipped with MU-MIMO to provide high-bandwidth Wi-Fi signal to multiple devices at the same time.
profile.reviewText:
...that comes at a premium price.

The D-Link DIR-885L/R AC router offers a mix of things I found very useful...and some surprising absences.

Pros:
-Hassle-free set up. Within 10 minutes of unboxing, this router was running and ready to support wired and wireless devices.
-Dual-frequency band  flexibility (2.4 and 5 GHZ bands)
-DLNA services for home media streaming
-Excellent user interface for set-up and configuration; one of the most user friendly I've ever used.
-4x wired ports (plus USB, WPS and a single-button option to use as an extender only)

Cons:
-No front panel indicators for connected wire ports (a common --and puzzling-- design choice on many current routers).
-QC issue: one of the four rubber feet (which are thicker than those found on most similar products) fell out of its mounting point as I unpacked this product.
-No way (that I found) to set up internally reserved IP addresses (I'm something of a control freak for my home network, and prefer to establish static IP addressees for my regularly connected devices).
-Bulky external 2.4 GHZ antennas. I understand (at least a little bit) about antenna physics, and while I understand how performance is usually improved by having larger external antennas, it's just not a look I like.
-Science fiction styling. Yes, totally subjective, but this look is going to be  a problem for the non-alpha geek members of a household.
profile.summary: Average features, good performance, unconventional styling...

profile.reviewText: The Roolen Breath is a compact and easy to use ultrasonic humidifier. It consists of just three user-accessible parts: the reservoir tank, the mister/fan unit and the AC adapter. After filling the tank with water (slightly less than a gallon), it fits over the mister. A single pushbutton cycles the Breath through four modes: standard, high, auto and standby. Standard mode offers about 24 hours of humidifier operation, high about 12 hours. The auto mode offers 24+ hours as the machine self regulates maintaining humidity between 40-55%. The standard and high modes run continuously. I operated the breath in room considerably larger than the 400 square feet that it's designed to treat. On a blustery fall day, it raised the RH in the room from 46 to 50% in 90 minutes and to 55% after 5 hours. When operating, a plume of cool-to-the-touch is visible about 10 to 12 inches above top of the humidifier, which as about 10 inches tall. It is very quiet in operation, and will likely not be heard over ambient sounds in even the quietest rooms. Roolen recommends filtered water, but tap water can be used if the tank is rinsed weekly. The Breath includes a good, complete user guide and excellent pictographs in full color printed on the carton. Less one star for no water level indicator or sight glass. Note: This item was provided for review purposes.
profile.summary: Compact, quiet and easy to use ultrasonic humidifier...

profile.reviewText: In the crowded marketplace of portable Bluetooth speakers, the first thing to pay attention to is the sound. On that account, I liked the Truffol DuraSound a lot. Its audio output is crisp, and I didn't notice any tendencies to over or under emphasize sounds in any area. Ergonomically, I like the rubberized texture of the the speaker case; adds confidence when handling. This speaker went into a pairing mode and readily paired with both an HTC EVO 4G LTE and an iPod Nano (7th generation) immediately on powering up. Power on/off, pairing and incoming call status are all indicated by voice announcements. Incoming and outgoing phone audio quality was excellent. Both a USB charging cable and a 3.5mm aux cable (for wired input) are included. The product description claims dust and splash resistance, but I'm not sure to what extent. Two minor issues separate this product from five stars: (1) The included user guide --which is otherwise well written-- does not address anywhere how to charge the speaker. Because I've used similar products, I knew it charges from a USB port...but a user new to wireless speakers would have to guess at this. (2) The black controls and and the input ports have black labels. In low light, very difficult to distinguish. These are noticeable, but forgivable shortcomings in a speaker that delivers excellent sound. Note: This item provided for review purposes.

profile.reviewText: ...that brings you into the premium price range. In all honesty, I may not have considered this table and chair set if had not been offered to me for reviewing. Its cost places it squarely at the threshold of premium pricing..and for a four-place setting, this will give some consumers pause. While it's certainly possible to spend both much more and much less, I won't know about the relative economy of this purchase until its sat outdoors for several seasons (which is when to expect the early demise of less expensive furniture). Other than to assume you've made your own budgeting decision, this review will NOT address price any further..even if it is quite an attention. This outdoor dining set is made of Highwood "synthetic wood", which the manufacturer describes as "closed cell", recyclable, PVC-free and resistant to splintering and fading. This set arrived in six flat pack boxes: one for the tabletop, one for the table legs, and four for the chairs. They were nicely packed and protected from scratching/fricthin with multiple applications of foam and cardboard packing materials. Assembly was relatively easy. It can be done by one able-bodied person, but anybody putting these together will benefit from a helper. Including unpackging, expect to spend about 30 minutes assembling the table and 15 to 20 minutes on each char. Assembly instructions are well written and well illustrated. The table and base assemble with 12 total bolts (all Allen head; one size for the base and a second for securing the base/legs to the tabletop. Great design feature: all four parts of the legs/base are identical! If you are not assembling the table where it will be used, plan on it being a two-person job to move it into place. Each chair assembles with 10 total bolts (also Allen head, all one size). Assembly hint: the two bolts that secure the arms to the rear of the seat can present a clearance problem for your Allen wrench. Turn these as far as you can by hand *before* tightening the rest of the arm bolts, and your assembly will be expedited. Outstanding fit and finish overall. The assembled items are very sturdy and the chairs are very comfortable. The Adirondack styling of the chairs mean they come with a slight recline...so you'll probably be sitting forward on the chair's forward edge for actual dining. Overall, this material offers the tactile experience similar to nicely inished wood. The chairs are very comfortable. The "weathered acorn" color is quite rich. Excellent outdoor dining set. Select with confidence.

Powerful, Detailed Sound Despite being just a little bit bigger than our original Boom Bar, this wireless speaker, with its passive radiator, is twice as powerful and twice as detailed, especially when positioned on the floor, as its angular design throws sound upwards. We are KitSound and we all commit ourselves to achieving one shared goal: Bringing people closer to their music. profile.reviewText: The SCUD USA BT-03 can help users of mobile devices overcome two common limitations while out and about: distance to the nearest AC power source as device batteries drain, and lack of a Bluetooth headset in these days when traffic laws frown on other than hands-free usage. Similar in size to an iPod, the unit consists of a 7800 mAh rechargeable battery pack that cradles a detachable Bluetooth headset and a USB charging cord. Four blue LED lights indicate that the unit is charging and remaining charge when in use. The Bluetooth headset charges while cradled in the main body. Bluetooth operation was effortless. profile.description: Logitech Wireless Rechargeable Touchpad T650
profile.reviewText:
Logitech has established a long history of high satisfaction with me because of the quality of its peripherals (keyboards, mice, speakers and webcams). The Touchpad T650 immediately lived up to the high expectations its predecessors established.

In the box:
-the touchpad
-the Logitech "unifying" wireless transceiver (which can connect up to six devices through a single USB port)
-a USB cable for charging the touchpad's battery.

Basic installation on PCs running Windows 7 and Windows 8 took less than 5 minutes:
(1) Plug in the unifying receiver to a USB port
(2) Turn on the touchpad.
Windows 7 and Windows 8 immediately recognized the touchpad as a pointing device.

The touchpad does not include an installation CD, so be sure to go Logitech's website to download their latest "SetPoint" software. This will give you advanced configuration options for the touchpad (including a battery charge indicator). The touchpad was sufficiently charged to begin operating out of the box, and was fully charged in less than 30 minutes. You can continue working while it charges, and the USB cable includes clips that help with management of the cable as a thoughful extra.

If you've not used a touchpad before, expect a slight learning curve to master the control gestures. The setup guide has some shown, but visit Logitech's support site for a complete list (and videos) of the default Windows 7 and Windows 8 gestures for this device.

For Linux geeks: This touchpad also worked under Ubuntu with its native drivers.

For Windows 8 users, the touchpad has default gestures that allow rapid switching between the Start and Desktop screens.

For both Windows 7 and Windows 8, all of the default settings and available gesture functions are fully customizable (and can be invoked with as few as one and as many as four fingers)
profile.summary: Really good interface device; Ubuntu-friendly too...

profile.description: Very bright LED safety running belt for men, women and children to be safe while running or playing at night. You can use for many different functions. Use instead of glow sticks for nighttime events, parties. Much brighter than reflective vest--highly visible and fashionably cool. Serves as money belt for travel and key holder for running, sporting events, walking. More highly visible than any reflective running vest. Can be used instead of reflective vest for biking. Flashes for 60 to 80 hours, available in red, yellow, blue, green, white, pink, orange and RGB colors. Easy to replace battery.
profile.reviewText: I share my house with a high energy dog (Jacob, the overly exuberant Weimaraner) and he *requires* daily walks to keep his indoor energy down and keep him from making his human pack crazy. In the wintertime, this often means walks after dark. Pedestrian safety is essential where I live (an exurban area where cozy relationships between the local government and developers have allowed too much subdividing with no requirement to improve formerly rural roads with sidewalks) as harried commuters regularly disregard posted speed limits while forgetting that pedestrians and cyclists are also entitled to a portion of the road. In concert with a safety vest, this LED belt has added a new dimension of safety as our visibility to oncoming drivers is improved. In fact, I wish we were given as much room by the same drivers in the daylight. So: as an illumination device: 5 stars. Light that won't diminish your own night vision even as you become visible at distances greater than 0.25 miles. The zippered storage pouch has limited utility. It will hold a standard key, but will be challenged by modern, bulky key fobs. In addition this arrived with no user guide. I was able to figure out the three-way operation (off, steady, slow flash and fast flash), but you have no insight into expected battery life, replacement ...or anything else. Does it's main thing very well; select with confidence. Note: this item provided for review purposes.
profile.summary: Excellent addition to your nighttime safety...

profile.description: Express yourself! Set of 2 replacement grills. Easy to fit and suitable for Jongo S3 speakers. Color coordinate to match your mood.
profile.reviewText: At its bottom line performance question (how does this small speaker sound), the Jongo S3 gets two great big thumbs up. The sound from this compact (approximately 5" on each side and 5.5" tall) speaker is very good. Clear midranges with a decisive (but not overpowering) bass presence. This speaker will provide nice audio for even the largest rooms in most homes. It can accept audio input from three sources: -Bluetooth (via an included adapter) -a wired 3.5mm aux cable -WiFi. Both the wired and Bluetooth connections were trouble free with this speaker. The wired is obviously simple, and this speaker readily connected and paired with both an iPod Nano (7th gen) and an HTC EVO 4G LTE Android phone. It's wifi connectivity offered more challenges..enough so that I could not get it work via this option. I'm not sure what the issue was, but the S3's default private IP address happens to be the same as my router's private IP address. Even I after I forced a change in my router address, I was unable to connect with the speaker. It also never appeared in either my router's attached devices list or appear as present in a list of wife devices available to my phone. Overall: -Really good sound -Two of three audio input options worked great. -Less one star for its inability to connect via wifi (if this is your only or primary option, this might mean more to you; it's not a deal-breaker for me).
profile.summary: Fine, room-filling sound and good wired, Bluetooth, Bluetooth connectivity (wifi: not so much)...

profile.description: Gorilla tape has taken duct tape to a new level. This double thick adhesive tape surpasses ordinary duct tapes, making the list of uses virtually endless. Made with double thick adhesive, strong reinforced backing, and a tough all-weather shell, its the biggest, strongest, toughest thing ever to happen to duct tape. Gorilla tape is manufactured with a highly concentrated rubber based adhesive  two to three times as thick as traditional duct tape. The result is a tape that fills gaps and penetrates Rough surfaces. It sticks to Rough and uneven surfaces, including wood, stone, stucco and brick, that ordinary duct tapes can't hold. To us, its made the way tape should be: the toughest on planet earth. Directions: use like any other tape. Tear Gorilla tape by hand or cut to size with a knife or scissors. It is important to clean the surface and brush off any loose particles and dirt before applying Gorilla tape. Apply the tape carefully, smoothing out any pockets or rolls. Thats it. Enjoy the strength and durability of Gorilla tape! to retain adhesive quality, store Gorilla tape in a cool, dry place. Keep out of direct sunlight. Try storing the tape vertically (rather than laying flat), on a hook or on wax paper. If you have multiple rolls, keep your excess Supply wrapped until theyre needed. Gorilla tape works best at temperatures above 32f (0c). for best results, always apply the tape at room temperature. If Gorilla tape freezes, it will work just fine Once it returns to room temperature. Gorilla tape can be removed, but with some difficulty and it may leave some residue. To remove any excess residue, we recommend using the tape itself as a blotter. Gorilla tape should not be used as an electrical tape. Weve found that Gorilla tape will last a lot longer than regular duct tapes when it comes in contact with moisture. Click on the Gorilla link at the top of this page to see other quality products from the Gorilla glue company.
profile.reviewText: As somebody whose handyman skills range from are limited (on my best days) to completely suspect (on most days): tape, --and especially abundant quantities of duct tape (or "duck tape" depending on where you first learned to use it)-- is a *major* part of a tool kit. While I once actually used duct tape on air conditioning duct in my house (how that came to be is a long story) this category of tape mostly gets used as a multi-purpose-temporary-to-permanent-fix-it measure for many kinds of repairs and holding jobs. Consider Gorilla Tape duct tape (or "duck" tape if you prefer) on steroids...or at least on a hardcore workout regime. In my opinion it holds tighter and lasts longer than other similar heavy duty tapes in most situations. Among the the things I've used this for in recent months: -reinforcing the hinge and lip areas of a wheeled storage trunk (which the manufacturer's website ironically calls a "gorilla on wheels...go figure) prior to shipping it to a southern Asia military base. The tape held up for the trip over, stayed in place while being stored there, and then got re-used when the trunk was repacked for return to the states. 7 months later of garage storage later, it's still sticking strongly. -When a battery retaining clip on my netbook computer snapped (trust me: *no* replacements for this are available), it was Gorilla Tape to the rescue to hold in the aftermarket 9-cell battery that probably overstressed the retainer in the first place. Gorilla Tape now overlaps the battery-netbook seam...and it's not going anyplace. -When my desktop telephone decided it needed to perpetually flash its "message waiting" LED (even when there were no more messages): a discretely placed piece of Gorilla Tape permanently and opaquely covered the annoying light. -When the plastic clips securing the rear panels of *both* front seats failed in our 1998 Nissan Maxima (exposing the interior springs and other parts of the seats), Gorilla tape successfully re-secured them. While it's hardly fine auto upholstery, we prefer the look of this repair to viewing the springs and other innards of the seats. Other reviewers have noted problems with this tape removing paint and other finishes from the surface it was stuck to. In my opinion, you have a choice here: protect the finish or hold something in place. If you want to protect the finish, use masking tape. By the time you escalate to this kind of tape, you've decided "holding" is more important than preserving the finish, and you can proceed accordingly. Buy with confidence and give it your toughest taping jobs.
profile.summary: Sticks like crazy; great for the toughest taping jobs...

profile.description: Canon Lasers Imageclass D1520 Monochrome Printer with Scanner & Copier
profile.reviewText:
This D1520 printer/scanner copier went right to work in a high use environment that included the printing demands of three school-aged users (in elementary, middle and high school) and a teleworking knowledge worker with a high demand for professionally printed (and shared) documents.

Its large paper capacity, legal-size scanner bed and relatively heaviness (60 pounds), you'll need to make sure you have sufficient space to accommodate a footprint larger than most home users are used to.  The payoff from this comes from its fast printing and ability to take on many document tasks.

Initial installation was trouble free. Once installed, it offers automatic double sided printing and copying (easily changed through the PC print dialog settings).

Scanning is managed from either a PC utility (easier) or direct via the printer's LCD display. In addition to now-ubiquitous .pdf and .jpg options, the scan function also includes the lossless .tiff format (an option now absent from many less expensive MFDs).

Excellent quality and fast printing.

Overall, the range of capabilities make up for the larger than average space this printer occupies.
profile.summary: Excellent choice for demading SOHO uses (if you have the space)...

profile.description: Upgrade to Dual-Band N to avoid interference and enjoy superior performance. Connect your computer with the speed and range of Dual-Band N to surf the web, share photos, stream videos, and game online. Enhance your computer with the flexibility and high performance of Dual-Band Wireless-N. Just plug the Adapter into your computer's USB port to wirelessly connect to a network or hotspot. With transfer rates up to 300 Mbps you'll enjoy a powerful networking experience for surfing, chatting, sharing, or playing online. Built with leading 802.11n wireless technology, the Linksys AE2500 offers optimal coverage and reliability. Multiple MIMO (multiple input multiple output) antennas boost signal strength so you can enjoy dependable wireless connectivity whether at home or at Wi-Fi hotspots on the go. Improve your wireless performance with dual-band N (operates at 2.4 or 5 GHz) designed to avoid interference and maximize throughput for smoother and faster video streaming, file transfers, and wireless gaming. Keep Wi-Fi freeloaders and Internet threats at bay with the latest in WPA2 security to help keep your network protected. The included setup wizard installs your adapter quickly and makes going wireless easy.
profile.reviewText:
After a recent desktop upgrade, I exiled a 5-year old PC from its wired connectivity next to a router to a spare bedroom about as far away from the wireless antennna as you can get in my house.

With no ethernet in that room, wireless became the only option.

The installation utility for this adapter ran in less than three minutes, and then invited me to plug it in to an available  USB port. Within a minute the device drivers were fully installed and it dectected and connected to my network's SSID. Even with three rooms and floor between the router and adapter, this device consistently connects to the router with strong signal strength displayed.

Very affordable, and worked right immediately upon installation: what's not to like ??
profile.summary: Works fine, even a long way from the router...

profile.description: The Dyson Cinetic Animal vacuum contains 54 ultra-efficient Dyson Cinetic tips which oscillate up to 5,000 times per second to separate the microscopic particles that clog other vacuums. Because of their efficiency, there's no filter that needs washing or replacing meaning there is no loss of suction.
profile.reviewText: ...with some surprising miscues for a firm as obsessed with design as Dyson. My household is currently enjoying the 12th year of service of a Dyson Animal (DC07) upright vacuum, so we are familiar with both the performance and premium pricing that comes with the Dyson brand. And while some of its parts are replacements and its motor bearings are offering groans of displeasure that suggest it's in the autumn of its service life, it has served well over a time when its cleaning abilities have been collectively challenged by five different dogs and seven different cats. So: both previous Dyson use and premium pricing set a high bar for the Dyson 65502401 Cinetic Ball Animal canister vacuum (Cinetic from here forward) to clear. It mostly does so, but with some surprises. PROS: -When it comes to a vacuum cleaner's primary function (sucking dirt off the floor), the Cinetic performs wonderfully. While I prefer uprights to other form factors, the Cinetic's large spherical roller (and articulating holder for the the canister) trail easily. Through attachments and hose/wand configurations, it is highly flexible for cleaning floors, upholstery, curtains, auto interiors...what have you. -Long (22 feet) power cord. Bonus: auto retracts. No more winding dirty cordage by hand. -No consumables (bags or filters). Over time, these add to the cost of any vacuum that uses them. CONS: -Surprisingly limited dustbin capacity. You'll be emptying this often. -Because there are no consumables, choose where/how you empty carefully, or expect to breath in some of the fine dust you've sucked up. -Surprisingly big footprint for storage. The extension wand slides into the ball assembly, bit the fore-to-aft footprint of the want and hose assembly will challenge those with limited storage space. -No provision for attaching the separate "turbine tool" to the canister or wand for storage; you'll need to be an organized housecleaner, or this may become orphaned. None of these are showstoppers, but collectively they are things anybody about to spend this much on a vacuum cleaner should know about. It cleans excellently; you'll have to decide for yourself if these shortcomings are acceptable at the premium prices that come with the Dyson label.
profile.summary: Oustanding suckage at a premium price...

profile.description: Pinzon's crisp, elegant Hotel Stitch shower curtain presents a subtle herringbone pattern in white, trimmed with a double row of satin stitching that adds just the right touch of color. Expertly crafted in Portugal from 100-percent single-ply cotton, the curtain is made with button holes across the top designed to fit with standard hanging hooks, which are not included. The shower curtain is offered in colors to match the Hotel Stitch towel collection and also to coordinate with the Hotel Stitch bedding collection. Tumble dry on low, remove promptly, and warm iron as needed. An Amazon Brand.
profile.reviewText:
I'm not sure what to say about a shower curtain. My tolerance for shopping excursions diminishes significantly if I'll be in a store where there is nothing that plugs in. Further, when it comes to functionality, I don't see any improvements in shower curtain performance between those that that cost $15 and the ones that cost $150.

This 100% cotton shower curtain feels nice to the touch; soft without being slick. The light color will fit with most decors, and the brown/could stripe provides a visual break to the otherwise broad expanse. You'll need to provide hooks and a liner.

It's a shower curtain. It hangs there and keeps water inside the tub. What else could anybody ask of it:-)
profile.summary: Not sure what makes one shower curtain better than another, but this one is fine...

profile.description: Righteous Camera Neck Strap
profile.reviewText:
I've been toting SLRs (film and digital) for avocational photography since Jimmy Carter was president. And at the end of long days of camera schlepping, it was my neck that paid the price...in sweat and strain.

The padding on this strap is wide. While it does make the strap harder to tuck into a bag or pack (the *only* downside to this product...hardly worth mentioning once you've made the commitment to haul around an SLR for your happy snaps), it also distributes the load far more evenly and significantly lessens the fatigue of a long day of shooting.

The length can be adjusted either where the straps attach to the camera (I simply set these once and then let them be) or by a sliding strap adjusters that begin where the padding ends.

The real payoff with this strap comes when you have a heavier lens mounted (like the 70-300 mm zoom I often carry).

Your neck will thank you; less time thinking about the stress of schlepping your gear may allow you concentrate more on your photos...
profile.summary: Necksaver: strong, light and comfortable...

profile.description: The iKN100 is a Bluetooth-enabled wireless stereo system with built-in speakerphone capability. Built-in NFC (near field communications) technology allows for instant Bluetooth connections from NFC-capable devices. Built-in rechargeable battery provides power on the go. Pop out removable battery with USB port to charge devices or extend portable operation. Stream wireless digital stereo audio via Bluetooth from your iPhone, iPad, Android, Windowsmost Bluetooth devices. Reson8 speaker enclosure plus Texas Instruments DSP for full, rich sound. Built-in mic, digital voice echo cancellation and answer and end controls make speakerphone use a pleasure. Aux-in jack for playing almost any audio device.
profile.reviewText:
The market for sub-$50 Bluetooth mono speakers is a crowded one, with little to distinguish one from another.

The distinguishing feature of this speaker is a dual-power supply. One is internal, and the other is a removable lithium-ion battery that can either extend the speaker life when the internal battery is exhausted or be removed to power another device (such as the the phone providing the source audio).

Overall the sound is clear. It's strong through the midrange and I didn't notice any over-emphasis on either bass or treble tomes.

It paired easily with both Android and an Apple media sources.

Why four stars instead of five?
The top panel control buttons (for Bluetooth, volume up/down, track forward/reverse and phone operation are all similarly sized with functions indicated by same-color raised symbols. This makes them difficult to distinguish except in the brightest direct light. Also, neither the amazon product description, user guide or iHome website show the charging capacity of the removable "K-Cell" battery. Ultimately, I discovered this specification engraved on the bottom of the batter case (2600mAH, which makes it a modest external power supply), but learning this should not have been a scavenger hunt.
profile.summary: Decent sound from an affordable speaker...
