input:
Generate the review text written by a reviewer who has a given an overall rating of "5.0" for a product with description "Title: Dune, Frank Herbert (Hardcover)
Binding: Hardcover
Classics of Modern Literature". The summary of the review text is "Every Grain of Sand...".
output:
I can see why Dune has such an enormous fan base. An amazingly imaginative piece of work, it sets a standard for "space opera" that is hard to approach given the immensity of detail, the intricacy of plot and the deployment of archetypal resonances author Frank Herbert brings to his sprawling narrative. Herbert definitely knew his Golden Bough and his Joseph Campbell, not to mention his Islamic history and his Isaac Asimov, whose Foundation stories are a clear influence, not least for the use of snippets from fictional works of "history" that headline each chapter.

Dune is the story of Paul Atreides, heir to his father's dukedom, who is forced to flee with his mother Jessica into the desert (very literally) where he finds his true calling among the Fremen, the despised and feared desert people who populate the arid world of Arrakis, the universe's only source of an immensely valuable material called Spice.

If you are a fan of the Star Wars movies, you owe yourself the pleasure of reading Dune. I'm sure George Lucas did.

My only real criticism of this monumental piece of imaginative literature is that after setting up the story to produce a dramatic conclusion, that conclusion is rushed through in about 50 pages, leaving lots of potential dramatic developments on the table.

Nevertheless, Dune is a magnificent achievement that needs to be on the reading list of anyone interested in science fiction and fantasy literature, in fact, of anyone interested in quality literature of any kind.

profile.description: Eric Arthur Blair (1903-1950), better known by his pen-name, George Orwell, was born in India, where his father worked for the Civil Service. An author and journalist, Orwell was one of the most prominent and influential figures in twentieth-century literature. His unique political allegory Animal Farm was published in 1945, and it was this novel, together with the dystopia of Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949), which brought him world-wide fame. His novels and non-fiction include Burmese Days, Down and Out in Paris and London, The Road to Wigan Pier and Homage to Catalonia.
profile.reviewText:
George Orwell's early-career poverty tour hit a high point with Keep the Aspidistra Flying (1936), which is perhaps the most perfect portrait of a total doofus ever written. Before becoming "George Orwell," aspiring young writer Eric Arthur Blair had already explored living on the extreme social/financial edge of the society of his time in his semi-non-fictional Down and Out in Paris and London (1933). Later came The Clergyman's Daughter (1935), which had the title character experience London's homeless culture for a portion of its narrative. And even in portions of the book where she's not on the streets she's wrestling with the problems of making ends meet on a very meager income. The following year Orwell would pen The Road to Wigan Pier (1937), which I will be getting to presently in my self-imposed reading regimen that has me chronologically touring the literature of the mid 1930s at present.

With Aspidistra, Orwell produced a novel about an aspiring poet who decides the best way to rebel against the "Money God" is by throwing up or refusing good jobs in favor of working in a dingy bookstore for sub-minimum wage and living in a rat trap. And when he gets in an especially tight money pinch, he does the noble thing--he sponges off his impoverished sister.

Orwell was very good at detailing the lives of down-and-outers because he had lived it, at least for a while. But while he was an ideological socialist, he had the intellectual integrity to see the fatuousnesses and hypocrisies of many of its adherents. Aspidistra's central character, Gordon Comstock, could have a conventionally successful life, which is something his family had scrimped and sacrificed to make possible. But he decides that society's definition of "success" is not for him, unless he could achieve it by becoming a successful poet. So he takes a menial job, one that holds no threat of being, you know, promising, and spends his nights writing poetry that he occasionally gets published. Why he couldn't do that while working a better job he doesn't explore too deeply.

Perhaps the most painfully marvelous episode in the book comes when Comstock unexpectedly comes into a bit of money and ends up blowing it in the most stupid possible way. That scene is a piece of riveting writing, but so are many other episodes in this very under-rated work. I especially liked the scene at the resort hotel restaurant where Comstock goes through yet another spasm of stupid spending just to keep up appearances...
profile.summary: Very under-rated Orwell work

profile.description: Unusual book
profile.reviewText:
Casino Royale is James Bond fresh out of the womb. Published in 1953, Ian Fleming's debut Bond book set the template for the 007 to follow, though that template underwent considerable subsequent adjustment, especially in the movie versions.

In this maiden voyage, Bond is a much less assured secret agent than the one we know today from the Bond films, one who survives and triumphs more by dumb luck than anything he does proactively. There are at least two instances where he should by rights have been a dead man except for a fortuitous deus ex machina.

Casino Royale also introduces us to Bond's sybaritic approach to fine food and drink (the famous Vesper Martini is here described for the first time) and his assured manner navigating the world of high-end European casinos. On the other hand, here he is a casual ladies man instead of a serial seducer (and a rather nasty misogynist to boot).

The first two thirds of Casino Royale make for engaging reading, especially the chapters describing an ultra high stakes baccarat showdown with Communist agent Le Chiffre (this book is definitely a product of the early Cold War and some of the chapters read like something out of John Le Carre's spy books). Unfortunately, instead of ending it after the Le Chiffre matter is disposed of, Fleming pads out his book with an extended coda that deals with a lovelorn Bond's growing infatuation with fellow agent Vesper Lynd. This episode does flesh out Bonds character somewhat and it does set up the sequels nicely, but as narrative it is not terribly interesting to read through unless you're into romance novels.

That caveat aside, Casino Royale is a great starter for anyone interested in the whole James Bond phenomenon and wants to get back to where it all began.
profile.summary: The Birth of Bond

profile.description: Please Read Notes: Brand New, International Softcover Edition, Printed in black and white pages, minor self wear on the cover or pages, Sale restriction may be printed on the book, but Book name, contents, and author are exactly same as Hardcover Edition. Fast delivery through DHL/FedEx express.
profile.reviewText:
And Then There Were None is reportedly the best-selling mystery novel of all time, and judging from the many five-star reviews here, it continues to be a favorite. So why only a four-star review from me?

Well, to begin with, let me acknowledge that I understand the accolades. The story premise is one of the most inventive and intriguing ever constructed. A mysterious stranger invites a group of ten individuals, all with a murder they have supposedly gotten away with in their backgrounds, to an isolated island where he then begins to dispense justice by knocking them off one at a time, with the successive murders each pegged to the text of the nursery rhyme "Ten Little Indians."

The group soon realizes that the mysterious stranger killing them is actually one of their number, but which one? As the bodies pile up and the list of suspects therefore dwindles, the drama intensifies. You can't help but be hooked.

But here's my quibble, which is serious enough that I docked the review one star: it's just too damn perfect, too mechanical. Strict adherence to the premise overwhelms any sense of reality as the necessities of the plot require the characters to act in dumbfounding ways.

What really are the odds that someone can bring ten people to an island and start murdering them--all in accordance with the strict requirements set down by the nursery rhyme and in that order--and keep doing it through to the end? Even after the group realizes that the nursery rhyme--which is posted in all their rooms--is the template for the killing, they do very little with it. For example, the butler, after knowing that the next killing will involve "chopping up sticks" decides to chop up sticks...by himself...in the early morning when he is alone. In this he is the idiot ancestor of the airhead teenagers in modern slasher movies who decide to investigate the basement in the middle of the night after being told there's a killer about.

Like in those movies, the killer in And Then There Were None is preternaturally competent and flawless--and lucky--because the plot requires it and no other real reason. To cap it off, there's that message-in-a-bottle "How I Did It" coda tacked on to satisfy a Golden Age detective fiction standard that requires a full explanation at the end.

I love mysteries, but what I love most about them is how they affect interesting characters, and how those characters interact. Here, the characters are mostly stock types (the adventurer, the old military guy, the old maid, etc.) who are not very well rounded out. Christie's short chapters don't help. You only get superficial glances at each person. The plot requires them to be pretty stupid or it wouldn't work.

Compare And Then There Were None with Raymond Chandler's The Big Sleep, published around the same time. Chandler's plot is not nearly so flawless (in fact, he neglects to account for at least one murder) but the characters are fascinating and the dialogue crackles. Look, I'm not telling you not to read And Then There Were None. In fact, I urge you to read it if you are a mystery fan. It is one of the most influential books in the genre ever written. And you won't be bored. But I just prefer a little more realism, fewer wires showing.
profile.summary: I just prefer a little more realism...

profile.description: Stylish reissue of a classic first published in the 1970s: Hunter S Thompson's ether-fuelled, savage journey to the heart of the American Dream. 'We were somewhere around Barstow on the edge of the desert when the drugs began to take hold! And suddenly there was a terrible roar all around us and the sky was full of what looked like huge bats, all swooping and screeching and diving around the car, which was going about a hundred miles an hour with the top down to Las Vegas!' As knights of old buckled on armour of supernatural power, so Hunter S. Thompson enters Las Vegas armed with a veritable arsenal of 'heinous chemicals'. His perilous, drug-enhanced confrontations with casino operators, bartenders, police officers and assorted representatives of the Silent Majority have a hallucinatory humour and nightmare terror never before seen on the printed page.
profile.reviewText:
I thoroughly enjoyed Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas (1971) despite the occasional cringe-worthy stunts of author Hunter Thompson and fellow-traveller Dr. Gonzo, who seem to operate under the premise that their drunken/drug-addled capers somehow elevate them over poor shrubs who only try to get through life in one piece.

I didn't mind their antics when they were directed at self-important authority figures like the attendees of the ridiculous drug enforcement convention Thompson is assigned to cover, but when they stooped to humiliating diner waitresses and terrifying hotel maids, they lost me. There is a kind of smug elitism in those episodes that undercuts the moral credibility Thompson is trying to build.

All that being said, this is still a marvelously funny and insightful personal narrative as well as a stylistic landmark in American journalism.
profile.summary: What Happens in Vegas...

profile.description: Told with deadpan humour and bitter irony, Kurt Vonnegut's cult tale of global destruction preys on our deepest fears of witnessing Armageddon and, worse still, surviving it ...Dr Felix Hoenikker, one of the founding 'fathers' of the atomic bomb, has left a deadly legacy to the world. For he is the inventor of 'ice-nine', a lethal chemical capable of freezing the entire planet. The search for its whereabouts leads to Hoenikker's three ecentric children, to a crazed dictator in the Caribbean, to madness. Felix Hoenikker's Death Wish comes true when his last, fatal gift to mankind brings about the end, that for all of us, is nigh.
profile.reviewText:
Cat's Cradle (1963), Kurt Vonnegut's fourth novel and one of his best known, is a very hard book for me to review because I enjoyed its sprightly pace, arch tone and clever prose but finally grew rather tired of the unrelenting, and frankly rather juvenile cynicism that undergirds the entire thing.

The story, told in first person by a young writer researching the life of an oddball deceased scientist who was famous for being the "father of the atomic bomb" dropped on Hiroshima near the end of World War II, takes the reader from the upstate New York town of Illium (based on Schenectady, where Vonnegut worked in PR for General Electric for a time) to the fictional Caribbean island nation of San Lorenzo. Along the way we meet eccentrics, weirdos, fools, knaves and misanthropes.

Vonnegut scores some wonderful satiric zingers about large organizations and third world dictatorships, and the book reads fluidly with short chapters and lots of entertaining dialogue. But underneath it all is the unmistakable message that life is a bad joke perpetrated by some demented deity with a sick sense of humor and mankind little more than deluded, self-important fools. There are reams of bad poetry out there written by teens dressed in all-black that convey the same message with the same level of sophisticated analysis.

I mostly enjoyed Vonnegut's first three books. Player Piano was a promising if flawed work by an obviously talented writer, The Sirens of Titan a stylistic breakthrough, though a bit of an unfocused mess, and Mother Night, the best of the lot, an excellent meditation on the nature of complicity in evil. Cat's Cradle is to my mind, despite its reputation, a step backwards.
profile.summary: Talking World War II Blues...

profile.description: Book by J.P. DONLEAVY
profile.reviewText:
The Ginger Man is an unholy confluence of James Joyce and Henry Miller that sets a Miller-esque hedonist loose in Joyce's Dublin. We are supposed to be enthralled with his ribald adventures becausewell, because Ireland is a repressed, priest-ridden society and Sebastian Dangerfield's adventures in seducing a series of dull-witted women, stealing anything not nailed down to hock with his "broker," mooching on his friends, chiseling tradesmen, getting plastered on the proceeds and generally making a hog of himself are all ways to stick it to the system and live authentically, you understand

Dangerfield is doubly offensive because he doesn't have to live like this. He comes from a well-to-do American family and is supposedly in Dublin to study law at Trinity College. But that is not nearly as much fun as taking advantage of people much less fortunate than he is. Picaresque adventure stories like this can be amusing, and there's no doubt J.P. Donleavy shows a masterful flair for language in telling his tale with a style that switches from third to first person narrative (so reader be warned) and some passages rise to poetic heights.

The book is also a wonderful evocation of Dublin at around mid-20th century, which seems not very different at all from the city of a half-century earlier described by Joyce in Ulysses. There is much beauty but also repressive religiosity that, for example, limits contraception choices to the rhythm method and pretty much ensures that most families have more kids than they can reasonably support. One can understand the frustration with such a society, but turning oneself into an amoral pig is not exactly the best countermeasure...

Ultimately, Dangerfield's adventures become wearing and repetitive and he finally decides to leave Dublin and move to London (which doesn't make sense since I assume it would have been a much higher cost of living city at the time). The last chapters may or may not be a fantasy creation of Dangerfield's booze-addled mind. I hope so since the gutter is what he richly deserves.
profile.summary: Lecherous, Drunk and Stupid Is No Way to Go Through Life, Son...

profile.description: The Source by James A Michener; Intern by Doctor X; Hotel St Gregory by Arthur Hailey; To Sir, With Love by ER Braithwaite
profile.reviewText:
Frederick Forsyth has a thing for detail and this obsession almost sinks his debut novel, The Day of the Jackal (1971) before it gets started. The first half of the book, which deals with how and why a movement opposing then French president Charles De Gaulle hired an anonymous killer to assassinate him, is so buried in details of politics, armory, topography and whatnot that a flesh and blood story gets submerged. I like realistic detail in a story as much as the next reader but enough is enough.

Fortunately, Forsyth pulls up on the gearhead stuff in the books second half, when a manhunt for the killer is undertaken to head him off before he can strike. Here, personalities finally take over, giving readers someone or someones to empathize with.

While one can assume that the killer, nicknamed The Jackal, won't succeed (after all, De Gaulle died of natural causes after being ousted from office), that doesnt seem to hinder the suspense, or at least, it didn't for me. This book was turned into a hit movie that I have yet to see but I can see how it would adapt to a cinematic treatment.

Forsyth does an excellent job down the stretch of showing how skill and luck mesh to produce the final resultwhich, I must say, does depend on a rather convenient turn of events. Nevertheless, I can see why The Day of the Jackal made Forsyth into a best seller list regular.
profile.summary: Hunting Very Big Game

profile.description: John Lanchester is a journalist, novelist and winner of the Whitbread First Novel Award. He is a regular contributor to the London Review of Books and the New Yorker, with a monthly column in Esquire. John was raised in South-East Asia and now lives in London.
profile.reviewText:
Okay, I call BS on The Drivers Seat (1970), Muriel Sparks self-consciously shocking ode to assisted self-slaughter. The (thankfully) short novella is about 34-year-old spinster Lise who goes on holiday for the first time in three years, apparently to Southern Italy, though its never specified.

Anyway, the geography doesnt matter. What does is that Lise will be found dead of multiple stab wounds a day after her arrival. This isn't a spoiler. We are told this early on.

I suppose there is a strong dramatic interest in finding out just how such a horrific crime came to be but the problem is that Lise is clearly irrational and not very sympathetic. She is confrontational and rather obnoxiously rude to numerous people she meets.

The message seems to be that despite all her problems and hangups, Lise is still in the drivers seat when it comes to ending her own life, and she manipulates several people to make it end the way she wants. Well hurrah for her

The writing is crisp and Lises actions perplexing enough to keep the dramatic drive going, especially given the short length it needs to be maintained. But in the end we are left with the rather banal conclusion that people off their rockers will do irrational things. From the author of such excellent fare as The Mandelbaum Gate, The Public Image, The Girls of Slender Means and, of course, The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie, I was expecting a bit more than cheap thrills.
profile.summary: Well, She Asked For It...

profile.description: In 1831 Nat Turner awaits death in a Virginia jail cell. He is a slave, a preacher, and the leader of the only effective slave revolt in the history of 'that peculiar institution'. William Styron's ambitious and stunningly accomplished novel is Turner's confession, made to his jailers under the duress of his God. Encompasses the betrayals, cruelties and humiliations that made up slavery - and that still sear the collective psyches of both races.
profile.reviewText:
After two stabs at writing a masterpiece novel (Lie Down in Darkness and Set This House on Fire), William Styron finally nailed it on his third try with The Confessions of Nat Turner (1967), a fictionalized but meticulously researched chronicle about the bloodiest slave uprising in the Antebellum American South, which led to dozens of deaths, both black and white.

Riveting from beginning to end, the story is told mostly in first-person flashback by Turner, who led the revolt, oversaw the massacres that resulted, and is sitting in jail awaiting execution when the novel opens. A broad outline of what happened is given early on, and then there is a long stretch of exposition as Turner gives us the history of his short life (he is only 31). Meanwhile, the reader is on pins and needles to find out the details of just how all the killings went down in the endespecially one particular killing. But thats all told only in a rush near the end of the book.

Most of The Confession chronicles Turners increasing frustration with his life as a slave, his growing messianic complex about leading his people out of bondage a la Old Testament figures like Joshua and Moses (Turner is an obsessive Bible reader) and his inner conflicts over the implications of his self-imposed mission, which, to put it bluntly, will require indiscriminate mass murder.

Styrons prose is exquisite in describing this world, and his characterizations shun the easy Manicheanism of the Django Unchained school, where caricatured heroes and villains manipulate rooting interests. Instead, as in real life, there are fools, knaves, tentative heroes and, mostly, unremarkable everyday people on both sides of the racial divide, forcing readers to think deeply about which way to sympathize. It is a society that seems strange and outrageous to us in the early 21st century, but one that was probably unremarkable to those who lived in it, having known nothing else.

Several characters throughout the novel remark how the idea of black slaves ever rising up to free themselves in this society is literally inconceivable, and certainly unprecedented. Turner achieves a modicum of success in bucking this trend through a combination of guile, perseverance, force of personality, psychological insight and plain, dumb luck. The 30-year-old carpenter Turner manages to gather a small group of disciples: yes, the New Testament allusions are obviously very deliberate, from Turner's sermon on the mount (delivered in a street) and his retreats to the wilderness to fast and pray (and where he has visions) to a last supper with his closest disciples.

After a short burst of very bloody success, however, Turner's rebellion fizzles. Part of the problem is that the forces he unleashes, brutalized by their slave experiences and haunted by their own demons, are not especially controllable. His last desperate attempt to reassert his authority leads to the climactic moment in the novel where Turner is forced to make a choice between his two most fundamental impulses. Does he choose wisely, badly or simply inevitably? Its up to each reader to make that determination.

Many critics of the book have taken Styron to task for his portrayal of Turner, a black slave, pining for the virginal white girl Margaret Whitehead as simply exploiting a crude and insulting stereotype. I disagree. Given Turners psychology, his sexual hangups and his life experiences, it is perfectly understandable and plausible. Forbidden fruit has always been a big turn-on (check out Alan Paton's excellent Too Late the Phalarope for a prominent example from the opposite perspective). Plus, from a simply artistic standpoint, it gives the novel its most powerful moments, both dramatic and thematic.

The Confessions of Nat Turner won Styron the Pulitzer Prize for fiction. They get no argument from me. This is a masterful piece of literature that is both thought provoking and engrossing from end to end.
profile.summary: 31 Years a Slave

profile.description: 5th Printing, July 1970.  Hardcover with dust jacket.  Inscription on inside cover page.  Dust jacket slightly worn.  Pages crisp and clean.
profile.reviewText:
Ball Four (1970) is the baseball version of Jerry Kramers famous football diary of a couple years earlier, except that Bouton is a lot more forthcoming about the secrets of the clubhouse and the real antics of the players. Hes also more bitter. Whereas Kramer was still a star player on a championship caliber team (the Super Bowl winning Green Bay Packers) when he chronicled his season, Bouton is a veteran pitcher with a shot arm trying to survive by throwing the knuckleball.

Reading Kramers Instant Replay, you would never think anything particularly interesting was happening in the world in 1967 other than the Packers run to a third straight NFL title. While Bouton doesnt dwell much on external developments either, he at least acknowledges that some pretty serious issues are in play in 1969 America, from the Vietnam War to civil rights, and he drops some of his opinions into his narrative.

However, most of the book is about Boutons struggles with what seems incredibly myopic management and coaching. For example, the front office of the Seattle Pilots for which Bouton played most of the 1969 season insisted players refrain from signing autographs before games, oblivious to the effect such standoffishness might have on the few fans who bothered to show up for the teams home games.

The seeds of the revolution that would sprout in the next decade that would grant players much greater freedom with the striking down of the reserve clause are already hinted at in the appallingly stupid penny pinching of baseball team management described by Bouton, penny pinching even the lordly New York Yankees for whom Bouton was briefly a star pitcher, were not immune to. There were literally contract squabbles about an extra $500 A YEAR in salary!

Bouton is an excellent and articulate chronicler who gives a very plausible view of the Major League clubhouse of the time. What was shocking in 1970, though, such as the Porkys level voyeurism of beaver shooting, seems almost absurdly quaint today. There are also entertaining hints of things to come that Bouton couldn't know the significance of, such as the offhand reference he makes to an exhibition season experiment that allowed designated hitters to hit for pitchers, a rule that would go into effect in the American League four years later and change the game. Young players briefly alluded toMike Marshall, Lou Piniellawould become much more prominent in years to come.

If you are a fan of baseball and baseball writing, Ball Four is a must-have.
profile.summary: Touch 'em All Time

profile.description: As he roams the US, Mexico, Morocco, Paris and London, Kerouac records life on the road in prose of pure poetry. Standing on the engine of a train as it rushes past fields of prickly cactus; witnessing his first bullfight in Mexico while high on opium; meditating on a sunlit roof in Tangiers or falling in love with Montmartre - Kerouac reveals both the endless diversity of human life and his own particular philosophy of self-fulfillment.
profile.reviewText:
Lonesome Traveller is a collection of travel essays published by On the Road author Jack Kerouac a few years after his breakthrough with that picaresque novel. Whereas On the Road was tightly structured around the adventures of Kerouac and Neil Cassidy (under pseudonyms), Lonesome Traveller is fragmented with each chapter essentially a self-contained adventure. They are also stylistically all over the place.

The best to me was the one about New York City, an excellent impressionistic view of the Big Apple in the 1950s, including  the name-dropping of numerous famous artists of the time, from Gregory Corso to Thelonius Monk. At the other end of the spectrum for me were the ones about Kerouac's adventures working on a railroad and on a ship. Both are very difficult reads, nearly incoherent in places, all done in the obscurantist style Kerouac had also deployed in earlier works like Dr. Sax. There's also one about his time working as a fire lookout for the Forest Service on Desolation Peak that basically replicates what had already been published in the last chapters of The Dharma Bums.

If you are a Kerouac-head, this one is a must. If not, it can still be interesting if you pick and choose among the chapters.
profile.summary: On the Road Some More...

profile.description: "Atlas Shrugged" is the astounding story of a man who said that he would stop the motor of the world - and did. Tremendous in scope, breathtaking in its suspense, "Atlas Shrugged" stretches the boundaries further than any book you have ever read. It is a mystery, not about the murder of a man's body, but about the murder - and rebirth - of man's spirit.
profile.reviewText:
What is it about Russians and long-ass novels? At over a thousand pages of microscopic print, Atlas Shrugged easily bests legendary megatomes like Anna Karenina and The Brothers Karamozov, and perhaps even approaches the grandaddy of them all, War and Peace.

Part mystery, part bodice ripper, part philosophical dissertation, part dystopian novel, part utopian novel and part revenge fantasy against prevailing cultural and intellectual trendsetters, Ayn Rand's 1957 pro-capitalist epic continues to sell in impressive numbers over a half century after its initial publication, a rather remarkable achievement.

At the plot's center is Dagny Taggart, who doggedly tries to keep her family's railroad business going despite the interference of her brother James, the self-pitying mediocrity who is nominal head of the company, as well as increasing government regulations, the crony capitalist machinations of other businessmen and the slow deterioration of society into disfunction that makes it hard to find either reliable suppliers or paying customers. Dagny is by far the novel's most rounded character, a woman torn between keeping faith with the vision and values of her ancestor Nat Taggert, who founded the railroad, and the compromises she must make to do so.

Those compromises are made harder by the mysterious John Galt, whose aim is to destroy both Dagny's company and the parasitic society that feeds off it. Galt, like most of the rest of the major characters (Hank Rearden is a partial exception), is more abstraction than man, an impossibly noble and brilliant personage who is the absolute yin to the yang of the novel's villains like James Taggart. Rand is not subtle with her characterizations, but then neither was, say, Frank Capra in It's a Wonderful Life or John  Steinbeck in The Grapes of Wrath. Rand is simply inverting the caricatures. Good for her.

Dagny's story is similar to that of that other great American female-in-a-male-world interloper, Scarlett O'Hara, in that other great iconoclastic American epic written by a defiantly independent-minded woman, Gone With the Wind. Though Scarlett starts life as a pampered Southern belle, she develops into a very hard-headed businesswoman very much like Dagny Taggart. Both women are also remarkably polyandrous given their cultures' mores and remarkably unapologetic about it.

What I really liked about Atlas Shrugged was the way Rand was able to maintain plot interest across over a thousand pages through a mix of extended narrative suspense, the creation of a fascinatingly FUBAR world and her parade of fabulous scene on scene of dramatic confrontation driven by crackling stichomythia laden dialogue. She also produces a number of set pieces that are positively brilliant in dissecting group behavior. My favorite was one that details how a passenger train rolls to its doom through a mixture of cowardice, arrogance, incompetence and cynicism.

The book develops from the early scenes that present an intriguing mysterywho is removing the titans of industry and whyto later scenes of a society in a death spiral and the growing, impotent panic of those in charge. The climax, straight out of the James Bond cliche book, is nevertheless well handled and dramatically presented.

There are times Rand gets carried away with her vision. For example, her ideal society in Galt's Gulch is about as plausible as James Hilton's Shangri-La. And her propensity, indulged more and more as the novel goes on, to preach to the reader repeatedly grinds the story to a halt. Galt's famously extended radio address is the most egregious but at least it was meant to be a set speech. Other instances, such as Francisco D'Anconia's Root of Money disquisition, come in the midst of dialogue, bringing the scenes to a screeching halt.

In a sense I give Rand some slack for this otherwise irritating habit, common among highly ideological writers, to bloviate rather than dramatize. She really is sui generis, so most readers are getting her contrarian philosophy for the first time in Atlas Shrugged. That she takes every opportunity to explain it is therefore somewhat defensible. But how much is too much?

The novel is also needlessly extended with numerous passages of bare exposition that go on and on. While Rand clearly has a talent for vivid description, whether it's the Rocky Mountains at sunset or NewYork City in winter, a couple of paragraphs would work better than a couple of pages in what is already an elephantine narrative.

There are also a few clunky scenes where I shook my head at the amateurishness, such as the highly implausible radio address describing the collapse of the D'Anconia Empire (this could have been done so much better with third-person description) and the treacly demise of the Wet Nurse, which would embarrass even Charles Dickens with its sentimentality.

But these are minor missteps compared to Rand's splendidly preposterous approach to romance and sex, which seeks to connect interpersonal love with external achievement but produces only a kind of I-love-you-dear-just-as-much-as-I-do-my-new-smelter ethos. Tedious, hilarious and creepy by turns (Rand seems to have a thing for rough foreplay, submissive women and dominant men), her romantic interludes are by far the novel's weakest points. On must also question the suspiciously convenient acceptance by Rand's parade of uber-alpha males of Dagny's fluctuating affections.

Nevertheless, this is a monumental work in scope, ambition, literary mastery and sheer balls. I had loved Rand's first book, We the Living, a much more traditional novel that promised the emergence of a talented writer. Anthem was an eccentric statement of purpose and The Fountainhead an Atlas Shrugged warm-up exercise that had a great premise but often floundered in bloated prose and sketchy characterization.

With Atlas Shrugged Rand nailed it. No wonder she never wrote another novel. Where was there left to go?
profile.summary: The Spirit of Enterprise

profile.description: When Joel Knox's mother dies, he is sent into the exotic unknown of the Deep South to live with a father he has never seen. But once he gets there, everyone is curiously evasive when Joel asks to see his father. Truman Capote's first novel, "Other Voices, Other Rooms" is a brilliant, searching study of homosexuality set in a shimmering landscape of heat, mystery and decadence.
profile.reviewText:
Truman Capote was one of a group of young American writers to emerge in the years following the Second World War, and few had more successful debuts. Other Voices, Other Rooms was a big best-seller, which is very interesting given its subject matter, a gay coming-of-age story. Capote's friend and mentor Carson McCullers had no end of grief with her own gay-themed Reflections in a Golden Eye only a few years before. I suppose it's possible readers didn't get the underlying implication and were caught up in Capote's wonderful prose, evocative setting and sharply drawn characters.

I very much enjoyed those elements as well, especially the protagonist Joel's relationships with the tomboyish Idabel and the black servant Zoo. If there was any disappointment it was the rather hasty wrapup at the end. But all in all and extremely rewarding read.
profile.summary: Truman Capote's Provocative Debut

profile.description: Henry Pulling, a retired bank manager, meets his old aunt for the first time in over 50 years. She persuades him to travel with her. Through his aunt, a veteran of Europe's hotel bedrooms, Henry joins a shiftless, twilight society coming alive after a dull suburban lifetime.
profile.reviewText: Travels With My Aunt (1969) is a late period Graham Greene novel that shows that the master had a rather severe creative slump following his great period from the late 30s through the late 50s, when he produced some of the best English novels of the period, especially The Heart of the Matter and The End of the Affair. Travels With My Aunt focuses on the relationship of middled aged bachelor Henry Pulling and his aunt Augusta, a bon vivant old lady who drags him on her international adventures to Istanbul and South America, where they tangle with rogues, adventurers and various exotics. All this is a significant change from the quiet life the retired Henry had been leading, when the highlight of his day was tending his dahlias. The adventures are somewhat interesting as are the characters but Henry remains rather a cypher and the strong undercurrent of philosophical seriousness of purpose that flavored Greenes best work seems to be missing, or at least not all that serious. The big revelations toward the end of the book don't come as a particular surprise and one wonders why they were shrouded in such mystery in the first place.
profile.summary: He's a Real Nowhere Man...

profile.description: Professor Timofey Pnin, previously of Tsarist Russia, is now precariously positioned at the heart of campus America. Battling with American life and language, Pnin must face great hazards in this new world: the ruination of his beautiful lumber-room-as-office; the removal of his teeth and the fitting of new ones; the search for a suitable boarding-house; and, the trials of taking the wrong train.
profile.reviewText:
Pnin (1957) was a placeholder novel cobbled together and fleshed out by Vladimir Nabokov from stories he had published in The New Yorker about an eccentric Russian emigre professor.  At the time, Nabokov was working to get his previous novel, Lolita, published in the United States (it had been published in France in 1955 but banned in the U.S. for obscenity).

As a result, Pnin is episodic and somewhat disjointed, but Nabokov's prose is so captivating, and the character so interesting, that it doesn't really matter. In addition, the book provides modern readers with a lively view of college town life in the Northeast in the 1950s as well as of the life of Russian emigrants in the U.S., caught in a strange new culture so different from what they had known.

Pnin is not a masterpiece like Lolita (almost nothing is) but it's more than a trifle and well worth checking out.
profile.summary: While Waiting for Lolita...

profile.description: Throughout his trial Jack had maintained his innocence, claiming he was hitchhiking on the night of the murder and he had been picked up by a middle-aged man in a dark car. Unable to locate this mystery man the police viewed Jacks story as a lie. Dr Arthur Calgary was the stranger in question, but he arrives too late for Ja
profile.reviewText:
Ordeal by Innocence presents an intriguing premise: a murder case that was thought solved two years earlier is suddenly reopened by compelling evidence that the man found guilty (and who had died in prison in the interim) didn't do it, which means that the murderer is still loose and is probably one of the members or close associates of the family of the murdered woman.

Ordeal by innocence is what each of the people in this group experiences due to suddenly becoming a suspect not only in the eyes of the police but of the other members of the group. Author Agatha Christie attempts to explore the intergroup dynamics caused by this psychological pressure but is hampered by her inability to create rounded, realistic characters.

Frankly, these people are simply not interesting enough to engage the reader, or at least they didn't engage me. They are variations on stereotypes, the types of characters that have always peopled Christie's novels, where for the most part they were harmless because Christie's best books are plot- rather than character-driven. However, Ordeal by Innocence is very much designed to be character-driven, which unwisely plays to the author's weaknesses.

In addition, the investigation of the newly reopened murder case seems to be pursued in a surprisingly desultory fashion by the authorities, leaving the field to a couple of amateurs. Christie had employed amateur sleuths as central characters before, with varying degrees of success. Here, I don't think it works very well, if only because she fragments the investigation among three people. It really could use a strong central investigator figure such as a Hercule Poirot to ground the plot.

When it finally comes, the resolution of the mystery is, frankly, disappointing, based as it is on a rather hoary stereotype. Finally, while we get some interesting Christie philosophizing about the perils of helicopter parenting, we also get some rather insulting views about adoptive families.
profile.summary: If He Didn't Do It, Then Who Done It?

profile.description: Published in 1962, this is an emotionally intense novel of love, hatred, race and liberal America in the 1960s. Set in Greenwhich Village, Harlem and France, ANOTHER COUNTRY tells the story of the suicide of jazz-musician Rufus Scott and the friends who search for an understanding of his life and death, discovering uncomfortable truths about themselves along the way.
profile.reviewText:
What, no lesbians? James Baldwin's 1962 novel Another Country has just about everything else to shock the sensibilities of readers of that era, from interracial relationships to gay male relationships to interracial gay male relationships.

The book details the interconnected lives and romances of a group of characters living in New York City in the 1950s. Most claim to be in love with a special someone, yet they are either ready to cheat on that special someone at the first opportunity (Vivaldo, Ida, Cass, Eric) or beat them up (Rufus). If this is lovegay or straightyou can have it

Not that there isn't a lot of fascinating stuff here as these profoundly silly, immature and self-important people go about their lives. I loved the many scenes of drama where tensions and confrontations either simmer below the conventional conversation surface or break out in fireworks. Baldwin has a great ear for dialogue and how to set scenes and deploys it to full effect. Some of it is melodrama, but great melodrama.

One caveat is that this seems a puzzlingly organized book. It starts off seemingly as the story of Rufus and his interracial affair with Leona. But that storyline is cut off less than a hundred pages into this 400-some page novel. It then focuses in turn on the other major characters, almost as if these were separate stories or aborted novels cobbled together. I wish Baldwin would have developed the Rufus/Leona relationship further instead of doing what he did (I won't spoil it if you haven't read it).

Still, this was a very entertaining book well worth a reader's time.
profile.summary: Ebony and Ivory With Not So Much Harmony...

profile.description: Chester Himes was born in Jefferson City, Missouri in 1909 and grew up in Cleveland. Aged 19 he was arrested for armed robbery and sentenced to 20 to 25 years in jail. In jail he began to write short stories, some of which were published in Esquire. Upon release he took a variety of jobs from working in a California shipyard to journalism to script-writing while continuing to write fiction. He later moved to Paris where he was commissioned by La Série Noire to write the first of his Harlem detective novels, La reine des pommes/A Rage in Harlem, which won the 1957 Grand Prix du Roman Policier. In 1969 Himes moved to Spain, where he died in 1984.
profile.reviewText:
A Rage in Harlem introduced Chester Himes' most famous characters, black detectives Gravedigger Jones and Coffin Ed Johnson, though they play fairly small supporting roles in this book. The novel is the first of what would become Himes' most successful line of writing, that of the crime/detective story set in the black neighborhoods of Harlem in New York City.

Himes had tried to write more serious stuff earlier in his career but it hadn't gone well. In the 1950s he settled in Paris and started writing potboilers like A Rage in Harlem. I haven't read his earlier, more serious work such as If He Hollers Let Him Go or Cast the First Stone but I can't believe they are any better than Rage in Harlem, which masterfully recreates a time and place with colorful, interesting characters, plenty of plot suspense and ripping but realistic dialogue.

Briefly, the story concerns Jackson, a somewhat dim-witted but basically good guy bedazzled by the sexy, manipulative Immaline. Jackson is rooked out of all his money by a pair of con men working with Immaline, who also force him to steal from his employer. So Jackson spends most of the novel on the run from the law while trying to get Immaline back (he continues to believe she is innocent and devoted to him despite all the evidence obvious to everyone else) and secure enough cash to make up for what he stole. He is helped in this by his brother Goldy, a con man and drug addict who spends a lot of his time posing as a nun soliciting donations on street corners.

The Harlem of the 1950s comes alive in Himes' pages just as it does in, say, James Baldwin's books of the same era such as Go Tell It on the Mountain (Baldwin was a fellow resident of Paris at the time).

It's not a profound book but a very entertaining one.
profile.summary: Do Wrong Woman, Do Right Man...

profile.description: Hardback 50th Anniversary Edition Doris Lessing brought the manuscript of THE GRASS IS SINGING, her classic first novel, with her when she left Southern Rhodesia and came to England in 1950. When it was first published it created an impact whose reverberations we are still feeling, and immediately established itself as a landmark in twentieth-century literature. This hardback edition is to celebrate the 50th anniversary of its publication.
profile.reviewText:
Doris Lessing's first novel, The Grass Is Singing, is a kind of reverse murder mystery, that is, a story that begins with the discovery of a body (and the identity of the supposed killer), and then goes back in time to show everything that led up to the death. In this respect, it's sort of like the movie Sunset Boulevard, which, coincidentally, came out at almost the same time Grass Is Singing was published.

The dead woman is Mary Turner, the middle aged wife of an indigent white farmer, Richard Turner, and her accused killer is Moses, a black laborer who had worked for the Turners. Lessing gives us the story of Mary's life, concentrating particularly on her marriage to Richard and her lonely life on his farm, which is located out in the sticks of Southern Africa (in present day Zimbabwe). Along the way we get a compelling tale of loneliness, frustration (emotional and sexual), naivet, perseverance and, ultimately, madness.

We also get a picture of society in South Africa in the 1930s and 1940s, society defined by a strict color line in which whites hold a privileged position and blacks are little more than beasts to be worked. The most curious aspect of it all for me was the paranoia whites had about any of their number descending to the socio-economic level of blacks because they feared it would give blacks the idea that they might be as good as some whites. Hence, the ne'er-do-well Turners are looked down on by other whites as being, in effect, a discredit to their race.

In addition to being an exploration of racial relations, The Grass Is Singing is also a feminist novel in the sense that it shows a woman trapped by cultural expectations into a life of misery and frustration. It reminded me of similar experiences described in books such as Giants in the Earth and The Awakening and in the Lilian Gish silent movie The Wind.

But Grass Is Singing is no ideological screed. Mary Turner is a fully realized and utterly believable character whose choo-choo slowly goes around the bend as the novel nears its conclusion, and the narrative following her perspective becomes disjointed as her sanity recedes. Frankly, the motivation for her getting killed is ambiguous and the actions leading up to it somewhat unconvincing given the characters and the setting. It is the weakest aspect of the book.

The Grass is Singing makes an interesting companion piece to another internationally renowned work coming out of South Africa at around the same time, Alan Paton's Cry the Beloved Country. That book also revolved around a murder of a white by a black and used that event to paint a picture of the larger society. It is also much better book in my opinion because it gives a broader perspective, including that of black characters. In Grass Is Singing, the blacks remain part of the background, a phenomenon of the physical environment like the bugs and the heat. Their thoughts and feelings remain mostly unexplored as Lessing concentrates on the story of Mary and, to a lesser extent, Richard.

Still, I can see why this was a successful debut for Lessing, who would go on to a distinguished writing career capped by a Nobel Prize for Literature in 2007. It is a strong first effort.
profile.summary: Working Back From a Murder

profile.description: Andrew Harlan is an Eternal, a man whose job it is to range through past and present Centuries, monitoring and, where necessary, altering Time's myriad cause-and-effect relationships. But when Harlan meets and falls for a non-Eternal woman, he seeks to use the awesome powers and techniques of the Eternals to twist time for his own purposes, so that he and his love can survive together.
profile.reviewText:
The End of Eternity shows how much a great core idea can raise a book from pedestrian to fascinating almost by itself. Isaac Asimov to this point in his career (1955) had produced some groundbreaking stuff, primarily the original Foundation series of stories, along with a couple of intriguing but flawed novels (Currents of Space, The Stars Like Dust, Pebble in the Sky).

The flaws that have dogged his bookscardboard characters, especially women, and pedestrian plottingare still here but are compensated for with a great premise. That premise is the existence of a kind of priesthood that travels back and forth through time while existing outside of it (in "Eternity"), continually adjusting events to keep mankind from destroying or severely harming itself.

The great flaw in that system is what drives the resolution of the plot but in the meantime there is enough impressive speculation and working out of how such a system might function that a reader is hooked. Had Asimov been able to create characters who are even remotely interesting, this would have been an utter masterpiece. Even without that it must be regarded as a seminal work in the science fiction genre, which is why I'm giving it five stars.
profile.summary: On Time and on Target

profile.description:
Lawrence Durrell's series of four novels set in Alexandria, Egypt during the 1940s. The lush and sensuous series consists of Justine (1957) Balthazar (1958) Mountolive (1958) Clea (1960).
Justine, Balthazar and Mountolive use varied viewpoints to relate a series of events in Alexandria before World War II. In Clea, the story continues into the years during the war. 
One L.G. Darley is the primary observer of the events, which include events in the lives of those he loves and those he knows. In Justine, Darley attempts to recover from and put into perspective his recently ended affair with a woman. Balthazar reinterprets the romantic perspective he placed on the affair and its aftermath in Justine, in more philosophical and intellectual terms. 

Mountolive tells a story minus interpretation, and Clea reveals Darley's healing, and coming to love another woman.
profile.reviewText:
Coming on the heels of three fabulous predecessors, Clea is a rather disappointing final chapter to Lawrence Durrell's Alexandria Quartet. Where the first three novels (Justine, Balthazar and Mountolive) presented an interesting and ever-widening storyline involving a growing set of interrelated characters, Clea has no real major developments to add, and that hurts the narrative interest quotient.

The book's narrator, Darley, who also narrated Justine and parts of Balthazar before disappearing almost completely in Mountolive, does take up here with Clea, a fairly minor character in the previous three books, but their relationship provides no fireworks since it is pretty uncontroversial. Neither is betraying anyone. Next to the dramatic tension of previous relationships (Darley/Justine, Nessim/Melissa, Mountolive/Leila, Pursewarden/Justine, etc.), this is very small beer indeed.

The big reveal is the incestuous relationship between Pursewarden and his sister Liza, already hinted at in Mountolive, but it's a minor development since Pursewarden is dead at the start of this book. More damaging is that some of the most fascinating characters from the first three books (Justine, Nessim, Mountolive) are almost totally absent here, and nothing really takes their place. Instead, Durrell turns here to a number of extended passages of raw philosophizing through clumsily rendered monologues or letters from various (dead) characters like Pursewarden. This is rarely a good move in a novel and it isn't here. These passages stop whatever narrative flow there is in its tracks.

Durrell's prose is still first rate and the portrait he presents of Alexandria during the Second World War years has its fascinations, but this is really a disappointing end to what had been a fantastic novel series.
profile.summary: Maybe Durrell Should Have Settled for the Alexandria Trilogy...

Mountolive tells a story minus interpretation, and Clea reveals Darley's healing, and coming to love another woman.
profile.reviewText:
Justine was published at a fortuitous time, in early 1957 just as the Suez Crisis was putting Egypt into headlines around the world. That country, or more precisely, the city of Alexandria, is one of the main "characters" of Justine and indeed of the four-pack of books that it initiated, The Alexandria Quartet. Indeed, in addition to the main story of the novel, I found the picture it presented of Alexandria's multicultural society quite fascinating on its own.

With The Alexandria Quartet, Lawrence Durrell, a good buddy of Henry Miller but lacking the latter's obsessive narcissism, penned what the Modern Library listed as one of the 100 Best English Language Novels of the 20th Century. I can't dispute that.

At heart it's a story of a romantic triangle, with the unnamed first-person narrator in love with Justine, the wife of good friend Nessim while two-timing his own live-in lover Melissa, who is suffering from tuberculosis. Melissa comes off as the most sympathetic of the major characters, if only because she gets relatively little face time in the narrative.

Nessim is a passive beta male in the hands of his flighty wife, to whom he seems to extend a free hand to indulge herself with lovers in the hope that she'll ultimately come to love him as a result. This rarely works, but some guys never learn.

The narrator bumbles into an affair with Justine and become obsessed with her, to the point of digging up her former husband's autobiographical novel about his relationship with Justine and memorizing frightfully large pieces of it. Justine herself comes off as a rather immature woman who may have been traumatized by an early rape (the narrative is unclear) but she certainly has no qualms about using people.

The style is not linear but impressionistic, with the narrator jumping around in the timeline. This has probably warned off a few readers but, honestly, I didn't think it was all that hard to follow. There are relatively few significant characters in addition to the Big Four, so if you pay attention and have a modicum of short term memory you should be fine.

The story is interesting on its own, as are the characters and the setting, and Durrell's style enhances rather than detracts front he pleasure of reading it. I'm very much looking forward to reading the other three books of the Alexandria Quartet.
profile.summary: The Problems of Three Little People Amounting to a Hill of Beans...

profile.description: Evelyn Waugh was born in Hampstead in 1903 and educated at Hertford College, Oxford. In 1928 he published his first novel, Decline and Fall, which was soon followed by Vile Bodies, Black Mischief (1932), A Handful of Dust (1934) and Scoop (1938). During these years he also travelled extensively and converted to Catholicism. In 1939 Waugh was commissioned in the Royal Marines and later transferred to the Royal Horse Guards, experiences which informed his Sword of Honour trilogy (1952-61). His most famous novel, Brideshead Revisited (1945), was written while on leave from the army. Waugh died in 1966.
profile.reviewText:
Scoop was Evelyn Waugh's fifth published novel and continued the author's exploration of the society of his time with his rather misanthropic attitude. It especially resembles Black Mischief, the novel Waugh had published six years earlier, which also was set in a fictional African country and treated the natives as amusing and somewhat childish figures. This can be construed as racist, realistic or consistent, or a combination of them, depending on your own biases. It is racist from our modern perspective in its condescending Western view of swarthier non-Westerners. It is realistic in that its portrait of Ishmaelia pretty much describes the internal politics of too many post-colonial African countries. And it is consistent in that Waugh savages everyone, from Africans to Europeans to Americans. In fact, in some ways, the Africans come off looking the best.

Scoop derives its immediate raw material from Waugh's own experiences as a foreign correspondent, and its portrait of the journalistic profession in pursuit of a "scoop" in a faraway land is merciless and rings true, skewed only slightly by satire. Certainly, today we are hardly free from reports from overseas (and even from our own country) by reporters clearly without the slightest clue as to what is actually going on but presenting an authoritative sounding spin on events that validates their own biases. Events of the time, especially the proxy war then going on in Spain between the fascist and Communist countries, provided additional fodder for Waugh's plot of outside powers manipulating Ishmaelia's various factions for their own ends. World War II, which would start a little more than a year after Scoop was published, would end this period of vicarious interwar international intrigue by commencing the real thing. So Scoop can also be viewed as a snapshot of the world on the brink of global war.

I gave this book only a four star rating because I don't think it quite lives up to its promise. I really enjoyed the first half and its emphasis on satirizing the journalistic profession, but it bogs down in the second half when a half-hearted romance narrative enters the picture and Waugh strays from politics to the personal. The central character, William Boot, is simply not interesting enough to support the story. I wish Waugh would have stuck with the broader satirical approach.

That's not to say that this is a failure. Waugh's Pythonesque cavalcade of fools, twits and naifs is always entertaining, and I laughed out loud several times while reading. I just wish Waugh had stuck to that.
profile.summary: Loved it...up to a point...

profile.description: Muriel Spark (19182006) was the author of dozens of novels, including The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie, Memento Mori, A Far Cry from Kensington, The Girls of Slender Means, The Ballad of Peckham Rye, The Drivers Seat, and many more. She became Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 1993.
profile.reviewText:
Curiously, Memento Mori was published around the same time as John Updike's The Poorhouse Fair. I note that seemingly random fact only because both are novels about aged characters written by young authors at or near the start of their careers. Updike was 26 and Poorhouse was his first novel; Spark was 41 but Memento Mori was only her third book. What possessed each to write about characters so much older than themselves is anyone's guess but Spark's work is clearly the superior one. In fact, it is almost certainly one of her best in a long and distinguished writing career that would go on for more than 45 years after Memento Mori (I hedge only because I haven't read most of her oeuvre yet but can't fathom that she could top this effort with any regularity).

A mature work by a master novelist with an assured grasp of character, situation, pace and structure, Memento Mori concerns a group of septu- and octogenerian characters with an interconnected history of kinship, friendship, romance and antagonism. Who slept with whom and who cheated on whom decades earlier is of critical importance to understanding the inter character dynamics and readers have to be careful to keep these in mind along with a rather extended dramatic personae list.

Spark spices up the drama with a conceit similar to the one she used in her first novel, The Comforters, where a character was plagued by hearing a voice narrating her life as if it were a novel. Here, the conceit is the mysterious phone call received repeatedly by just about every character admonishing them to remember that they will die (which is what "memento mori" means in Latin). Who placed the calls remains unexplained, baffling the police who suspect mass delusion.

Memento Mori is an outstanding and insightful piece of work about human relationships and the effects of the consciousness of mortality felt by characters with every reason to be conscious of it.

profile.description: Donald Hamilton is the creator of Matt Helm, star of 27 novels that have sold more than 20 million copies worldwide. He was born in Uppsala, Sweden, attended the University of Chicago, and served in the U.S. Naval Reserve. His writing career began in 1946 with short stories for Collier's and The Saturday Evening Post. His first novel was Date With Darkness, published in 1947, and altogether he published 38 novels. The first Matt Helm novel, Death of a Citizen, was originally published in 1960, at the height of the Cold War.
profile.reviewText:
The third Matt Helm novel from Donald Hamilton, The Removers gives us a very cold blooded anti-hero protagonist who has no conscience about seeing bad things happen to the woman he supposedly loved through a 15-year marriage. We had already seen Helm as a compunctionless killer in the first two books (and again here) but an incident toward the end of this book ups the ante considerably. James Bond may have been the agent licensed to kill, but Helm is the one who takes to such a role with nary a hesitation. You wonder how he was ever the quiet family man he was first introduced as.

In The Removers, Helm is assigned to find a sleeper enemy agent hiding out as a right-hand-man for an American gangster. This involves reconnecting with his now remarried ex-wife because her new husband has a connection with the gangster. There is also a "Helm Girl" in the form of the gangster's daughter, who I thought was a very good character, very much up to the standards of the best Bond Girls and not a dumb bunny at all.

The plot, I thought, wasn't quite as engaging as those from the first two Helm books but the fleshing out of the Helm character and his background, as well as the Helm Girl (and her dog!) made up for it and it was worth the read.
profile.summary: Family Man No More...

profile.reviewText:
Our Friends From Frolix 8 (1970) is tighter in plot than many other Phillip K. Dick novels, but the story is still undercooked with a number of promising plot strands left hanging or underdeveloped.

The story is set in a future world in which a fairly small aristocracy of New Men (high IQ bubble heads) and Unusuals (those with physic and precognitive powers) rule over the vast majority of Old Men (those with no special powers of any sort). An underground movement disseminates subversive, illegal literature containing the writings of the imprisoned rebel intellectual Cordon. Meanwhile, another rebel leader, Thors Provoni, has escaped Earth to find an alien ally who might help the Old Men overthrow the New Men/Unusuals tyranny.

The central character, Nick Appleton, however, is another of Dicks ordinary Joe figures who winds up enmeshed in a Hitchcockian web of intrigue far beyond his pay grade. Appleton gets involved with the rebels when he falls for the jailbait girlfriend of one of the rebels and spends a good portion of the book on the run.

By the way, this isn't the first time Dick gives us an underage object of middle aged male lust and one begins to wonder is this is coincidental

Anyway, Provoni eventually turns up accompanied by the titular friend from Frolix 8, a massive alien he insists is benevolent. Is it? Thats just one strand of the story that doesnt seem to be explored enough. Ditto Earths politics, especially the relationship between the New Men and the Unusuals. i would rather have had more of that than Appletons mid-life crisis difficulties.

One thing I did appreciate is that unlike in many of his earlier novels, Dick in Friends From Frolix 8 keeps a tight hold on his plot lines instead of pouring on more characters and situations that fly off in all directions with few satisfactory resolutions.
