profile.reviewText:
I didn't know anything about these characters aside from a quick cameo they made in the animated Avengers TV series.  Knowing that there was a talking raccoon in the movie, I was aware of how easily this could go badly.  When I finally saw it on opening day, my fears were put to rest and I thoroughly enjoyed the movie.  So much so, I saw it again in an Atmos screening the next day and have seen the film in theaters ten times, beating out the old record holders of Lord Of The Rings and Star Wars, which were 6 and 5 times respectively.

The movie was shot in 2D, with the stereoscopic effect done in post, which never looks as good as real 3D, and sure enough, the flaws of that process were distracting; stars at wrong depths, feet not where they should be, weird ripples around moving objects, and the worst offenders were reflections that look like they're painted on.

So, why did I get the 3D version?  Well, since the studio wanted to get people to pay more for the 3D versions and the realized the 3D part alone wasn't enough, they decided to load it up with extras that the 2D version doesn't have.  One of those is the changing aspect ratio that the IMAX version had, which, again, was only available to the 3D version of the film.  So, I sprung for the 3D version here to get those larger screen filling shots, which I could watch in 2D by simply turning off the 3D feature on my TV. That leaves me with the original 2D image, which doesn't have any of the 3D flaws.

This was also my calibration disc since the image contains so much detail and color.  I had my TV calibrated professionally earlier this year and this was the first disc I played on that TV.  Even though the TV was pretty close to optimal out of the box, an hour of calibration really brought out the details, and I recommend it to anyone that is serious about their home theater.

I just watched this a couple more times this week, and I'm looking forward to the next movie.

As I mentioned, this is one of my calibration discs now, due to the high quality image and the full range of colors.  Surround sound is quite full as well, probably a result of the original ATMOS mix.  If this gets re-released with an ATMOS audio track, I may just have to upgrade my sound system for it.

If your system is not 3D capable, or you just aren't interested in the aspect changing, then stick with the 2D version; the 3D really didn't do anything for this movie, as it wasn't shot for 3D.
profile.summary: A movie that surprised me by instantly becoming my favorite.

profile.description: From Marvel, the studio that brought you the global blockbuster franchises of Iron Man, Thor, Captain America and The Avengers, comes a new team  the Guardians of the Galaxy. An action-packed, epic space adventure, Marvels Guardians of the Galaxy expands the Marvel Cinematic Universe into the cosmos, where brash adventurer Peter Quill finds himself the object of an unrelenting bounty hunt after stealing a mysterious orb coveted by Ronan, a powerful villain with ambitions that threaten the entire universe. To evade the ever-persistent Ronan, Quill is forced into an uneasy truce with an uneasy truce with a quarter of disparate misfits  Rocket, a gun-toting racoon, Groot, a tree-like humanoid, the deadly and enigmatic Gamora and the revenge-driven Drax the Destroyer. But when Peter discovers the true power of the orb and the menace it poses to the cosmos, he must do his best to rally his ragtag rivals for a last, desperate stand  with the galaxys fate in the balance.
profile.reviewText:
I didn't know anything about these characters aside from a quick cameo they made in the animated Avengers TV series.  Knowing that there was a talking raccoon in the movie, I was aware of how easily this could go badly.  When I finally saw it on opening day, my fears were put to rest and I thoroughly enjoyed the movie.  So much so, I saw it again in an Atmos screening the next day and have seen the film in theaters ten times, beating out the old record holders of Lord Of The Rings and Star Wars, which were 6 and 5 times respectively.

The movie was shot in 2D, with the stereoscopic effect done in post, which never looks as good as real 3D, and sure enough, the flaws of that process were distracting; stars at wrong depths, feet not where they should be, weird ripples around moving objects, and the worst offenders were reflections that look like they're painted on.

So, why did I get the 3D version?  Well, since the studio wanted to get people to pay more for the 3D versions and the realized the 3D part alone wasn't enough, they decided to load it up with extras that the 2D version doesn't have.  One of those is the changing aspect ratio that the IMAX version had, which, again, was only available to the 3D version of the film.  So, I sprung for the 3D version here to get those larger screen filling shots, which I could watch in 2D by simply turning off the 3D feature on my TV. That leaves me with the original 2D image, which doesn't have any of the 3D flaws.

This was also my calibration disc since the image contains so much detail and color.  I had my TV calibrated professionally earlier this year and this was the first disc I played on that TV.  Even though the TV was pretty close to optimal out of the box, an hour of calibration really brought out the details, and I recommend it to anyone that is serious about their home theater.

I just watched this a couple more times this week, and I'm looking forward to the next movie.

As I mentioned, this is one of my calibration discs now, due to the high quality image and the full range of colors.  Surround sound is quite full as well, probably a result of the original ATMOS mix.  If this gets re-released with an ATMOS audio track, I may just have to upgrade my sound system for it.

If your system is not 3D capable, or you just aren't interested in the aspect changing, then stick with the 2D version; the 3D really didn't do anything for this movie, as it wasn't shot for 3D.
profile.summary: A movie that surprised me by instantly becoming my favorite.

profile.description: In the 19th century, The NoMad District of New York was the meeting place of the eras elite - from Oscar Wilde to Charles Dickens, Mark Twain to Nikola Tesla. The vision was to create a deck of cards that would serve as a monument to The NoMad. The result is a timeless blend of beauty and elegance - NoMad Playing Cards.
profile.reviewText:
The box for this one is outstanding!  It ranks up there with Theory 11's Artisan deck for beauty.  The box is made from a black card stock, that is then printed with opaque white and gray inks, which really stand out.  To finish it off, Theory 11 also used some gold foil stamping and some sharp embossing to really set this off.  The back design is actually on the front of the box, while the label is on the back.  The inside of the box is also printed with a repeating pattern of the Nomad logo in gray ink.  The box is sealed with a rather long sticker that has the seal of NY on it twice.  Since the box is made with uncoated stock, it's more susceptible to moisture damage, so take care.

There are 56 cards in this deck, with two nearly identical Jokers.  Nearly identical, meaning the artwork is identical but the faux foxing on the cards is heavier on one than the other, making them different.  There are two additional black ad cards for The Nomad Hotel, which this deck was designed for.

All the cards have a foxing texture on the background, on both front and back, to varying degrees.  There are several patterns to this and if you look for it, you can find the same pattern on different cards.  The artwork is traditional, but using a very dark red for the red suits and a golden tan for the yellow in the face cards, which utilize only the dark red, tan and black colors; there are no blues used.  The Ace of Spade is entirely custom and even uses a different font for the value.

The backs have the design that appears on the front of the box, but in black line art, over the foxing pattern.  Without that foxing, the backs would probably much less appealing.

The cards are Bicycle stock, printed by the USPCC, and are high quality.  Interestingly, this is the first deck of cards I've run into that had defective cards in it; five cards have creases down the faces - 7H, AC, 2D, 9C and 10D.  There's no sign of this on their backs, so I wonder, given the overall stained nature of the designs, if this was intentional, as there's no sign the cards were actually bent; the creases are only on the face, like it happened when the paper was glued together to make the card stock.  If so, kudos on that!

This is a nice deck in one of the most beautiful boxes I've seen.  In fact, I would love to have a poster of that box front.
profile.summary: An absolutely gorgeous box and another design win from Theory 11.

profile.description: Use your home's existing power outlets to network your pc's, gaming consoles, BlueRay players and other ethernet enabled devices.
profile.reviewText:
I got this in the hopes of improving our LAN, but unfortunately, the wiring in our place isn't up to the challenge.  We used to use the Actiontec units in our old place and they worked well, but in the new place, they all show the orange connection light, meaning the connection is poor.  Since those are also a couple years old now, I hoped a newer set of units would solve the issue.

Well, first things first, these worked, right out of the box, without any setup.  Which is good because the instruction sheet, if you can call it that, really doesn't say much.  I've seen more informative business cards. They don't even tall you want the lights on the units indicate, and the little pictograms on them don't help much.  I've always wondered why companies choose to keep things like this so obscure. It is really so prohibitively expensive to actually LABEL the lights with full words, rather than overly shortened abbreviations or unintuitive pictures?

These units are both two-prong plugs, and are designed in such a way that the second port on an outlet is still accessible to two-pronged plugs.  A three pronged plug will probably be a tight fit at best.

These are good units, but since they didn't solve my current problem, I'll be returning these.  It's too bad, because I do like them.  But, surprisingly enough, our Dark Knight router we got earlier this year has such good WiFi performance, it actually works much better and fast to use WiFi for the devices I got these for (TV, receiver, PS3/4).  That, I did not expect.
profile.summary: Easy setup and works right out of the box.

profile.description: Gallium is a soft, silvery metal, and elemental gallium is a brittle solid at low temperatures. If it is held in the human hand long enough, gallium will melt, since it melts at the temperature of about 29.76 C (85.57 F),
profile.reviewText:
Gallium is an interesting metal because it melts at body temperature, looking a lot like mercury when it's a liquid, but safe to touch.

This comes in a small plastic vial with an attached cap.  If it's cold enough, the gallium inside will be solid, making it virtually impossible to remove.  Just run hot water over the vial and it will melt and you can then just pour it out.  Take care though, because this can separate into tiny drops that can easily get away, and, being a metal, it won't exactly soak into a paper towel or sponge.  I found the easiest way to return it to the vial is to scoop it up with a piece of paper or plastic sheet.  If it's on a smooth surface, you can use ice to harden it and make it easier to pick up.

Warning.  This is a soft metal, and will melt easily, and as such,it will readily mark surfaces if it rubbed across.  If you're handling it with your hands, your hands will get dirty.  It's best to keep it over a protective surface like a plastic sheet to prevent this from marking up a table to counter-top.  And whatever you do, avoid dropping it on cloth or on a carpet!  It will be practically impossible to get it out.

This stuff works great in ice cube molds.
profile.summary: Possibly the most fun element ever.

profile.description: Based on the same basic matching concept of hit party games Apples to Apples () and Cards Against Humanity (), the game is simple to play. One player reads a question card out loud. The other players each submit an answer card. The best answer wins. The results are as hilarious, embarrassing, depraved, and satisfying as marriage itself. (* - Not actually guaranteed to do anything.)
profile.reviewText:
This is sold as a stand-alone game, and it's quite hilarious that way.  However, it only gets better when you combine it with Cards Against Humanity and the various expansions sets for that.  Yes, these are shades of blue, but that shouldn't detract from the fun, especially if you're just playing this on its own.

As you probably have already guessed, the cards here are all themed around weddings, and the humor can get pretty raunchy at times.  We've played with these cards a few times now, both alone, and with other decks, and had some of the best games ever with them.  You don't have to limit playing these to just weddings; they're great any time, and some of the topics are relatable to just about everyone.

And that's where a lot of the real humor comes from, the cards that everyone can relate to in one way or another.  There are no wildly fantastical cards in here; no David Bowie flying on a tiger made of lightning, no snorting coke off a clown's boner, or anything else that outlandish.  These are down to earth topics that nearly everyone has at least had a near miss with; the good, the bad, and the awkwardly embarrassing.  Goodies like Knowing way too much about each others bathroom habits., Getting tired of being on top., A lifetime of judgmental glances from your in-laws., or Your dad showing up drunk. Like always..  'Black' cards include gems like ________ doesn't count as cheating.,  The only thing worse than ________ at a wedding is ________., and What will the groom think of when he first sees the bride on their wedding day?  There's a lot of wrong stuff in here that's all just so right.

The box is pretty much identical to the box that Cards Against Humanity comes in, but smaller and more colorful.  The cards are the same card stock and size (though they're smoother), so they mix in well with that game as well.  Plus, the logo is pure genius.

This is slightly larger than half the size of the original Cards Against Humanity game; there are 55 'black' cards and 230 'white' cards, which will take a few hours to get through;.  Normally with that high a percentage of black cards, you'll run out of white cards quite fast.  Fortunately, only three of the cards in this set have two blanks, so the white cards will last a bit longer.  Mix these with another deck and it'll take a long time to run out of cards.

Yes, these are blue, but they still work with CAH; we haven't had any issues with the different colors, as long as the card czar doesn't see who put down the colorful cards.  Yes, this is designed as a stand alone game, but when mixed with CAH and the various expansions, you're in for a real treat.

I hope Zapler comes out with their own expansions for this soon.
profile.summary: Great for more than just weddings.

profile.description: Finely chiseled metallic grip inlaid with soft latex-free pads. Dual-function pocket clip releases heavy spring mechanism to retract tip. Sophisticated brushed metal barrel. Writes crisp, .5mm fine lines of consistent density. Refillable with Pentel Super Hi-Polymer Lead and Z2-1 refill eraser.
profile.reviewText:
This is the first review I've ever written about a pencil, something I never thought I'd be doing.  But here goes.

For the past few years I've carried a Moleskin notebook with me, and something to write in it, which was one form or another of mechanical pencil.  They all had the same drawbacks  the lead would easily break off in my pocket, the plastic parts could get damaged, and the points would either poke holes in the pockets (not nice when it's a leather jacket), or poke holes in me when I reached in to get them.  In the past couple months, I've had two other pencils get damaged, and one no longer works, while the other had to have some repairs done.  I needed something sturdier.

I saw this one had a lot of reviews, but what really attracted me was the metal body, and the price.  So, I sprung for this, while also ordering a pair of other pencils (also from Pentel).  They all arrived together.

This one was packaged in a simple plastic bag; there was no box or blister pack, so, basically, you're not paying for excessive packaging here.

I took it out, and it felt nice in the hands.  The grip can be turned to change the dial that shows the lead hardness; something I've seen on more expensive technical pencils before.  I pressed the button a few times and the lead slid out nicely.  Now, here's where things get a bit strange, in a very good way.

With other pencils, if you hold the button down, you can press the lead back up into the barrel.  You cannot do that with this one; the lead is one way only.  I tried all sorts of ways, and that lead will not slide back in.  Seems like a design flaw, but not really.  The pocket clip on the side is also a hinged lock  When you press on the top, it will open and unlock the barrel mechanism, which will shoot back inside the pencil tip.  While this is unlocked, the lead itself can be pushed back into the barrel if needed.  And since the barrel is now tucked up safely inside the tip, there's no sharp point sticking out that can cause damage, or be damaged; the tip is essentially as blunt as the button on the eraser end.  You can see this in the product photos, as well as my own.  Pressing the button again will extend the barrel once more and the clip will lock it into place.

The button pulls off to reveal a small white eraser.  That can also be pulled out to open the lead chamber for refilling.

As I stated, this comes in bare minimum packaging, and without any instructions, which explains why there are customer questions about it.

I've used this a bit and compared to some other more expensive  Koh-I-Noor Rapidomatic  pencils I've used in the past, this is much more comfortable to use.  I still like the Rapidomatic, but I have had one break because of the plastic body it has. The GraphGear feels a lot more solid.  Plus, it has some gel grip pads on the knurled barrel for more comfort.
profile.summary: Quickly became my favorite mechanical pencil, over some that were much more expensive.

profile.description: Artisan Playing Cards are back in an all NEW white print edition - a breathtaking union of style, elegance, and sophistication. These premium, luxury playing cards feature elegant gold foil hot stamped onto ultra-lux black paper. Sealed with a red tax-stamp, vintage sticker seal marked with the exact month and year of print.
profile.reviewText:
Let me just say this...  These cards are frikken gorgeous!

Everything about these screams excellence and luxury, right down to the metallic seal.  The boxes are made from very nice card stock with one of the most matte finishes I've seen in paper.  The black box, in particular, is an incredibly deep black that you'd normally only expect from a gloss finish, and this sets off the gold foil artwork ablaze, yet the embossing effect is still visible.  The white deck has the same artwork, but on a white, almost cream colored card stock instead.  There is no coating on these boxes; these are bare card stock, and as such, are extremely susceptible to water damage.  Both come with stamp-like seals with edition numbers, which are also present on the aces.

The cards themselves are top quality, as is expected from the USPCC.  The backs have a thin white border, about half as thick as regular cards, and this thin border also serves to showcase the attention to detail present here; it's extremely uniform all around.  When you put a border this thin on something that will be cut later, the slightest registration errors will be far more noticeable.  I see none, and I've sorted several regular decks so their thin borders are all on the same sides.

The black deck has a black pattern printed over a pale bronze metallic background.  Similarly, the Ace of Spade uses black and metallic to great effect, mimicking the design on the box, but without the foil or embossing. The white deck has the same design on the back, but without the black ink; the design is made up entirely by the metallic ink and the white card stock.

The faces are identical on both decks, and have no more than three colors printed on them; black, a burgundy red and the metallic bronze (it's a bit dull to be gold really).  There are two identical Jokers, which have a circular emblem with "The Guild Of Artisans" across the top and "The U. S. Playing Card Company" on the bottom, also using the three inks.  The decks also contain one double-backer and a promo card for Theory 11.

I normally remove the seals on my decks, carefully to avoid ripping the boxes, and toss the cellophane wrap as well.  I made exceptions for these decks, leaving the seal in place, and keeping the boxes in what's left of the wrap to keep them protected.  The seals, due to the embossing of the boxes, are easily peeled up to allow opening.  Even with limited, gentle handling, I know these will eventually start to show signs of wear and I'm already planning to get at least one more set for backups.  At $16 for the pair, they're a great bargain, but they're so nice, you'd hate to see any harm come to them.  As such, these will appeal to collectors more than anyone, and few would actually want to put these through the wear & tear of game play.

Personally, I think Theory 11 outdid themselves on these decks.  But to be sure, I'm collecting their other decks now.  The designs of these two just caught my eye first.
profile.summary: Probably the most luxurious cards I've ever seen.  A must for collectors.

profile.description: Great collection for Farscape fans. Includes all seasons and The Peacekeeper Wars - all 42 DVDs. Region 2, 2004 edition, purchased in 2008 from Australia. Home collection.
profile.reviewText:
First of all, this is a nice, and very convenient set, well worth the money.  If you've never bought any Farscape episodes before, or you have limited space to store a collection, then this set is probably for you.  That said, there are some caveats. I did a back to back comparison of the original ADV discs and the newer ones in this set. There's three things that jump out.

1. The bit rate is about 2/3 of the ADV discs. I expected this to be lower since A&E is squeezing about twice the number of episodes onto a disc - ADV put two episodes while this set piles on four per disc. The only way to do this is to compress the programs more. Quality-wise, the image is still remarkably good, and I didn't hear any differences in the audio quality.

2. Unlike the ADV discs, these are not progressive scan encoded - the video is interlaced. Some players don't handle interlaced video properly when they try to convert it to progressive scan output, and jittering can appear in motion. This drops the image quality on players that are outputting a progressive video.

3. For some reason, A&E didn't bother using the original source material, and instead, used their broadcast edits. At the beginning of each episode, they have the "Dolby Surround Where Available" bug in the lower right corner, which is unacceptable to me. This just makes it look like they recorded it off TV.

On the bright side, the set takes up about a tenth of the space of the entire ADV set does (the main reason I even bothered to buy this set), and has some extra features the original doesn't. It also costs about as much as about 10 of the ADV episodes did. The cases also use the new Bluray style clips that hold the discs in place, so there's much less risk of getting a set with loose (and thus, scratched) discs.

If you're not a big stickler for quality, then this set is for you - the price is just amazing, and most people won't care about the lower bitrate or encoding method. Videophiles, however, should probably steer clear and stick with the ADV sets, or wait until a new set is released with higher quality.
profile.summary: A nice set, but it won't be replacing my ADV discs

profile.description: Medallion Playing Cards offer a blend of sheer elegance and striking beauty. A timeless object infused with supreme luxury from the Victorian era. The design is accented by embossed stitch elements in the front and sealed with theory11's signature precision printed gold foil sticker seal.
profile.reviewText:
Another top notch deck by Theory 11.  Along with their Artisan, Nomad and Tycoon decks, this is on of what I consider their top five decks, coming in at fifth place.  Why fifth?  For the same reason I put off buying this deck for so long; I find the backs are a bit flat and dull compared to the others.

First, top score again on their box.  This is a dark chocolate brown, uncoated card stock that's entirely printed with a gold foil stamp and embossing.  There is some additional embossing on the box that isn't foiled, and therefor quite subtle; almost too subtle.  The box is sealed with a fairly thick foil sticker cut like a postage stamp. As with other uncoated boxes, this means the seal leaves sticky residue on the card stock that very difficult to remove.  Too much effort on this can start removing the foil stamping in the area.  This also means the box is more susceptible to moisture damage.

The deck comes with two identical Jokers, with a medallion design that is not on the box.  Although it's difficult to see, these are printed in two colors; the design is printed in the same dark chocolate brown as the backs, but the Joker index is in black.  The two additional cards are a double backer and an ad card for Theory 11.  The Ace of Spades has the medallion design in it, and like the Jokers, is printed in the dark brown color with black indexes.

The suits are standard art, though the red is a dark burgundy color instead of the brighter traditional red.  The royals are mostly traditional art, but with custom artwork added, featuring a medallion motif on each, and new faces.  These are printed with black, dark red, dark brown and a pale metallic gold.

The backs are all a simple two-color design, printed in a dark chocolate brown.  I think it would have been nicer if they added some metallic highlights in the design, so I find this to be a bit on the flat side, and put off buying a set for a while, though it was always near the top of my list.

Overall, this is another top notch deck, from a group that has quickly become on of my favorites.

The cards are high quality Bicycle stock with the USPCC's Air Cushion finish, so these handle very well.
profile.summary: Another must for collectors.

profile.description:
This precision made brass prop makes dreams come true - it doubles money like magic. The magician places a stack of nickels on the table and covers it with a brass cap. Instantly, the nickels have turned into a stack of dimes! 


There is no sleight of hand involved in the trick. Complete with detailed instructions and all necessary apparatus. The cap can be examined before and after the trick by the most attentive spectator. There's nothing to find! 


Made in the USA by FUN Incorporated.
profile.reviewText: This is a cute little gag, that's pretty effective, and fairly examinable at the end. Basically, you cover four nickels with a brass cap, wait a bit and then remove the cap to show the nickels have changed to dimes. Or, pretty much anything else you can fit in the cap. I like shrink the nickels, or just make them vanish entirely, or go into a scotch & sodawith one of the dimes, or even a tiny card reveal; it's up to your imagination. This is one of those tricks I carry with me almost everywhere. My main issue with this is that the gimmick doesn't have a nickel design on it, so it has to be covered all the time by a real nickel (one is included). You get the device, which is two pieces, and a bang ring, in a box, as you can see in my photos. What you turn the nickels into, you supply. It's a simple trick and pretty easy to reset, and takes literally minutes to learn.
profile.summary: A fun trick, which can be easily taken advantage of for other tricks.

profile.description: A great new color for your card act! These orange-backed cards are officially printed by the U.S. Playing Card Company and can be used in any number of card routines. Bring a bit of color to your card routine!.
profile.reviewText:
Just like standard red or blue backed Bicycle decks, but with orange instead.

The box is the standard Bicycle brand box, with orange where there would normally be red or blue.  Aside from that, the only other difference is the UPC code.

The deck comes with 56 cards.  There are two Jokers, both featuring the full B&W 808 Joker design, but on has a star symbol instead of the US designation in the corners.  The two additional cards are both blank faced cards.  The backs are standard Rider Back designs, but printed in orange.  Other than that, these are standard Bicycle cards.

With one minor difference...

These cards are slightly thinner and more flexible than standard Bicycle cards. In fact, these seem to be the same stock that the Aristocrat and newer Mandolin Back decks are made from.  Whether this is a bad thing or not is up to you.  If you like the way Aristocrats feel, then you'll like these.

Finally, these are standard cut, like most Bicycle decks these days.
profile.summary: Orange is the new back.

profile.description: BEAUTIFUL VINTAGE STYLE RHAPSODY BICYCLE PLAYING CARD DECKS WITH DETAILED BACKS IN DARK RED AND PURPLE
profile.reviewText:
These aren't bad cards, but they're not great either.  This is apparently a design made by the United States Playing Card Company to be sold in Walmarts and a few other stores primarily.  This is actually common with many stores having their own branded, or unbranded, playing cards.

As the item description states, there are two decks of cards included; one red and the other purple.  While the fronts show a fairly noticeable color difference, the backs of the cards are not so different; the red and purple colors are pretty dark as you can see in the photos.  In a not brightly lit room these can be hard to tell apart.

The boxes are standard tuck boxes, made with standard coated card stock.  The backs show a full size card back design in the appropriate color, just like the more popular, older style Bicycle Rider Back decks or the newer Mandolin Backs.

There are 56 cards per deck.  These include two standard 808 Jokers, the main one being colored in the same dark red & purple the backs are printed in, and other is a standard guarantee joker.  The two additional cards are a backed ad card and a promo card with links to Bicycle's social media pages.

The faces are all traditional artwork, though the colors on both decks are identical and use the same red and purple colors instead of the more traditional bright red & blue.  The artwork for the Ace of Spades is new and features the musical emblem instead of a spade.

The backs are as shown on the boxes, and have an nice old style feel to the design.  This is a pretty obvious one way design.

The card stock is a bit thinner than the standard Bicycle stock; it's the same thickness as the Mandolin backs and Aristocrats, leading me to believe it is Aristocrat stock, which is a good card stock.  Surprisingly, these were also traditionally cut, meaning these will faro shuffle quite well face-down.

The cards feel good, handle well and in all other ways, are typical of the high quality standards of the USPCC. All in all, it's a good deal; two very playable decks for a total of $8.50.

Why just four stars?  I have other decks that I like more than these, so it's just personal preference and nothing to do with the quality.  I would give them 4.5 stars if I could.
profile.summary: A pair of very good, inexpensive decks of cards, great for when you're tired of the same old rider backs.

profile.description: This is a professional quality reproduction poster. Item is 24x36 inches. This is an industry standard reproduction print 44lb. 165gsm 7mil gloss. This is a Certified Print with Holographic Sequential Numbering for Authenticity
profile.reviewText:
This is NOT an original poster.  It is an ok scan or photo of the original and you can see the edge of the original poster in it.  The image was obviously a JPEG as you can easily see the compression artifacts in the green smoke and around the text.  Some image sharpening has also been done as there is a noticeable outlining around all the text.  The text on the bottom is quite soft, and the original printing and copyright info on the bottom is completely unreadable.  The effective resolution of this poster is roughly 30-40 pixels per inch.

This was printed on a pretty good large format printer, so there's that.  As this is a copy of the original, blacks are not solid.  Colors are nice, though they suffer from the original JPEG compression and scanning. Text also has a dark band around it, which is normally seen with edge enhancement (sharpening), and also frequently a side effect of too much JPEG compression.  Whites are also clipped, which isn't really a surprise when the image is a JPEG.  Small scratches and marks on the original poster are also visible.

There is a 1/8 white border around the image, which has a roughly 1/2 white border itself, which is slightly darker.
profile.summary: An okay print job... of a JPEG of the original poster.

profile.description: You are bidding on a new sealed rare deck of cards. Cards Feature a Tie Dye Designed Back that can be used in any standard 52 card game and even includes 2 Gaff cards to do a magic card trick called Million Dollar Monte. The jokers are a Dove and a Patriotic colored Piece Sign, there is also a a piece sign on the center of the Ace of Spades and check out the pictures, look real close at the suicide King of Hearts which normally has him holding a knife thru his head, but this deck has something different instead of the knife, Check it out, very cool. Cards measure standard poker size 2.5" x 3.5" regular index and are made with High Quality Bicycle Playing Card Stock
profile.reviewText:
Very colorful deck.  I liked the tie-dye color swirls, which is the main reason I got this deck.  The backs are a very obvious one-way design (any card turned around is very easy to spot), but they're great for fanning.  The Rider Back design appear to be a transparent grey or black over those colors, and has a sort of antique feel to it.  The card faces are all standard colors and designs, except for the Jokers.  One Joker is a line art drawing of a dove, while the other is the peace symbol with a US flag design running through it.  I thought this deck would be great for some color change effects, but the full bleed of the back design limits that ability as well; it cannot be hidden easily in a normal deck as the back colors do wrap around a bit to the front.

The additional gaff cards are for the Million Dollar Monte, though, due to the obvious one way nature of the backs, their use is a bit limited as well.

I also suspect these will not be reprinted due to the USPCC's policy update regarding the Rider Back design.  These cards probably infringe on that.  Which is probably why the product entry states they're rare.

As for the cards themselves, they're quality Bicycle stock, finish and printing.
profile.summary: A very colorful addition to a collection.

profile.description: A high quality, Linoid finish makes Tally-Ho playing cards the premiere choice among flourishers and card magicians alike. The classic Circle Back design exudes elegance, quality, and sophistication. Made in the USA.
profile.reviewText:
This is probably the favorite back design.  I recently picked up a red deck so I felt obligated to get the blue as well.

These decks probably have the largest Ace of Spades design I've seen, which nearly pushes the indexes out of the way.  The deck come with two Jokers, one with the Tally Ho! joker in color with red & yellow, and the other is the guarantee joker.  The faces are all traditional art and colors, and there are no additional cards included, though some decks my have an ad card or two, like current Bicycle decks.

These are printed by the United States Playing Card Company, so you get the same high quality they're known for.  The cards handle perfectly, fan well, and look great.
profile.summary: A perfect compliment to the red back version.

profile.description: USPCC brought back one of their most popular designs; their bank note back. This deck features a high quality linen finish and legendary Aristocrat stock.
profile.reviewText:
I remember these cards from when I was a kid.  I didn't think they were made anymore.

Once again, these are top quality cards by the USPCC, with a fine back design of thin lines like you find on bank notes, hence the name.  The two Jokers are identical and have some nice artwork, the faces of the cards are all standard, but the red suits are printed with a darker, burgundy red color, which matches the red backs.  The royals have a metallic bronze ink in their designs, which makes them pop.  Also included in each deck is a blank faced card, and an ad card listing other brands that the USPCC prints.

The backs are just nice to look at, and hide a subtle one-way design in the frame.

These are nice, all-purpose cards that handle well and look great.
profile.summary: A classic design that everyone can enjoy.

profile.description: You are buying a new sealed rare deck of cards. These are the 2nd in the TIE DYE collection. Cards Feature a Tie Dye Designed Back that can be used in any standard 52 card game and even includes 2 Gaff cards to do a magic card trick called Million Dollar Monte. The jokers are a Love & a Peace colored button pin. There is also a a peace sign on each of the pips of every card, the court cards clothing show they have interesting style, and look real close at the suicide King of Hearts which normally has him holding a knife thru his head, but this deck has something different instead of the knife. Check it out, very cool. Cards measure standard poker size 2.5" x 3.5" regular index and are made with High Quality Bicycle Playing Card Stock. I only have a limited supply of these and might they not ever be produced again so if you are a collector please buy these early before they are gone. Check out my other Merz67 decks. Thanks for looking.
profile.reviewText:
These are really colorful cards.  The tie-dye design is the same as the original deck, but with a different color. My only real complaint is the use of the peace symbol on all the pips

The back feature the same design, but with one different color; the pink in the other deck is replaced with a dark purple here, which blurs with the yellow more.  The Rider Back design is actually a negative, printed in black on this deck.

As for the faces, as stated in the description, every pip has a peace symbol on it.  I could do without that.  As I pointed out in my review of the original deck, these could have been useful for color change effects, but that's diminished some by the addition of details like this.

The two Jokers are different again, one being a round button with "PEACE" written across it in shaded of blue, over a peace symbol, and the other is a button with the word "LOVE" in rainbow colors.  The royals are pretty cool though, with the tie-dye effect on each.

Finally, the two gaff cards are for the Million Dollar Monte, and again, due to the nature of the back design, I'm not sure they'll be that effective.

Still, it's a cool deck.
profile.summary: Same as the first deck, but different colors, and new Jokers.

profile.description: The BCW Storage Box is the highest quality, most competitively priced cardboard storage box on the market today. They are constructed of white corrugated paper and have a 200 lb. test strength. Use this box for store and protect collectible trading cards like: baseball cards, basketball cards, football cards, Magic The Gathering, VS, Yu-Gi-Oh, Pokemon, Dragonball Z and others.
profile.reviewText:
Yes, this is a review of a cardboard box; one of those things most of us never even consider that we might write one day.

So, this is a box for cards.  As the description states, it can hold 800 cards.  Well, give or take a few depending on their thickness, and whether they're in sleeves or not.  I ordered two of these, one for 800 and one for 930. This one shipped already folded, and arrived in a huge box, while the other was shipped flat, but was also in a box about 5" thick.  Strange, but it did make me look incredibly strong as I carried two large boxes in one hand as I brought them back from the front office where they were delivered.  I am mighty!

I'm using these for storing some of my collection of playing cards.  However, I'm not overly thrilled by the color options that include white, or, if I fold it backwards, cardboard brown.  Personally, I'd prefer a nice classic black.  To that end, I found some of the contact paper available on Amazon to be ideal for dressing these up:  I used some chalkboard paper (http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B00MXDZBB0) to give these a matte black exterior and lined them with some red velvet paper (http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B00IV60ARI).  It worked well, though I think I may give it another shot on more boxes to get a better result, now that I know where I screwed up (mainly the notches in the lid)

As stated, this is designed to hold 800 cards, give or take, or 20 regular decks of cards, or about a ten Cards Against Humanity expansions.  The boxes are quite study, which is handy since a full box does weight a fair bit.

The photos show the box as it arrived, with the contact paper coating, next to the larger 930 version, and the third shows the box all 'decked' out.
profile.summary: It holds cards.  It does that quite well.  It's not very stylish though.

profile.description: Cock Pack One: Just the Tip - Card fronts appear in "Fair Use Blue" and "Copyright Compliant Navy", while card backs are traditional black and white, making them playable with other card games with similar initials. - Nearly 100% of the proceeds from every purchase will be converted into either single malt Scotch or small-batch Bourbon.
profile.reviewText:
There are some really great cards in this set, making this one one of the best sets so far.

Like many players of Cards Against Humanity, I've noticed the game starts to get dull and predictable with the same old cards, after you've played it a few times.  The creators know this as well, and have created six expansions to date, as well as several smaller themed additions.  Third party support is growing as well, with expansions from Crabs Adjust Humidity, Cards & Punishment, Cads About Matrimony, and now Cocks Abreast Hostility.

At $15 for 125 cards, it's not bad  about average for an expansion of this size -  but if you consider that CAH are charging $10 for their smaller 30-card packs (Holiday packs, science pack, etc.), this doesn't seem too costly.

The content is good, and not quite as lewd as the package implies (I've seen much ruder cards), but there are a few cards that are definitely 'not safe for kids', and it does have a few recurring themes in it; making fun of Hitler for one.  We've played with these cards a few times now and they seem to get used faster than the official cards.  These are great on their own, though with three or more players, you can expect to run out of 'white' cards well before you get through the 'black' ones.  Mixed in with the main game, you're not likely to run out of any cards, and these really do make for a better game.  I've included photos of some of the better, 'safe' cards, but there are many really good ones, with quite a few more being quite funny on their own, that are just a bit less kid-safe.  Some good ones include Shamelessly being the little spoon., Inappropriate eye contact in a threesome., and Being required by federal law to introduce yourself to your neighbors.

The cards themselves appear to be the same card stock the original game uses; the calendaring texture only seems to be present on the faces, but the backs are smooth, like the many of the current CAH cards.  The backs are the familiar black and white, so when shuffled into the main game, they don't stand out, other than the title being different, and in a different sans serif font.  The faces of the cards have a blue background, as stated on the box; "Card fronts appear in Fair Use Blue and Copyright Compliant Navy".  Well, that's a very dark navy blue, and appears almost pure black under normal room lighting.  The lighter blue is the blue you see on the front of the box. I don't know if they're being humorous about the naming of the colors, or if there were some legal issues presented to them, since other brands are able to freely use the standard black & white color scheme, which is not restricted to just Cards Against Humanity (there are other games that use the same black & white color scheme).  While the colors can be a bit jarring, they do not adversely affect game play

I find the horizontal aspect of the box design a bit odd, as it might lead people to believe the cards themselves are also horizontal; they're not.  The cards are vertical, as the images show.

All in all, this is a great addition to the game, and I eagerly look forward to their next set, and I really hope they make one.  My only complaint is that this is another set where the creators felt compelled to use the C, A, H initials, which really isn't necessary, but this had no bearing on my rating.
profile.summary: Well worth your lousy fifteen bucks.

profile.reviewText:
Wow, are the cheapest pieces of plastic I've ever seen that carry electricity; they're even inferior to cheap plastic toys for kids or pets, what with gobs and strings of melted plastic stuck to the ends and flaps of plastic along the mould lines.  Even the wiring looks cheap. They look like something you'd get out of a cheap vending machine as a prize.

But they work, so far.  They kinda worked right out of the box, for a few seconds, until the charge they had died.  I stuck the solar cell into the 4pm sunlight streaming through our window and let that charge it up for about 3 hours.  I hung them on our balcony, and they turned on around 7:30pm.  It's almost 2am now and they're still going strong.

These are not bright lights; they're about the same brightness as a typical power light on a computer - pretty much 1990's LED brightness here.  They're pretty, and from a few feet away, you're not going to notice how cheap and crappy their construction is, much like the product photo shows.  But, opening that box... yikes.

Edit:  I've had these since May, so that's about three months.  The batteries are already nearly dead.  The lights still come on but only for about two hours or so before they fade out.  It's too bad because at night, these looked pretty nice.
profile.summary: Very cheap looking, but when they're on, they're probably worth the $14, but not for very long.

profile.description: Love Cards Against Humanity but find yourself playing with the same old cards all alone? Have some empty space burning a hole on one side of your Bigger, Blacker Box? Want to spice up your game and be the coolest uncool kid in the neighborhood? Then Cards & Punishment is the expansion pack for you! This deck was designed to be used as an addition to your original game and make you a better person! Please note, this is now the second printing. Size issues have been fixed, meaning reviews of cards being too big are so last year. Now, they're just what your mother ordered. Card backs are still black and white with a minor formatting change. Card front colors are now Dark I Just Blue Myself and Tainted Ejaculate Light Yellow.
profile.reviewText:
Updated review:

I originally got the first deck last summer, which came in a black & white box with red artwork, and unfortunately, some bad card stock.  C&P have just reprinted that deck along with a long anticipated volume 2, and this review is updated to reflect the new printing, unofficially called volume 1.1.

First, I love the content on the cards.  That's what I really wanted.  And wow, they really pack that box full.  I mean, so full it's hard to even open.  I really like the artwork on the box and how it breaks away from the 'traditional' type design of the original Cards Against Humanity sets.  Also, bonus points for not following the CAH initials like so many other third parties. The box is the same size as the official CAH expansions.

The cards are basically the same content as their version 1 release, but with a few additions and some changes.  First, all the text has been redone, typos fixed and a new, easier to read font has been used.  The card backs are still the traditional black & white, but the title has been reduced to two lines of text; Cards & Punishment, apparently to appease the CAH guys.  The card faces have added color, much like Cocks Abreast Hostility; the white cards have a pale yellow background and the black cards have white text on a dark purple background.  Under dimmer lighting, this will be marginally discernible from black & white, and is apparently another concession to CAH.  Their box also has the same color changes, as you can see in the product photos.  Not exactly a game killer here, and the reprint does improve the clarity of their box art.

The new card stock is very similar to most other decks now, and in most cases, the cards glide and fan pretty well.  The few I have in this specific deck that don't will when shuffled and broken in, so that's not an issue.  If your deck has 'clumps', give it time  My deck is pretty fresh off the press, and  I've found with other fresh decks like these that they improve over time.  The cards are smooth on the backs, and have a very light calendaring pattern on the faces, and, unlike the original printing, these are cut to the correct size (63mm x 88mm), so they'll fit in with other decks better.

The content on the cards covers a lot and is really good.  The inclusion of the F***, marry, kill. card is nice; I like seeing variations on the game like that, as it adds a bit of a change during play.  The cards are remarkably clean, making use of the fewest of the seven words you're not allowed to say on television.  Some of the cards are bit more obscure, and a few are pretty generic (which is a good thing as they can have multiple interpretations), but overall, they're all good.

A few changes have been made, which I first noticed when trying to replicate the photos from the first review.  The original deck had 115 cards; this one gives you 110, which necessitated a few alterations. Not counting a few corrected typos, there are ten white cards and one black card that have been removed, 3 black cards and 5 white cards have been reworded, and 6 new white cards have been added.  You can blame Leonardo DiCaprio's Oscar win for one of these.

This is a great deck, and I highly recommend it.
profile.summary: A very worthy addition to the game.

profile.description: A package of two clip on chair trays designed to fit most recliners and chairs with A type frame. Provides perfect place to set a cup, plate or book. Installs in seconds with no tools. Made of durable plastic. 14 inches x 9 inches x 1.5 inches. Will not fit Elite chairs and rockers.
profile.reviewText:
I recently got a couple Zero Gravity chairs and after not having anywhere close to put a drink on, I ordered these.  They snapped onto the chairs with no trouble, and stay pretty well attached.  I have knocked one loose a couple times, but only when reaching for something under the chair and bumping the tray from below, but it was easy enough to lock back in place.

There are two cup holders on these, one with a notch for a handle.  These are only about two inches deep, so you might want to use shorter glasses on them as a tall one could be knocked over.  Someone mentioned lining the holders with some felt, which is a good idea.  There are also two rectangular sockets for a phone, calculator or anything else that's a bit less than an inch thick.

I frequently get in & out of the chair while a drink is on the tray, and it's pretty sturdy, though, you should be careful; the chairs are not very heavy, and a large drink on the tray can make the chair off balanced.  Reclining the chairs isn't a problem, though the locking latch is close to the tray, and can be hard to work with when a drink is on it.  Again, it's good to be careful; the chairs are light enough they're easily rocked enough to spill anything on the tray, especially on uneven ground.
profile.summary: A very nice, convenient drink tray for your Zero Gravity chair.

profile.description: SodaStream soda mixes let you add new flavors to your repertoire for parties, dinners and other gatherings. When used as directed, these economy-sized syrup bottles make 12 liters of soda (about 33 cans). Be able to create your favorite flavor of fresh, fizzy soda in minutes from our large collection of regular and diet sodas, as well as energy drinks, teas, natural cane sugar flavors and even your favorite brands of soft drinks. For longest shelf life, please keep tightly closed and keep in a cool, dry place.
profile.reviewText:
I've wanted to try this ever since I found a bottle at a local store, but they wouldn't sell it to me because it was past the expiration date.  I never found it anywhere since, until I looked on Amazon.  When it arrived, I immediately poured some into a pre-fizzed bottle and gave it a tray.  At first, it was ok, and then the horrible sucralose aftertaste hit and hit hard.

That's the problem with most of Sodastream's  flavors; they use sucralose to sweeten their syrups, instead of sugar.  Yes, it's great that it doesn't use corn syrup, but I'd rather have corn syrup over sucralose, or any other artificial sweetener.

Well, my curiosity has been satisfied, while my tongue wasn't.  I doubt I'll be buying this again.  I'll be getting my cream soda fixes using a third party brand, like Monin, which has some extremely delicious syrups.
profile.summary: Cream Soda, ruined by sucralose.
